-#+title: User Journey: Publish conventions from data quality
-#+description: A data quality operator publishes the curated ORE conventions dataset into a tenant, reads the counts each kind lands with, learns why 33 rows are skipped on every party after the first, and finds that a re-publish does not carry a corrected curated term.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:refdata:dq:
-#+created: 2026-10-18
-#+updated: 2026-10-18
-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A data quality operator publishes the curated conventions dataset into a tenant and reads what landed.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"The curated ORE conventions are the ones we trade on. I need them in the tenant,
-for the party that trades, and I need to know what arrived, what did not, and
-what a second publish will do before I run it."
-
-This journey is how every convention a party holds actually arrives. ACME holds
-10,991 convention rows across 26 kinds, and 25 of those kinds came from a DQ
-publish. The person is not authoring a term and not choosing one: they are
-moving a curated catalogue into a tenant and reading the receipt.
-
-The journey is done when the person can state four things: which kinds the
-publish covers, how many rows each kind landed with, why part of the receipt is
-a skip rather than an insert, and what a re-publish would and would not change.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-The actor is a data quality operator or a tenant administrator. Publishing a
-dataset is a DQ permission and reading what it wrote is a reference data
-permission; in a small tenant one person holds both. A data quality operator
-arrives with a dataset that has been curated or corrected. A tenant
-administrator arrives because a party has been added or because a term in the
-tenant is stale.
-
-The trigger is three different things and the same journey covers all three: a
-new tenant or party that needs the curated set, a curated row that has been
-corrected upstream and should now be in the tenant, and a publish that returned a
-skip count nobody can explain. The journey starts at the dataset and ends when
-the person has read the counts against what they expected.
-
-The journey writes through the DQ publish path and sends no per-kind convention
-write. It does not author a term, does not choose which document a run takes,
-and does not run a report.
-
-The journey keeps no server state of its own. The publish does: it runs as a
-workflow instance, and progress is read from the instance and not from the
-client.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Read the dataset.* The person opens the dataset and reads what it is. There
-   are two for conventions:
-   - =ore.conventions=, named *ORE Instrument Conventions*, artefact type
-     =conventions=, catalogue *ORE Analytics*, subject area *Trading*, domain
-     *Reference Data*;
-   - =refdata.currency_pair_conventions=, named *Standard Currency Pair
-     Conventions*, artefact type =currency_pair_conventions=, catalogue *FX Market
-     Conventions*, subject area *Currency Pairs*.
-   The person also reads the third, =refdata.currency_pair_convention_calendars=,
-   which carries the calendars a currency pair advances on, because a pair
-   without its calendars is half a convention.
-2. *Read what each dataset covers, and count the kinds.* The first dataset's
-   artefact type names 24 artefact tables and one subject,
-   =refdata.v1.ops.publish_conventions_from_dq=. The function behind it loops an
-   array of exactly those 24 kinds and dispatches =ores_dq_<kind>_conventions_artefact_tbl=
-   into =ores_refdata_<kind>_conventions_tbl=. The second dataset covers
-   =currency_pair= alone, on its own subject. Together that is **25 kinds of the
-   26**. The person is shown the 26th explicitly, because a publish that silently
-   covers 25 of 26 is a trap: =tenor= has no DQ route at all. There is no
-   =ores_dq_tenor_conventions_artefact_tbl=, so no function can copy it, and its
-   4 rows are not published — they are copied from the system tenant when the
-   tenant is created. The screen says so on the =tenor= row rather than leaving
-   the count to be discovered.
-3. *Read the bundle that carries it, and who it publishes for.* The two datasets
-   travel in different bundles, and the difference decides who they land for.
-   =ore.conventions= is a member of =party_essentials=, which is published **once
-   per party** with a ={"party_id": "..."}= parameter. =refdata.currency_pair_conventions=
-   and its calendars are members of =base=, which is published **once per
-   tenant**. The person reads this before publishing, because "publish the
-   conventions" means one thing per party and another per tenant, and a person
-   who publishes =base= expecting party rows gets none.
-4. *Publish.* The person publishes. The operation is
-   =dq.v1.ops.publish_bundle=, which the shell spells =bundles publish <bundle>
-   --party-id <id> --wait=. The service starts a workflow instance and the
-   publication walks the bundle's datasets in dependency order, one step per
-   dataset. The conventions step is one step of that run and not a run of its own.
-   With =--wait= the person watches step transitions and the command returns when
-   the instance reaches a terminal state. Without it they hold an instance id and
-   read progress from =workflow.v1.ops.get_workflow_steps=.
-5. *Read the counts the publish returns.* The step's result is four counts:
-   =records_inserted=, =records_updated=, =records_skipped= and
-   =records_deleted=. ACME's actual receipts, in publish order:
-   - the first party: **2,188 inserted, 0 skipped, 0 updated**;
-   - each of the next four parties: **2,155 inserted, 33 skipped, 0 updated**;
-   - a later re-publish of the same party: **0 inserted, 2,188 skipped, 0
-     updated**.
-   The person reads all three against each other, because the difference between
-   them is the whole of this journey's remaining steps.
-6. *Explain the 33.* 2,188 is 2,155 plus 33, and the 33 is not a defect. Four of
-   the 26 kinds are tenant-scoped — their table carries no =party_id= column — and
-   two of them are in the 24-kind array: =ibor_index= with 10 rows and
-   =overnight_index= with 23. 10 + 23 = 33. The publish's insert is guarded by
-   "this key does not exist for this tenant and party", and for a table with no
-   party column that guard finds the row the first party's publish wrote. So the
-   first party's publish writes them and every later party's publish reports them
-   as skipped, because they are not that party's rows to write. The person reads
-   the 33 as *already present, tenant-wide*, and not as a failure. The screen
-   states the arithmetic and names the two kinds, because a skip count of 33 with
-   no account of it is unreadable.
-7. *Explain what a re-publish will and will not do, before running it.* This is
-   the step the journey exists for. The 24-kind function writes with an insert
-   guarded by "the row is not already there", and it has no update path: its
-   result carries no =updated= count and the function's own body never updates a
-   row. So **a curated row corrected in the dataset does not reach a tenant that
-   already holds it** — the re-publish reports it as skipped and the tenant keeps
-   the old terms. A re-publish of a party that already has its rows is 2,188
-   skipped and 0 inserted. The exception is =currency_pair=: its own function
-   inserts with the store's version-replace, and its second publish reports
-   **179 updated**. So 25 of the 26 kinds cannot take a correction and 1 can, and
-   the person is told which is which on the row rather than from a run's
-   surprise. Correcting a convention a tenant already holds is
-   [[id:FA1CC25B-9745-4172-BAE8-4B6413958077][Change the convention a party uses
-   for one kind]]'s job, done per row.
-8. *Read what the publish cannot show.* The person asks what the curated rows
-   actually say before publishing them. Nothing answers. There is no read of an
-   =ores_dq_*_artefact_tbl= over NATS: DQ publishes artefact *types* and
-   *datasets*, and the rows they stage are readable only in the database. So the
-   person can read what landed in the tenant, kind by kind, and cannot read what
-   is about to land. The screen says so and does not draw an artefact preview it
-   cannot fill.
-9. *Read where the =tenor= rows came from, and when.* The four =tenor= rows were
-   copied from the system tenant when the tenant was provisioned, by
-   =ores_iam_provision_tenant_fn=, with =change_reason_code= =system.new_record=
-   and the commentary "Copied from the system tenant during provisioning". That
-   copy happens once per tenant and never again. A change to the system tenant's
-   tenor conventions reaches a new tenant and does not reach an existing one, and
-   no publish refreshes it. The row says so.
-10. *Leave, or go on.* The person has the receipt. They either go to the party's
-    conventions to verify what a run will read
-    ([[id:0DC107D4-170D-478B-9476-570343806888][See the conventions a party
-    uses]]), or to a kind to correct a term the publish could not carry
-    ([[id:FA1CC25B-9745-4172-BAE8-4B6413958077][Change the convention a party
-    uses for one kind]]).
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen: the dataset in the header, the kinds it covers with their counts, the
-bundle and the scope it publishes for, the publish action with its instance, and
-the receipt. The receipt is the largest panel, because the counts are the answer
-and the same four counts mean different things on the first publish, the fourth
-and a re-publish. The screen shows the last publish's counts beside what the
-person expected, so a skip count is read against an expectation rather than in
-isolation.
-
-The screen never shows artefact rows. There is no operation that returns them,
-and a panel that drew an empty table would be claiming a read that does not
-exist.
-
-#+caption: Publish conventions from data quality: the two datasets with the 25 of 26 kinds they cover, the tenor exception, the bundle and scope per dataset, and the receipt as it reads on the first party, a later party, and a re-publish.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/conventions/wireframe_publish_conventions_from_data_quality.png]]
-
-* Prototype
-
-No prototype is written for this journey in this pass, and none should be until
-the artefact read exists. The screen's central panel is a receipt the person
-compares against an expectation, and half the expectation — what the curated
-rows say — cannot be read at all. A prototype would have to fake the half that
-matters.
-
-What a prototype must draw when the read exists is stated here so it is not lost:
-the four counts, in three columns, one per publish act; the 33 accounted for by
-the two tenant kinds; the =tenor= row marked as not published; and the one kind
-that updates marked apart from the 25 that do not.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =dataset= | The two convention datasets, their names, their artefact types and their catalogue | |
-| =artefact_type= | What each dataset stages and publishes as, and the subject that carries it | |
-| =dataset_bundle=, =dataset_bundle_member= | The bundle each dataset travels in, and therefore whether it publishes per tenant or per party | |
-| The 26 convention tables | Where the rows land. 22 carry =party_id= and are written per party; four carry none and are written once per tenant. | one per kind; see below |
-| =change_reason= | =system.external_data_import= for a published row and =system.new_record= for a copied one, which is how a row states its own provenance | |
-| =party= | The party a =party_essentials= publish writes for | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Kind | Route | Rows per party | Rows per tenant | Re-publish behaviour |
-|------+-------+----------------+-----------------+---------------------|
-| the 22 party kinds | =refdata.v1.ops.publish_conventions_from_dq= | 2,155 | — | insert only; a correction is skipped |
-| =currency_pair= | =refdata.v1.ops.publish_currency_pair_conventions_from_dq= | — | 179 | version replace; a correction is written as an update |
-| =ibor_index= | the 24-kind subject | — | 10 | skipped after the first party, because it has no party column |
-| =overnight_index= | the 24-kind subject | — | 23 | skipped after the first party, for the same reason |
-| =tenor= | none | — | 4 | copied at tenant provisioning, never republished |
-
-The models the rows land in:
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =swap_convention= | The worked example of a party kind: 320 rows per party from 320 staged rows | [[id:F68E18C5-A704-40E8-A37B-4B8F5DCB5089][ores.refdata.swap_convention]] |
-| =deposit_convention= | The contrast, 163 rows per party | [[id:F7C5287B-7781-45EA-BA4C-63F077E36A89][ores.refdata.deposit_convention]] |
-| =ibor_index_convention= | One of the two tenant kinds in the 24-kind array, and part of the 33 | [[id:852FE06C-70D9-48BC-B768-D99D87D0D796][ores.refdata.ibor_index_convention]] |
-| =overnight_index_convention= | The other one, and the larger part of the 33 | [[id:B72547F3-83B5-4F83-AA65-BBE16C191089][ores.refdata.overnight_index_convention]] |
-| =tenor_convention= | The kind with no DQ route | [[id:C4D8A2E6-3B7F-4A1D-9C5E-8F2A6D3B1E90][ores.refdata.tenor_convention]] |
-| =currency_pair_convention= | The kind with its own subject and its own bundle | [[id:1B88215B-1FE0-4CAF-B6AB-53F471963CA6][ores.refdata.currency_pair_convention]] |
-
-The publish copies the live table's own data columns, read from
-=information_schema= at call time, less the columns it stamps. That is why one
-function spans 24 kinds: a new kind costs one array entry and one artefact table,
-not a function. It also means the published row's key is the artefact's key, so
-a curated document keeps one key across every tenant that publishes it.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Read the dataset | List the datasets | =dq.v1.datasets.list= | exists |
-| Read the dataset | Read one dataset | =dq.v1.datasets.get= | exists |
-| Read the dataset | Read the artefact types | =dq.v1.artefact_types.list= | exists |
-| Read the bundle | List the bundles | =dq.v1.dataset_bundles.list= | exists |
-| Read the bundle | Read a bundle's members | =dq.v1.dataset_bundle_members.list= | exists |
-| Publish | Publish a bundle | =dq.v1.ops.publish_bundle= | exists |
-| Publish | Publish one dataset | =dq.v1.ops.publish_datasets= | exists |
-| Publish | Watch the run's steps | =workflow.v1.ops.get_workflow_steps= | exists |
-| Publish | List the instances | =workflow.v1.instances.list= | exists |
-| Read the receipt | The counts the publish returns | the step's =result_json=: =records_inserted=, =records_updated=, =records_skipped=, =records_deleted= | partial |
-| Read the receipt | List the tenant's published conventions | =refdata.v1.<kind>_conventions.list= | exists |
-| Read the receipt | Read the party's whole conventions document | =refdata.v1.conventions_documents.get= | exists, not reachable by a person |
-| Read what is about to land | Read an artefact table's rows | (no read of =ores_dq_*_artefact_tbl= over NATS) | missing |
-| Read the receipt | Read one publish's counts and its whole receipt | (no read of a publication's result; the counts are on the workflow step) | missing |
-| Read the receipt | Attribute a skip count to a kind | (the function returns one total, not a breakdown) | missing |
-
-The publish steps that the function serves are subscribed by the reference data
-service's =publish_from_dq_handler=, one handler for every
-=publish_*_from_dq= subject, and each call reaches a =security definer= SQL
-function. The counts reach the caller through the workflow step's result and not
-through a service read of the tenant's own tables.
-
-No BFF route serves DQ. This journey adds one, for example
-=GET /api/dq/datasets/<code>/conventions=, which returns the kinds the dataset
-covers, the artefact suite count, the bundle and the scope, and the last
-publication's counts per kind. That read has to be built on a per-kind count and
-does not exist today.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *A corrected curated row never reaches a tenant that already holds it.* The
-   24-kind publish function has no update path: it inserts where the row is
-   absent and counts everything else as skipped. Its result type carries no
-   =updated= count, and its body performs no update. A re-publish after a
-   correction returns 2,188 skipped and 0 inserted, and the tenant keeps the old
-   terms. This is the most consequential gap in the group: the curated dataset is
-   the source of truth for 25 kinds and it cannot be corrected downstream.
-   =currency_pair= is the only kind whose function replaces the row it finds.
-2. *A skip count is a total, not an account.* The function returns one
-   =records_skipped= for the whole 24-kind loop. The person who sees 33 cannot
-   learn from the server that 10 are =ibor_index= and 23 are =overnight_index=.
-   The arithmetic is derivable by counting the tenant-scoped kinds' rows, and the
-   server does not state it.
-3. *Nothing reads the curated rows.* No operation returns an
-   =ores_dq_*_artefact_tbl= row. DQ exposes artefact types and datasets and not
-   the rows they stage, so a person can read what landed in a tenant and cannot
-   read what is about to land. Comparing a curated document against the tenant's
-   copy is a database query and not a screen.
-4. *No read states a publication's outcome.* The counts exist on the workflow
-   step's =result_json=, and no operation returns a publication with its counts
-   and the dataset it published. A person reads a workflow instance to learn what
-   a dataset did.
-5. *`tenor` has no publish route at all.* There is no
-   =ores_dq_tenor_conventions_artefact_tbl= and no subject. Its 4 rows come from
-   a one-time copy at tenant provisioning, so a corrected tenor convention
-   reaches only tenants created after the correction. A DQ artefact table and a
-   subject would close it, and until then this is the one kind whose curation
-   cannot be shipped.
-6. *A tenant-scoped kind publishes once and is then reported as skipped forever.*
-   =ibor_index= and =overnight_index= are in the 24-kind array and their tables
-   carry no =party_id=, so the insert's "already present" guard fires for every
-   party after the first. The behaviour is correct and the receipt is not: a
-   person publishing a party is told 33 rows were skipped without being told that
-   they are present, tenant-wide, and were written for someone else.
-7. *A tenant-scoped kind cannot be published per party even if a tenant wanted
-   it.* =currency_pair='s function writes the whole tenant, and =currency_pair=
-   is in =base=, a tenant bundle. There is no way to give one party a different
-   pair convention, which is consistent with the 1:1 pair model and is a limit a
-   reader should be told rather than discover.
-8. *The publish cannot be scoped to a kind.* One subject publishes 24 kinds
-   together. A person who needs one kind refreshed cannot ask for it, and a failed
-   step is a failed publish of all 24. There is no per-kind publish subject, and
-   the function's array is the only partition.
-9. *No dry run.* The mode is =upsert=, =insert_only= or =replace_all=, and there
-   is no mode that reports what it would do. On a function that skips rather than
-   updates, a dry run is the only way to learn what a publish would change, and
-   there is not one.
-10. *`replace_all` is offered and closes rows before it writes.* The 24-kind
-    function does not honour =replace_all= at all — it ignores the mode and its
-    contract says the mode has no effect — while =currency_pair='s function does
-    honour it and closes every current pair convention in the tenant before
-    inserting. A caller reading "all publish functions take the same modes" would
-    be wrong here, and a person who sends =replace_all= to the currency pair
-    function removes what the dataset no longer carries.

-#+title: User Journey: See the conventions a party uses
-#+description: A person asks which market terms the next run of their party will read, gets the 26 kinds with what each holds, and finds that no document is marked as the one a run takes.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:refdata:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-18
-#+updated: 2026-10-18
-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A person asks which market terms the next run of their party will read, and cannot be answered from what is stored.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"Something in this run looks wrong and I think it is a convention. Which terms
-does the run read, kind by kind, and which one of them is the one that counts?"
-
-The person opens the conventions of one party and gets one row per convention
-kind. Each row answers three questions: how many documents of that kind the
-party holds, what the terms of one of them say in words, and where the kind
-came from. The journey is done when the person can say, for the kind they
-suspect, which document a run takes.
-
-Today the third question has no answer for any kind, and the row has to say so.
-There is no default marker anywhere, no name column to look a document up by,
-and the conventions configuration a report binds carries no rows that would
-name one. *What is missing* states all three, and each is a fact about the
-server rather than an opinion about the screen.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-Three actors read the same rows: the market risk function, the trading desk and
-the tenant administrator. A market risk reader arrives after a run produced
-numbers they did not expect, and wants the terms behind one instrument family.
-A trading desk arrives with a booking in front of them and asks what the
-convention for that family states. A tenant administrator arrives when a party
-reports a term that has moved, and reads across the tenant's parties. The three
-read the same activity over different visible sets, and the sets are the
-permissions and the row-level policy, not three screens.
-
-The trigger is a run whose figures are doubted, or a term that is known to have
-moved. The journey starts when the person opens the conventions of a party and
-ends when they have read the terms of the kind they came for, and have read that
-which document a run takes is not recorded.
-
-This is a read-only journey. It creates nothing, changes nothing and destroys
-nothing. It reaches one write only from a row: the link to
-[[id:FA1CC25B-9745-4172-BAE8-4B6413958077][Change the convention a party uses
-for one kind]].
-
-The journey keeps no server state. No step waits on the server after its reply.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Open the conventions of the party.* The person opens the conventions area
-   with a party in view. The system shows one screen: a header that names the
-   tenant and the party, a summary that counts the kinds and the documents, and
-   a table with one row per convention kind. ACME's one operational party holds
-   2,155 rows across the 22 kinds that carry a party column, and the tenant
-   holds 216 more across the four kinds that do not. A party that holds nothing
-   is stated as such, and the row says what a run would write instead: a
-   conventions file with no rows for the 22 kinds.
-2. *Read the 26 kinds.* There are 26 convention tables and the table draws one
-   row per table: =average_ois=, =bma_basis_swap=, =bond_yield=, =cds=,
-   =cms_spread_option=, =commodity_forward=, =commodity_future=,
-   =cross_currency_basis=, =cross_currency_fix_float=, =currency_pair=,
-   =deposit=, =fra=, =future=, =fx_option=, =ibor_index=, =inflation_swap=,
-   =intraday_power_load=, =ois=, =overnight_index=, =swap=, =swap_index=,
-   =tenor=, =tenor_basis_swap=, =tenor_basis_two_swap=, =zero= and
-   =zero_inflation_index=. Each row states the kind's name, how many term
-   columns its table carries, how many documents the party holds, and whether
-   the party or the tenant owns them. The two are not the same claim, so the
-   row states which: 22 kinds belong to the party and four belong to the tenant.
-3. *Read the terms of one kind in words.* The person opens the kind they
-   suspect. The system shows the kind's documents, each with its terms said in
-   words rather than as codes: "The AED calendar, modified following as the
-   business-day rule, ACT/360 as its day count, settlement 2 business days after
-   the trade." Every convention table states its terms as text columns and a
-   term that is a pick holds the list's code, never its label, so the words on
-   the screen are the screen's reading of the codes.
-4. *Look for the document that counts, and find nothing.* The person asks which
-   of the swap kind's 320 documents a run takes. The system has no answer. No
-   convention table carries a default marker: the only =%default%= column in the
-   whole of =ores.refdata= is =pays_at_default_time= on =cds_convention=, which
-   is a business term about a credit event and not a mark on a document. So the
-   row states the count and states, on the row, that nothing records which of
-   them a run reads.
-5. *Look a document up by name, and find that a name is derived.* No convention
-   table has a name column. One has a description: =tenor= carries a nullable
-   =description=, and the row =CREDIT_CDS_IMM= states
-   "Credit/CDS curves: tenors resolve to the first business day following the
-   appropriate IMM roll date, not a fixed offset from an anchor." For the other
-   25 kinds the name is read off the terms: an index-based document by its
-   index, and a terms-based one by its calendar, its convention, its day count
-   and its settlement days. The screen says the name is derived, and says the
-   consequence: a derived name does not identify a document. ACME's party holds
-   320 swap documents stating 201 distinct sets of terms, so 201 derived names
-   stand for 320 documents and 119 rows carry a name another row also carries.
-   The primary key sits beside every name for that reason.
-6. *Follow the run back to its configuration and find a label.* A person who
-   reasoned "the report knows" opens the report definition and reads the
-   conventions configuration it binds. Each of ACME's 78 definitions binds one,
-   and there are four of them: *US conventions* with 22 definitions,
-   *UK conventions* with 24, *HK conventions* with 22 and *Group conventions*
-   with 10. The names are read; the contents are not. Every one of the four is a
-   header with no rows: no market binding, no parameter and no analytic hangs off
-   it. The system therefore shows the configuration's name and states that the
-   configuration names no document.
-7. *Read what the run actually writes.* The person asks the question one step
-   further back: when a run writes its conventions file, which rows go in? The
-   export reads the party's whole conventions document and nothing else, and it
-   does not read the configuration's id at all. So every definition of a party
-   writes the same conventions file, and it holds every document the party owns
-   for the 22 party kinds plus the tenant's 216 for the four tenant kinds. The
-   four configuration names describe different intents and select the same rows.
-   The screen states this rather than drawing four configurations as four sets.
-   In ACME each party binds one of the four for all of its definitions, so the
-   coincidence hides: a tenant that gave one party two conventions configurations
-   would find the two produce one file.
-8. *Read where a document came from.* Each row states its provenance, because
-   "provisioned" is not "authored". 25 of the 26 kinds arrived from a DQ publish
-   and their rows carry =system.external_data_import= with the dataset's name in
-   the commentary. =tenor='s 4 rows carry =system.new_record= and the commentary
-   "Copied from the system tenant during provisioning". A row a person wrote
-   carries the change reason that person chose. A reader who wants the publish
-   itself reads [[id:99481EA8-1D2B-426D-A4E6-5E834FF5FFCE][Publish conventions
-   from data quality]].
-9. *Read one document's versions.* The person opens one document's history and
-   reads every saved version with the field-level difference from the one before,
-   by whom and why. This is the only place the screen can say when a term
-   changed, because no run records the version it read.
-10. *Leave, or go on.* The person either has the answer, or has found the term
-    that is wrong and goes to
-    [[id:FA1CC25B-9745-4172-BAE8-4B6413958077][Change the convention a party
-    uses for one kind]]. A person with no permission to write terminates a
-    read-only copy of the same screen; there is no read/write pair of screens.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen. The party header, the summary counts, the kind table and the open
-kind's terms are panels of that screen, because the person reads them as one
-answer. The screen is read-only: it creates nothing, changes nothing and
-destroys nothing. The table is the whole answer, and a row carries its count, its
-terms in words, its provenance and the statement that no default is recorded, so
-that no row needs opening to be understood.
-
-#+caption: See the conventions a party uses: the 26 kinds with their counts and terms in words, a kind open with its 320 documents and 201 distinct term sets, and the four configuration names that select the same rows.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%

-
-* Prototype
-
-No prototype answers this journey today. The prototype that used to draw the
-26-kind table inside the reporting group has been retired: it was built on a
-conventions configuration that carries no children, and the conventions are now
-named convention sets rather than a per-kind list a person assembles. This pass
-writes no prototype.
-
-Conventions are named convention sets: a set carries a name, a purpose and a
-description, a system holds few of them, and a report binds one by choosing it.
-The choosing surface is drawn in
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/create-a-report/][Create a report]] and
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/change-what-a-report-runs/][Change what a
-report runs]]: one page of sets, a radio to bind one, and one link out to the
-authoring UX. The authoring prototype is deferred to its own work and is not in
-this MR. The decision, and the three absences this journey records — no default
-marker, no name, and a configuration that holds nothing — are stated in the story
-[[file:../../../agile/versions/v0/sprint_28/name-the-convention-sets-a-report-chooses/story.org][Name
-the convention sets a report chooses]] (DE6C0BDA-D12A-4E31-AA86-C323F5A7E016).
-Two points the retired prototype raised are kept here rather than lost: a party
-with no conventions does not fall back to the curated document for the kind, and
-no such fallback exists (see *What is missing*); and the retired note said
-thirty-one definitions bind the conventions configuration, where each of ACME's
-78 definitions binds one.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| The 26 convention tables | The rows themselves: one table per kind, each with its own terms. The 22 party kinds carry =party_id=; the four tenant kinds carry none. | see the table below |
-| =configuration= | The four conventions configurations a report binds, by name and type | [[id:6B3D9E27-5C41-4A86-8F19-2E7B0D4C6A53][ores.reporting.configuration]] |
-| =report_configuration= | The binding of one definition to its conventions configuration | [[id:7F2C8A41-6E93-4B57-A0D4-3C9E1B5D7826][ores.reporting.report_configuration]] |
-| =report_definition= | The definition whose next run carries the terms, and the party the export reads the document for | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the 22 party kinds in the header, and the party the export resolves | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-The four kinds whose table carries no =party_id= are the ones the table has to
-mark, because their count is the tenant's and not the party's:
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Kind | Key column | ACME rows | Why it has no party |
-|------+------------+-----------+---------------------|
-| =currency_pair= | =pair_code= | 179 | One convention per pair for the tenant, 1:1 with the pair |
-| =ibor_index= | =id= | 10 | The index terms belong to the index, not to a party |
-| =overnight_index= | =id= | 23 | The same |
-| =tenor= | =code= | 4 | The label resolves once for the tenant |
-
-The two worked term sets, and the two model documents the rest of this group
-cites:
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =swap_convention= | The worked example: seven term columns, 320 documents per party, 201 distinct sets | [[id:F68E18C5-A704-40E8-A37B-4B8F5DCB5089][ores.refdata.swap_convention]] |
-| =deposit_convention= | The simpler contrast: =index_based= decides whether the row states its own terms or inherits them from the index | [[id:F7C5287B-7781-45EA-BA4C-63F077E36A89][ores.refdata.deposit_convention]] |
-| =ibor_index_convention= | The kind that cannot name itself: its table carries a fixing calendar, a day count, settlement days and a business-day rule, and no index column | [[id:852FE06C-70D9-48BC-B768-D99D87D0D796][ores.refdata.ibor_index_convention]] |
-| =tenor_convention= | The one kind with a description column, and the one kind with no DQ route | [[id:C4D8A2E6-3B7F-4A1D-9C5E-8F2A6D3B1E90][ores.refdata.tenor_convention]] |
-| =currency_pair_convention= | The one tenant kind that arrives on its own subject and its own dataset | [[id:1B88215B-1FE0-4CAF-B6AB-53F471963CA6][ores.refdata.currency_pair_convention]] |
-
-Every one of these tables is bitemporal: a term edited today leaves the earlier
-version readable, so the history view reads saved versions and the current row
-reads the latest. The party-scoped kinds are party-scoped by row-level security
-and not by a filter the screen applies.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Open the screen | List the party's convention rows of one kind | =refdata.v1.<kind>_conventions.list= | exists |
-| Open the screen | Read one convention | =refdata.v1.<kind>_conventions.get= | exists |
-| Open the screen | Read many conventions by key | =refdata.v1.<kind>_conventions.get_many= | exists |
-| Read the terms | Read the term lists the codes come from | =refdata.v1.calendar_names.list=, =refdata.v1.day_count_fraction_types.list=, =refdata.v1.business_day_convention_types.list=, =refdata.v1.payment_frequencies.list=, =refdata.v1.floating_index_types.list= | exists |
-| Read one document's versions | List a document's versions | =refdata.v1.<kind>_conventions_versions.list= | exists |
-| Read one document's versions | Read every version with its diff | =refdata.v1.history.get= (=entity_type= = =ores.refdata.<kind>_convention=) | exists |
-| Follow the run back | Read the configurations a definition binds | =reporting.v1.report_configurations.list= | exists |
-| Follow the run back | Read the configurations of type =conventions= | =reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code= | exists |
-| Read the whole party document in one answer | Read the party's conventions document | =refdata.v1.conventions_documents.get= | exists, not reachable by a person |
-| Read the whole party document in one answer | Write the party's conventions document | =refdata.v1.conventions_documents.put= | exists, held by no role |
-| Search a kind by a term | Filter a convention list by anything but the key | (the filter is =id_one_of= and nothing else) | missing |
-| Name the document a run takes | Read the default of a kind | (no default column, no default row) | missing |
-| Read what a configuration names | Read the documents a conventions configuration holds | (a conventions configuration has no children to read) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Read 26 kinds for one party in one answer | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-The per-kind subjects are the generated ones: =refdata.v1.swap_conventions.list=
-and its equals for every one of the 26 kinds, under the kind's own plural. A
-tenant kind's subject is the same shape, and its key holds no party:
-=refdata.v1.ibor_index_conventions.get= takes an =id= alone.
-
-=refdata.v1.conventions_documents.get= is the read that would answer this
-journey in one call: it returns every convention the party holds, kind by kind,
-in one message. It is not available to the person who asks the question. Its
-permission is =refdata::conventions:read= and the two roles that hold it are
-=OreService= and =ReportRun=. =refdata::conventions:write= is held by no role at
-all, so the document write is reachable only by =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=,
-which hold =*=. The person who reads conventions for a living holds
-=refdata::swap_conventions:read= and its siblings under =Operations=, and reads
-them one kind at a time.
-
-No BFF route serves conventions. This journey adds one, for example
-=GET /api/refdata/parties/<party-id>/conventions=, which reads the party's
-document once, joins the term lists, derives the names and returns the 26 rows
-with their counts and their provenance.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *No default marker exists anywhere.* Nothing on any of the 26 tables and
-   nothing keyed by tenant and kind says which document a run takes. The only
-   =%default%= column in =ores.refdata= is =pays_at_default_time= on
-   =cds_convention=, a business term about a credit event. A real default needs
-   either a per-kind default column on =ores_refdata_<kind>_conventions_tbl= or a
-   per-kind default row keyed by tenant and kind. This is the gap that makes the
-   journey's own goal unanswerable, and it is the first thing to build.
-2. *No convention has a name or a description column.* Only =tenor= has a
-   nullable =description=. Every other kind must be named from its terms, and a
-   derived name does not identify a document: ACME's party holds 320 swap
-   documents stating 201 distinct term sets, so 201 names stand for 320
-   documents. The deposit kind holds 163 documents stating 141 sets. A screen
-   cannot offer a person a name to choose by until a name is stored.
-3. *A conventions configuration carries no rows, so naming one selects nothing.*
-   All four of ACME's conventions configurations are headers with no market
-   binding, no parameter and no analytic. The reporting model can say a
-   definition binds *US conventions*; it cannot say what *US conventions* holds.
-4. *The export ignores the configuration entirely, so every report of a party
-   reads the same rows.* When a run's files are assembled, the conventions file
-   is written from the party's whole conventions document and the bound
-   configuration's id is not read. Rebinding a definition to a different
-   conventions configuration would change nothing. This is not a screen defect
-   and no screen can paper over it: four configurations that name four intentions
-   select one set.
-5. *`refdata::conventions:read` sits where no person can reach it.* It is held by
-   =OreService= and =ReportRun=. =refdata::conventions:write= is held by no role
-   below =TenantAdmin=. So the one operation that answers the journey in a single
-   call is reachable by a service and by two administrative roles, and the person
-   who runs reference data reads 26 lists instead.
-6. *A convention list cannot be searched by a term.* The generated filter takes
-   =id_one_of= and nothing else, so a person who knows the index, the calendar or
-   the day count and not the key cannot reach the document. The screen says so on
-   the field and pages the list for the client to filter, which does not reach
-   320 documents in a browser.
-7. *One kind cannot name itself at all.* =ibor_index_convention= carries a fixing
-   calendar, a day count, settlement days and a business-day rule, and no index
-   column. Its terms do not state which index they belong to, so no naming rule
-   recovers it, and two IBOR indices with the same conventions are
-   indistinguishable in every column the table has.
-8. *The four tenant kinds belong to no party, and a party reader is not told.*
-   216 of ACME's 10,991 rows are held once for the tenant: =currency_pair= 179,
-   =overnight_index= 23, =ibor_index= 10 and =tenor= 4. A change one party makes
-   to the IBOR convention changes what every party reads, and nothing on the row
-   says so. The screen marks the owning scope per kind; the server does not
-   report it.
-9. *No operation returns how many distinct term sets a kind holds.* The 201 of
-   320 is a =count(distinct (…))= over seven columns that the screen performs. No
-   read states it, so the person learning that a derived name collides learns it
-   from a count the client made.
-10. *No run records the version of a convention it read.* The history view can
-    say when a term changed and cannot say which run was affected. The person who
-    asks "did the AED number change because the term changed" has a timeline and
-    two separate facts, and no join between them.
-11. *A party with no conventions has no fallback, whatever the design note says.*
-    The party's document read returns the rows the party holds; for a new party
-    that is nothing for the 22 party kinds. The export writes that file. Nothing
-    in the tree substitutes a curated document, and nothing refuses the run. See
-    [[id:AD7E6FC0-392E-46A9-8E28-23B7B4946A88][Onboard a party and verify its
-    conventions]] for what fills the gap instead.

-salt
-{
-  <b>PUBLISH CONVENTIONS FROM DATA QUALITY</b>  { Datasets | Coverage | Bundle | Receipt }
-  --
-  {
-    {
-      <b>The datasets</b>
-      --
-      {#
-        Code | Name | Artefact type | Catalogue
-        <b>ore.conventions</b> | ORE Instrument Conventions | conventions | ORE Analytics
-        refdata.currency_pair_conventions | Standard Currency Pair Conventions | currency_pair_conventions | FX Market Conventions
-        refdata.currency_pair_convention_calendars | Currency Pair Convention Calendars | ... | FX Market Conventions
-      }
-      <i>Payload: a curated artefact row per party, seeded in the system tenant.</i>
-      --
-      <b>What the person cannot read</b>
-      <b>No read of an ores_dq_*_artefact_tbl over NATS.</b>
-      DQ publishes artefact types and datasets, not the rows they stage.
-      What is about to land is readable only in the database.
-    } | {
-      <b>What the publish covers: 25 of 26 kinds</b>
-      --
-      {#
-        Route | Kinds | Subject
-        the 24-kind array | 24 | refdata.v1.ops.publish_conventions_from_dq
-        currency pair | 1 | refdata.v1.ops.publish_currency_pair_conventions_from_dq
-        <b>tenor</b> | <b>0</b> | (no artefact table, no subject)
-      }
-      <i>The function loops a 24-kind array and dispatches by name transform.</i>
-      <i>ores_dq_&lt;kind&gt;_conventions_artefact_tbl into ores_refdata_&lt;kind&gt;_conventions_tbl.</i>
-      <i>A new kind costs one array entry and one artefact table, not a function.</i>
-      --
-      <b>tenor is the 26th</b>
-      No ores_dq_tenor_conventions_artefact_tbl exists, so no function can copy it.
-      Its 4 rows are copied from the system tenant by ores_iam_provision_tenant_fn
-      when the tenant is created, reason system.new_record, and never refreshed.
-    }
-  }
-  --
-  {
-    {
-      <b>Which bundle, and who it publishes for</b>
-      --
-      {#
-        Dataset | Bundle | Scope | Param
-        ore.conventions | <b>party_essentials</b> | once per <b>party</b> | {"party_id": "..."}
-        refdata.currency_pair_conventions | <b>base</b> | once per <b>tenant</b> | (none)
-      }
-      --
-      The shell spells it: bundles publish party_essentials, with the party id, and wait.
-      That reaches dq.v1.ops.publish_bundle, which starts a workflow instance: one step per dataset.
-      The conventions step is refdata.v1.ops.publish_conventions_from_dq.
-      [ Publish ] | [ Read the run ]
-    } | {
-      <b>Receipt: the four counts the step returns</b>
-      --
-      {#
-        The publish | inserted | updated | skipped | deleted
-        first party, ore.conventions | <b>2,188</b> | 0 | 0 | 0
-        each later party | <b>2,155</b> | 0 | <b>33</b> | 0
-        a re-publish of the same party | 0 | 0 | <b>2,188</b> | 0
-        currency_pair, second publish | 0 | <b>179</b> | 0 | 0
-      }
-      --
-      <b>The 33 is not a defect</b>
-      Four kinds carry no party_id. Two of them are in the 24-kind array:
-      ibor_index 10 + overnight_index 23 = 33. The insert is guarded by
-      "this key is not already here for this tenant and party", and with no party
-      column it finds the row the first party's publish wrote.
-      <b>The 33 reads: already present, tenant-wide.</b>
-      --
-      <b>A re-publish does not carry a corrected curated row</b>
-      The 24-kind function has no update path: it inserts where the row is absent
-      and counts everything else as skipped. Its result carries no updated count.
-      <b>25 of the 26 kinds cannot take a correction. currency_pair is the one that can.</b>
-      <i>Correcting a row a tenant already holds is the change journey's job, per row.</i>
-    }
-  }
-}

-@enduml

-:PROPERTIES:
-:ID: 87B9678E-2085-4968-8AEA-7184D1384F1D
-:END:
-#+title: User Journey: Change what a report runs
-#+description: A market-risk owner or a tenant administrator reads the analytics a report configuration carries, opens the one screen that manages them, and reads what a change to that set reaches: which definitions it reads, that past runs keep their configuration, and that a run either side of the change is not comparable.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A market-risk owner or a tenant administrator reads the analytics a report configuration carries, opens the screen that manages them, and reads what the change does and does not reach.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"This report does not produce what I need any more, so I want to add one
-analytic, take another away, and know what that does to the runs I already
-have." The person owns a report definition for a party and reads its runs. A run
-came back with the measures they knew, and without the one they asked for. They
-want the missing measure produced by the next run, they want a measure they no
-longer read to stop costing a run, and they want one setting inside a measure
-adjusted. The journey is done when the definition runs the analytics the person
-meant, and the person has read what the change does and does not reach: which
-rows now carry what, which configuration moved, which runs keep the
-configuration they ran with, and which comparison stops being a comparison.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-A market-risk owner or a tenant administrator runs this journey. The owner knows
-what the desk reads and asks for the measure; the administrator holds the
-definition and makes the change. The person acts inside their own tenant, on a
-definition their party owns, and the configurations they can change are the
-party's own.
-
-The trigger is a run that came back without the measure the person asked for, or
-with a measure nobody reads any more, or with one setting of a measure that is
-wrong for the book. The person opens the definition from
-[[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]], and
-the journey ends when the analytics read the way they meant them to.
-
-This journey reaches the analytics of the configuration the definition binds. It
-does not write the definition's name, its schedule, its concurrency policy, its
-processing phases or its bindings, and it does not run the report. The next run of
-the definition carries the change; nothing here makes one.
-
-The journey is a wizard of three panels, titled *What this report runs*: the
-definition and the configurations it binds, the analytics the bound configuration
-carries, and what a change to that set reaches. The analytics themselves are set
-on **Manage the analytics**, one screen that owns them, and step 2 opens it. This
-journey is that screen's owner.
-
-* Steps
-
-** Step 1: the definition and the configurations it binds
-
-1. *Read what the definition binds.* The wizard opens on step 1, titled =The
-   definition and the configurations it binds=. The panel states the definition's
-   =name=, =report_type=, =party_id=, and the configurations it binds. A
-   definition binds configurations of exactly five types: =conventions=,
-   =pricing_engines=, =todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and
-   =risk_report_config=. It reads them through =report_configurations= and
-   reads the configurations themselves, all five named on the panel.
-2. *See what each configuration supplies.* Each of the five is shown with what it
-   puts into a run: conventions supplies the calendars, day-count rules,
-   business-day rules and currency pairs every analytic reads; pricing_engines
-   says which engine prices which product family; todays_market carries the
-   market data of the valuation date; curve_configuration says how each curve is
-   built; and risk_report_config carries the analytics, their order and their
-   parameters.
-3. *See where each configuration's data lives, and follow it where a screen
-   exists.* A conventions configuration is a named convention set, so the panel
-   shows the set this report uses and one page of the sets the party holds: a row
-   per set with its name, its purpose, the kinds it covers and whether it is the
-   one this report uses, and a radio that chooses it. One link leaves that page
-   for the authoring UX, and it is marked as not in this MR. The panel draws no
-   per-kind table, because what a set holds is decided in authoring. The names,
-   purposes and counts on the page are a fixture: no table stores a set's name or
-   purpose, nothing marks the document a run reads for a kind, and the
-   configuration carries no children. The other four, =pricing_engines=,
-   =todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and =risk_report_config=, have no
-   screen and no route, so the panel states the link as missing rather than
-   drawing one that would not resolve. The panel never invents a route.
-4. *Read who else is bound to the analytics.* The configurations in the first four
-   slots are the party's own. The one in the fifth, =risk_report_config=, carries
-   the analytics, and it is shared: three other definitions bind the same
-   configuration in this fixture. The panel names them before offering a change,
-   because "change this report" and "change these four reports" are different
-   decisions.
-
-** Step 2: the analytics
-
-5. *Read the set the configuration carries.* Step 2, titled =The analytics=,
-   states the set of the run settings configuration the definition binds: the
-   count that is on, every row with its =display_order= and a one-line statement
-   of what that analytic produces, and the rows that are on the configuration and
-   off. It reads =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.list_by_configuration_id=
-   and the vocabulary with =reporting.v1.analytic_types.list=. The fourteen types
-   are =npv=, =sensitivity=, =cashflow=, =curves=, =simulation=, =saccr=,
-   =parametricVar=, =portfolioDetails=, =creditcurves=, =pfe=, =calibration=,
-   =pnlExplain=, =historicalSimulationVar= and =xva=. The panel names the codes in
-   words, and it keeps three states apart: a type that is on, a type that owns a
-   row that is off, and a type the configuration has never carried.
-6. *Read what the panel does not draw.* Step 2 is read only. It draws no switch,
-   no parameter and no add action, because **the analytics are managed on one
-   screen and this is the reading of that screen's result**. A panel that also
-   drew the controls would be a second implementation of the same interaction,
-   and the two would drift.
-
-*** The shared screen: manage the analytics
-
-7. *Open the screen that manages them.* Step 2 links to Manage the analytics,
-   =doc/prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/=. That screen owns the whole
-   analytic interaction of a run settings configuration, and
-   [[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][Create a report]] hands the work
-   there too. It opens on a switchboard: every analytic type, one row each, with
-   the on/off control, the =display_order= and a one-line summary, and a type the
-   configuration carries no row for says so and offers to add it. It then gives
-   one step to each analytic that is on, in =display_order=, titled with the
-   analytic's name, and it ends on a step that reads the set back.
-8. *Read what the analytic is, and set every parameter it takes.* Each analytic
-   step carries what the analytic is, how it is calculated in plain words, and
-   every parameter it takes with a helpful control, a note on what the parameter
-   means and what a normal value is. The control follows the parameter's shape: a
-   number field for a count or a size, a select for an enumeration, a toggle for a
-   boolean, and a text field for a name. An analytic that takes no parameter says
-   so rather than showing an empty list. The fixture carries settings for the
-   fourteen types, so almost every analytic that is on opens a step with something
-   to set.
-9. *Turn one off.* The person sets the row's =active= to false. The row stays.
-   **An analytic is turned off by setting =active= false, not by deleting the
-   row**, because the history must show that it was turned off: a person who
-   reads the configuration later sees the measure, its =display_order= and its
-   parameters, and sees that it is off. Deleting the row would erase the fact
-   that the report ever produced it. The shared screen asks first, because the
-   parameter values leave the rail with the step, and it states the write in
-   those words. **No control anywhere on either screen removes a row.**
-10. *Turn one on.* Turning an analytic on, or adding one the configuration never
-    carried, is the switch on the switchboard, and the switch is the only way to
-    add one. It writes the row with the default value of every parameter at the
-    next =display_order= and gives the analytic a step of its own, so the person
-    is offered the step the switch just created. A row that exists and is off is
-    turned back on with the settings it kept.
-11. *Read where the editor is deferred.* =simulation= and =pfe= need
-    purpose-built editors for the cube, the shift and the time grid. The shared
-    screen says so on the parameter itself: these are drawn as plain fields for
-    now, each labelled a deferred editor, and the purpose-built editor is a later
-    task. The page never presents a plain field as the final design.
-12. *Read the set back.* The last step of the shared screen names the rows rather
-    than counting them: each active analytic with its =display_order= and its
-    number of parameter rows, the rows kept off with their order, every parameter
-    value with its position, and the definitions bound to the configuration that
-    read the set. It is the final step, so it offers no Back, and it offers the
-    way back to the report.
-
-** The rule between analytics
-
-13. *See the incompatibility as a state, not as prose.* =pfe= reads a cube that
-     =simulation= writes, so =pfe= on without =simulation= cannot work. Both
-     screens show that as a visible state: the rule strip names the rule and
-     marks the set as one that cannot run, both rows are marked in red, and on
-     the shared screen the toggle that would write either row of the pair is
-     refused and its last step refuses to read the set back. The rule lives in
-     the ACME seeder, in =generate_risk_config_data.py=, function
-     =check_exposure_needs_simulation=, and **no service validates it**. The write
-     would be accepted and the run would fail later, so the shared screen refuses
-     what the server would not, and says that is what it is doing.
-
-** Step 3: what a change reaches
-
-14. *Review what a change does and does not reach.* Step 3, titled =What a change
-     reaches=, states the reach before anything is written. It reaches the next
-     run of every definition bound to this configuration, including the three the
-     person did not open. It does not reach a run already produced: a run keeps
-     the configuration it ran with, and its outputs and its errors are that run's
-     own record. It does not reach the definition's scheduling, its processing
-     phases, its concurrency policy or its other four configurations.
-15. *Read that the comparison stops being a comparison.* A run made after the
-     change is not comparable with a run made before it, because the two runs did
-     not produce the same measures. The difference between them is then a
-     difference of configuration and not a difference of the book, and the
-     comparison states a change that did not happen. The panel says so plainly,
-     and names the definition's runs from before the write as the runs it makes
-     incomparable.
-16. *Read where the write happens.* The write is the shared screen's and not this
-     wizard's. The set is sent in one call, so a turned-on analytic, a
-     turned-off one and a changed parameter land together and a half-written
-     configuration is not left behind; one setting alone is written one row at a
-     time. Step 3 names the operations, states that this page stages nothing and
-     writes nothing, and points at the screen that does. No step anywhere deletes
-     a row.
-17. *See the version history.* The person reads the definition's version history:
-     the versions it has had, and what each one states. This is the record of the
-     change, and it is also the only timeline the screen has to place a run
-     against. It is not a complete answer. **No operation says which runs were
-     made with which configuration version.** The best the screen can do is
-     compare a run's own start time with the definition's version history and say
-     that a run started before a version, which is an inference and not a fact,
-     because the analytics live on the configuration and the configuration's own
-     version history is not read here. *What is missing* records all of it.
-18. *Leave, or go on.* The person returns to the definition's latest run, or runs
-     the report to see the new measures. The run is
-     [[id:76431668-8656-4276-9F9B-F292FE45B2CA][Run a report and watch it
-     finish]]'s page, and its figures are
-     [[id:969C14D2-4280-4D7C-8F51-1D395B521C83][Read what a run produced]]'s.
-     This journey changes what the next run produces and nothing else.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-Two screens. The wizard has three panels: step 1 shows the definition header and
-the five configurations it binds, each with what it supplies and a link to the
-screen that holds its data; step 2 shows the analytics of the bound run settings
-configuration as a read-only summary — the count on, the display order, the rows
-kept off, and the pair marked when it cannot run — and links to the shared
-screen; step 3 shows what a change reaches and the runs it makes incomparable.
-The person reads the three as one answer: what this report runs, and what
-changing it does.
-
-Manage the analytics is the second screen, and it owns the analytic interaction
-for every journey that needs it. It is the standard steps UI: a switchboard of
-the fourteen types, one rail step per analytic that is on in =display_order=
-carrying that analytic's explanation, calculation and every parameter with a
-control chosen for its shape, and a final step that reads the set back and
-refuses to read a set that cannot run. The rail is computed from the set, so
-turning an analytic on adds a step and turning one off removes it.
-
-The two screens write two things and read eight. They write the analytic rows and
-their parameter rows, both from the shared screen. They read the definition, its
-bindings, the five configurations, the configuration's analytics, their
-parameters, the analytic types, the definition's versions, and the configurations
-grouped by type. They run nothing and they schedule nothing.
-
-The wizard keeps four statements beside the summary, because a person who reads
-only the wizard must still read them. Turning an analytic off sets =active= to
-false and leaves the row. A configuration is shared, so the change can reach
-definitions the person did not open. A run keeps the configuration it ran with,
-and nothing says which configuration version that was. And a run after the change
-is not comparable with a run before it. The wizard draws the incomparable runs by
-their start times and says the placement is an inference.
-
-#+caption: What this report runs: the wizard's three panels with the analytics of the bound configuration summarised and the pfe and simulation pair marked, and the shared screen the panel hands the work to.

-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_change_what_a_report_runs.png]]

-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/][manage the analytics
-prototype]] owns this journey, and
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics.org][its design note]] says
-what it argues, which states it can reach and what is fake. It belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/=.
-
-It is one screen on the standard steps UI, and it draws the whole analytic
-interaction: the switchboard with every analytic type as one row, the on/off
-control, the =display_order= and a one-line summary; a rail step for each
-analytic that is on in =display_order=, titled with its name, carrying what the
-analytic is, how it is calculated, and every parameter with a control chosen for
-its shape and a note on its meaning and its normal value; and a final step that
-reads the set back and offers the way to the report. It must show the =pfe=
-incompatibility as a visible state — the rule strip, both rows marked, the toggle
-refused and the last step refusing to read the set back — and it must name the
-rule and the seeder it lives in. It must state that an analytic is turned off by
-setting =active= false and never by deleting the row, and no control on it may
-remove a row. It must say that the complex editors for =simulation= and =pfe= are
-deferred, and label each as it draws it. It carries =?variant=A|B|C= as three
-readings of the per-analytic step, because that layout is the open question. Every
-value on the page is a fixture, and the page says so.
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/change-what-a-report-runs/][change what a
-report runs prototype]] is the same journey's wizard, and
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/change-what-a-report-runs.org][its design
-note]] says what it argues. It belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/change-what-a-report-runs/=. It must draw step 1 with
-the definition's five bindings, each with what it supplies and a link that is real
-for conventions and stated missing for the other four; step 2 as the read-only
-summary of the bound configuration's analytics, with the =active= flag shown, the
-display order, the incompatibility as a visible state, and the link to the shared
-prototype; and step 3 with what a change reaches and the runs it makes
-incomparable, placed by start time against the definition's version history and
-marked an inference. It must state the server's silence beside the rule, say that
-past runs keep their configuration, that the configuration is shared, and that a
-new run is not comparable with an older one. It draws no analytic control, because
-the shared prototype owns them.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_definition= | The definition whose analytics change: =name=, =report_type=, =party_id=, and the version history an edit writes | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =report_configuration= | The slot a configuration fills: =configuration_type_code= and =configuration_id=, five of them per definition | [[id:7F2C8A41-6E93-4B57-A0D4-3C9E1B5D7826][ores.reporting.report_configuration]] |
-| =configuration= | The configurations step 1 names, and the one the analytics belong to, which several definitions can bind | [[id:6B3D9E27-5C41-4A86-8F19-2E7B0D4C6A53][ores.reporting.configuration]] |
-| =configuration_analytic= | One measure the configuration asks for: =analytic_type_code=, =display_order= and =active= | [[id:ABEA22FE-C92F-4522-8256-72DE1804295B][ores.reporting.configuration_analytic]] |
-| =configuration_analytic_parameter= | One setting of one measure: =parameter_name= and =value= | [[id:BFDAC96E-3774-45F8-9013-DFDDF0EE7335][ores.reporting.configuration_analytic_parameter]] |
-| =analytic_type= | The vocabulary the =analytic_type_code= comes from: the fourteen types, their names, and what the switchboard offers | [[id:F92E7855-D5F5-41AE-AD3E-9F61BCC3830F][ores.reporting.analytic_type]] |
-| =report_instance= | The runs, which keep the configuration they ran with, and whose start times are what the screen places against the version history | [[id:9FCCF6C8-9C10-403B-BDA4-C3E28706BD67][ores.reporting.report_instance]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the definition and the configuration | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-The rows this journey edits are =configuration_analytic= and
-=configuration_analytic_parameter=, and neither belongs to the definition. The
-definition reaches them through =report_configuration=, one row per configuration
-type, and the configuration in the fifth type, =risk_report_config=, is the one
-that carries the analytics. The definition's own fields are shown to the person
-but not written here:
-=schedule_expression=, =concurrency_policy=, =pre_processing=,
-=prepared_input_key=, =post_processing= and =is_official= all stay as they are.
-
-The definition is bitemporal. An edit writes a new version, older versions stay
-readable, and a run keeps the configuration it ran with. That is what makes the
-change safe to make and hard to read afterwards: nothing is destroyed, and
-nothing names the version a run used.
-
-Every entity above carries =party_id= and is party-scoped by row-level security.
-The analytic and its parameters carry the tenant as well, because a
-configuration's analytics are written by the session that writes the
-configuration.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Step 1, read the definition | Read the definition | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Step 1, read the definition | List the party's definitions | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.list= | exists |
-| Step 1, read the bindings | Read the configurations the definition binds | =reporting.v1.report_configurations.list= | exists |
-| Step 1, read the bindings | Read the configurations themselves | =reporting.v1.configurations.list= | exists |
-| Step 1, read the bindings | Read the configurations of one type | =reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code= | exists |
-| Step 2, read the set | Read the analytics of one configuration | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.list_by_configuration_id= | exists |
-| Step 2, read the set | Read the analytic type vocabulary | =reporting.v1.analytic_types.list= | exists |
-| The shared screen, read one analytic's settings | Read one analytic's parameters | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytic_parameters.list_by_configuration_analytic_id= | exists |
-| The shared screen, turn one off | Write one analytic's =active= and order | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.put= | exists |
-| The shared screen, turn one on | Write the new analytic and its parameters | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.put= and =reporting.v1.configuration_analytic_parameters.put= | exists |
-| The shared screen, the set | Write the whole set in one call | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.put_many= | exists |
-| The shared screen, one setting | Write one parameter's value | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytic_parameters.put= | exists |
-| The shared screen, read back | Read the stored analytics again | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.list_by_configuration_id= | exists |
-| Step 3, review what the change does not reach | Read the configuration's market roles, which this journey leaves alone | =reporting.v1.configuration_market_bindings.list_by_configuration_id= | exists |
-| Step 3, the version history | List the definition's versions | =reporting.v1.report_definitions_versions.list= | exists |
-| Step 3, the version history | Read one version | =reporting.v1.report_definitions_versions.get= | exists |
-| Not sent here | Write a definition's binding to a configuration | =reporting.v1.report_configurations.put= | exists |
-| Not sent here | Write a configuration row | =reporting.v1.configurations.put= | exists |
-| Not sent here | Write a configuration's market roles | =reporting.v1.configuration_market_bindings.put= | exists |
-| Not sent here | Write the definition itself | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.put= | exists |
-| Which runs ran with which configuration | Name the configuration version behind a run | (no operation returns it) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Read and change analytics from the browser | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-Two operations are this journey's writes, and =configuration_analytics.put_many=
-carries the set. A person toggles rows, adds one with the switch, and the shared
-screen sends the whole set at once, so added, turned-off and reordered analytics
-land together and a half-written configuration is not left behind.
-=configuration_analytic_parameters.put= writes one parameter at a time, because
-a parameter is one row with one value and the set of parameters a person edits is
-not a unit. Both belong to the shared screen; the wizard sends neither.
-
-=report_configurations.put=, =configurations.put= and =report_definitions.put=
-exist, and this journey sends none. Reaching into another configuration,
-rebinding the definition to a different one, or editing the definition's own
-fields is a different change: it would move every analytic at once and leave the
-old configuration running for whoever else binds it. A person who wants that has
-not asked to change what a report runs; they have asked to change which
-configuration it uses, or what the definition says.
-
-No BFF route serves reporting. The shared screen adds one, for example
-=GET /api/reporting/configurations/<configuration-id>/analytics= for the read and
-=PUT /api/reporting/configurations/<configuration-id>/analytics= for the write,
-which calls =configuration_analytics.put_many= and the parameter write behind it.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *A route and a screen for reporting.* No BFF route serves reporting, and
-   nothing in the web application shows a report today. The wizard, the summary,
-   the shared analytics screen and the read-back are new.
-2. *No screen exists for four of the five configuration types.* Step 1 names the
-   five configurations the definition binds, says what each supplies, and links
-   each to the screen that holds its data. **Only conventions has a screen
-   today**: =PATHS.conventions= is =/refdata/conventions=, a real route in
-   =projects/ores.web/packages/web/src/shell/paths.ts=. The other four,
-   =pricing_engines=, =todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and
-   =risk_report_config=, have no screen and no route, so step 1 states the link
-   as missing rather than drawing one that would not resolve. A person who wants
-   to change the engines, the market data or the curves behind a run has nowhere
-   to go, and the wizard says so instead of hiding it.
-3. *The complex editors for simulation and pfe are deferred.* =simulation= and
-   =pfe= each need a purpose-built editor: one for the cube, one for the shift,
-   one for the time grid. Manage the analytics draws those settings as plain
-   fields, =time_grid= as a select and =exposure_cube= as a text field, and it
-   says on the parameter that the purpose-built editor is a later task. A plain
-   field is not the design, and the page never pretends it is.
-4. *Nothing validates the =pfe= rule.* =pfe= reads a cube that =simulation=
-   writes, so =pfe= on without =simulation= cannot work. That rule lives
-   in the ACME seeder, in =generate_risk_config_data.py=, function
-   =check_exposure_needs_simulation=, and nowhere else. The reporting service
-   does not check it when a configuration is written, so
-   =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.put_many= accepts the set and the
-   failure arrives in the run. A screen cannot rely on a refusal it does not get,
-   so the summary marks the pair, the shared screen refuses the toggle and its
-   last step refuses to read the set back, and all three name the rule. That is a
-   screen defending itself against a server that does not, and it is the
-   second-best answer; a validation on the write is the first.
-5. *No operation says which runs used which configuration.* A run keeps the
-   configuration it ran with, and nothing reads that configuration back with the
-   run. The screen can place a run against the definition's version history by
-   the run's own start time, and that is an inference: the analytics live on the
-   configuration, and the definition's version history says what the definition
-   changed, not what the configuration held. A person who needs "this run predates
-   my change" has an inference and no fact, which is why the panel marks it.
-6. *No read of a configuration's version history.* A configuration carries a
-   version, and no operation in this journey's set returns the versions of one
-   configuration or the version a definition bound at a time. The definition's
-   history is the only history the screen can read, and it is a history of a
-   different row.
-7. *The comparison is marked partial for errors and not for a changed set of
-   analytics.* The results screen compares a run with a previous run of the same
-   definition and marks the comparison partial where either side carried errors.
-   It cannot mark it invalid because the analytics changed, because nothing tells
-   it that they did. A person reading a comparison across the change is reading
-   two different sets of measures side by side, and the screen shows the change
-   as a change in the figures.
-8. *The allowed values of a parameter are not readable here.* A parameter's kind
-   comes from the definition behind it, and the operations in this journey's set
-   read the configuration's parameter rows and the analytic types. No operation
-   in the set returns the value domain of a parameter, so the shared screen draws
-   a select only where the fixture knows the enumeration, and a text field where
-   it does not, and cannot tell the person whether a value is one the analytic
-   accepts. A run is where a wrong value shows up.
