-#+title: User Journey: Choose when a report runs
-#+description: A tenant administrator gives a report definition a schedule so it runs every morning, changes that schedule, runs the report now, pauses the schedule, or takes it away, and reads what each action does and does not reach.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A tenant administrator gives a report definition a schedule so it runs every morning, changes that schedule, runs the report now, pauses the schedule, or takes it away, and reads what each action does and does not reach.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"Make this report run every morning." The person owns a report definition for a
-party and wants it produced without anybody pressing a button: at the close, at
-the start of the trading day, or at whatever time the desk reads it. They also
-want four separate answers as the routine changes. They want one run now, without
-waiting for the schedule. They want the schedule to stop firing for a while and
-to keep it. They want the same recurrence to fire again afterwards. They want the
-schedule gone when the report is no longer read each morning. The journey is done
-when the definition carries the schedule the person meant, or no schedule at all,
-and the person has read what the change does and does not reach.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-The tenant administrator runs this journey. Choosing when a report runs is a
-tenant-level decision: it changes what the tenant's parties produce every day,
-and it is not a desk's choice for the afternoon. The administrator acts inside
-their tenant, and the definitions they can schedule are the tenant's own, party
-by party. A trading desk asks for the schedule; the administrator sets it.
-
-The trigger is a decision about routine. A report that has been run by hand
-every morning is wanted on a schedule. A schedule that fires too early or too
-late is wanted at another time. A report wanted today and not at 06:00 tomorrow
-is wanted run now. A schedule that fires into a quiet week is wanted paused, and
-back on the same recurrence afterwards. A report that is no longer read each
-morning is wanted off the schedule. The person opens the definition from
-[[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]], and
-the journey ends when the definition's row reads the way they meant it to.
-
-This journey writes three ways. Scheduling and unscheduling change the definition
-and the scheduler job that carries the recurrence. Running the report now creates
-a run and changes no schedule. Pausing and resuming would change neither the
-expression nor the job, only whether the job fires, and no operation does it
-today. No action here touches a run that has already happened.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Open the definition and read its schedule.* The person opens one definition
-   and reads its schedule panel. The panel states the definition's
-   =schedule_expression=, the cron expression that drives the report's
-   recurrence, and whether the definition is scheduled at all. A definition with
-   a =scheduler_job_id= is scheduled and names the job that holds its recurrence;
-   one without it is on-demand. The panel states which of the two the person is
-   looking at before offering to change it, because "every morning" is already
-   true for some definitions and a person should not schedule one twice. The
-   panel cannot state that a schedule is paused. The scheduler job carries an
-   =is_active= flag and no read in this journey returns it, so a paused schedule
-   and a live one read the same here, and *What is missing* records that.
-2. *Write the expression.* The person states the recurrence as a cron
-   expression. The screen accepts the expression and shows it back, and it does
-   not pretend to evaluate it: the next firing is the scheduler's to compute,
-   and the personal reading of a cron expression is not a fact the definition
-   stores. A person who wants "every morning" states the expression the
-   installation's scheduler understands; the screen offers no natural-language
-   promise it cannot keep.
-3. *Press Schedule.* The system asks the person to confirm, restating the
-   definition, its party and the expression. On confirmation the screen sends
-   =reporting.v1.ops.schedule_report_definitions= for the definition. The
-   reporting service validates the expression and asks the scheduler to hold the
-   definition's job; the definition records the job in =scheduler_job_id=. The
-   service answers, and the screen reads the definition again so the panel shows
-   the stored expression and the job, not the value the person typed.
-4. *Read what the schedule now covers.* The panel states that the definition is
-   scheduled, with its expression and its scheduler job. The front door's row
-   for this definition now reads *scheduled*, and the next firing creates a run
-   there. The screen says plainly what it cannot say: it cannot show the job's
-   next due time, the last time the schedule fired, or the scheduler's own state,
-   because no read in this journey's set returns them. A person who wants "every
-   morning, starting tomorrow" has to trust the expression and the scheduler,
-   and *What is missing* records that.
-5. *Change the time.* The person edits the expression and presses Schedule
-   again. The same operation is sent with the new expression and the service
-   reconciles the definition's schedule. The screen does not simulate the
-   change: it sends it, reads the definition back, and states the result.
-6. *Run now.* A person who wants one run without waiting for the next firing
-   presses Run now. The system asks the person to confirm, and the confirmation
-   states what the action reaches: it starts one run at once, and it does not
-   change the schedule, the expression or the scheduler job. On confirmation the
-   screen sends =reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance= for the definition.
-   The reporting service applies the definition's concurrency policy, creates a
-   =report_instance=, and dispatches the execution workflow. The screen does not
-   wait for the run: it states that the run started and hands the person to
-   [[id:76431668-8656-4276-9F9B-F292FE45B2CA][Run a report and watch it finish]].
-   Run now serves an on-demand definition as well as a scheduled one, because
-   running when a person asks is what an on-demand definition is for. The
-   scheduler sends the same operation when a job fires, so a build that offers
-   it to a person must name the permission that gates a person's call.
-7. *Pause.* A person who wants the schedule to stop firing, and to keep it,
-   presses Pause. The system asks the person to confirm, and the confirmation
-   states what the action does and does not reach: the recurrence stays on the
-   definition, the scheduler job stays, and nothing fires until the person
-   resumes; the next fire time is unknown while the schedule is paused, and the
-   screen says so instead of drawing one. **No operation does this today.** The
-   scheduler job carries =is_active= in =ores_scheduler_job_definitions_tbl=, so
-   the data can express a paused schedule, and nothing exposes it to a reporting
-   screen. This journey names the action because a person asks for it, and
-   records the operation as missing rather than inventing a subject for it.
-8. *Play.* A person whose schedule is paused presses Play. The system asks the
-   person to confirm, and the confirmation states that firing starts again on
-   the same schedule: same expression, same job, and the next time the
-   expression names. Nothing is re-entered and no run is created by the action
-   itself. **No operation does this today**, for the same reason: the state would
-   live in the job's =is_active= and nothing writes it from a reporting screen.
-9. *Unschedule.* A report that is no longer wanted on a schedule is unscheduled
-   with =reporting.v1.ops.unschedule_report_definitions=. The system confirms,
-   because taking a schedule away changes what the tenant produces every day.
-   On confirmation the service removes the definition's schedule, and the
-   definition no longer names a scheduler job. The definition stays, and it
-   becomes on-demand: a person who wants the report can still run it now.
-   Unscheduling is not pausing. It removes the expression and the job with it,
-   so there is no recurrence left to resume.
-10. *Read what these actions do not do.* The runs already produced stay, with
-    their outputs and their errors. No action here deletes history, and none
-    stops a run that is in flight: there is no operation in this journey that
-    cancels a run. Run now does not change the schedule, and pausing does not
-    remove a run. The screen says all of it, so a person who expected
-    "unschedule" to mean "stop everything" is not left believing it did.
-11. *Leave, or go on.* The person returns to the front door and checks the row,
-    or opens the definition's latest run to see what the schedule last produced.
-    The run the schedule produces is
-    [[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]]'s
-    row and [[id:76431668-8656-4276-9F9B-F292FE45B2CA][Run a report and watch it
-    finish]]'s page; this journey changes when that happens and nothing else.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen. The definition header, the schedule panel, the expression editor and
-the actions are panels of the same screen, because the person reads them as one
-answer. Each action carries its own confirmation, a dialog that restates the
-definition, the party and the expression, because the change outlives the
-person's session. The confirmation also says what the action does not reach, so
-Run now, Pause and Unschedule cannot be read as one another.
-
-The screen writes three ways at most: it schedules, it unschedules, and it
-starts one run. Every other message on it is a read. The panel distinguishes
-"scheduled" from "on-demand" by the presence of the definition's scheduler job.
-It cannot distinguish a paused schedule from a live one, because the job's
-=is_active= is unread here. It says what it cannot show rather than drawing a
-next-run time it did not read.
-
-#+caption: Choose when a report runs: the definition, its current expression, the schedule editor, and what the schedule does and does not cover.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_choose_when_a_report_runs.png]]
-
-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/choose-when-a-report-runs/][prototype]] argues this journey in three interpretations, and [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/choose-when-a-report-runs.org][its design note]] says what each argues and what is fake. This journey is the design intent for the schedule panel, and its
-prototype belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/choose-when-a-report-runs/=. The prototype must draw a
-definition that is on-demand with no scheduler job; the confirmation that sets a
-schedule; the same definition scheduled, with its expression and its job; the
-change of an expression; the confirmation that runs the definition now; the
-confirmation that pauses a schedule, and the same definition resumed; the
-confirmation that unschedules; and the definition back on-demand with its past
-runs still listed. It must draw Run now, Pause or Play, and Unschedule as three
-separate actions, and it must show a paused definition as paused while its
-expression stays readable. Pause and Play have no operation, so the prototype
-draws them as a fixture and says so. It must also draw the panel's honest
-statement that the next firing and the last firing are not readable, so the
-prototype does not imply a next-run time.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_definition= | The definition whose recurrence changes: =schedule_expression=, =scheduler_job_id=, =concurrency_policy= and the party that owns it | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =report_instance= | The runs the schedule has already produced, which unscheduling leaves in place | [[id:9FCCF6C8-9C10-403B-BDA4-C3E28706BD67][ores.reporting.report_instance]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the definition whose routine changes | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-The definition is the row this journey edits, and =scheduler_job_id= is how the
-screen knows the definition has a schedule. The runs are the definition's
-history, and they are not part of the schedule: unscheduling does not remove
-them. The firing a schedule produces is a =report_trigger_event=, immutable and
-written once; it is named here because it is what the screen would read to
-answer "did the schedule fire", and no read serves it.
-
-The paused state does not live on the definition. It lives in the scheduler job:
-=ores_scheduler_job_definitions_tbl= carries =is_active=, and a paused schedule
-would be a job whose =is_active= is false. The definition stores only the job's
-identifier, so a screen that reads the definition alone reads a paused schedule
-and a live one the same. The table is named here because it is where the state
-belongs, and no operation in this journey reads or writes that column.
-
-Every entity above carries =party_id= and is party-scoped by row-level security.
-The definition and the run are bitemporal, so a schedule change is a new version
-of the definition and the earlier version stays readable. The trigger event is
-an immutable event.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Open the definition | Read the definition and its expression | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Open the definition | List the party's definitions | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.list= | exists |
-| Schedule | Give the definition a schedule | =reporting.v1.ops.schedule_report_definitions= | exists |
-| Schedule | Read the definition back after the write | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Change the time | Give the definition a new schedule | =reporting.v1.ops.schedule_report_definitions= | exists |
-| Run now | Start one run immediately, without touching the schedule | =reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance= | exists |
-| Run now | Follow the run the trigger created | =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= | exists |
-| Pause | Stop the schedule firing and keep it | (no pause operation; the state would be the job's =is_active=) | missing |
-| Play | Start firing again on the same schedule | (no play operation; the state would be the job's =is_active=) | missing |
-| Unschedule | Take the schedule away | =reporting.v1.ops.unschedule_report_definitions= | exists |
-| Unschedule | Read the definition back after the write | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Read the past runs | List the runs the schedule already produced | =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= | exists |
-| Read the firing | Read when the schedule last fired, and what it triggered | (no read of =report_trigger_event= over NATS) | missing |
-| Read the scheduler job | Read the job's state or its next due time | (no scheduler read is named in this set) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Read and change a schedule from the browser | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-Three operations are this journey's writes, and run now is one of them. The two
-schedule operations are served by the reporting service, which asks the
-scheduler to hold one job per definition. =trigger_report_instance= is served by
-the same service: it applies the definition's concurrency policy, creates a
-=report_instance=, and dispatches the execution workflow. The scheduler sends
-that same operation when a job fires, so its caller is normally a service and
-not a person. The definition read returns =schedule_expression= and
-=scheduler_job_id=, so the screen can state whether a definition is scheduled
-and what expression it carries. It cannot state the job's own state or its next
-due time, because those belong to the scheduler and no operation here reads
-them.
-
-The permission that gates these operations is not uniform. The scheduling handler
-checks a permission before it schedules or unschedules, so those two writes are
-gated. The run-now handler checks none. It serves
-=reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance= and contains no permission test
-anywhere, while its own documentation states that the caller's permission check
-is what decides whether it may act in a tenant. Any authenticated caller can
-therefore trigger a run today. The definition read is gated by
-=reporting::report_definitions:read=. The tenant administrator holds
-=*= and reaches all three. A role below the administrator has no stated code to
-be granted for the schedule writes, and needs none at all for run now, which
-*What is missing* records.
-
-No BFF route serves this screen. The prototype adds one, for example
-=GET /api/reporting/reports/<definition-id>/schedule= for the read,
-=PUT /api/reporting/reports/<definition-id>/schedule= for the schedule and
-unschedule writes, and =POST /api/reporting/reports/<definition-id>/runs= for
-run now, which calls =trigger_report_instance=. The handler authenticates the
-caller's token and checks the definition read and run write codes.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *A route and a screen.* No BFF route serves reporting, and nothing in the web
-   application shows a report today. The schedule panel, its editor and its
-   confirmations are new.
-2. *The firing is stored and unreadable.* =report_trigger_event= records every
-   firing with its definition, its trigger type, its scheduler job and its time.
-   There is no read of it over NATS. The screen can say a definition is
-   scheduled, and it cannot say when the schedule last fired, whether it fired
-   at all, or which run a firing produced. That is the central gap for a person
-   who has set a schedule and is waiting for the first result.
-3. *No read of the scheduler job.* The definition stores =scheduler_job_id=, and
-   no operation in this set reads the job behind it. The screen cannot show the
-   job's state, its next due time or the scheduler's own view of the expression,
-   so "every morning" is a promise the screen can only repeat, not verify.
-4. *No time zone.* =report_definition= states a cron expression and no time
-   zone. A tenant whose morning is not the installation's morning cannot state
-   which morning it means, and the screen cannot say whose clock the expression
-   is read on. A time zone on the definition, or a stated installation default,
-   is the missing field.
-5. *The write permission is not named, and run now is not gated at all.* The two
-   schedule operations have no permission code in this journey's set.
-   =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin= hold =*= and can call them; no role below the
-   administrator can be granted the capability because there is no code to
-   grant. A write code for the definition is the missing piece. Run now is
-   worse than unnamed: its handler performs no permission test, so any
-   authenticated caller can start a run. The handler's own documentation claims
-   the caller's permission check decides, and no such check exists.
-6. *No pause and no play.* The scheduler's job row carries =is_active= in
-   =ores_scheduler_job_definitions_tbl=, so the data can express a paused
-   schedule, and nothing exposes it to a reporting screen.
-   =reporting.v1.ops.schedule_report_definitions= and
-   =reporting.v1.ops.unschedule_report_definitions= are the only two schedule
-   operations, and neither sets =is_active=. A pause operation and a play
-   operation are the missing pair, and a read of the flag is the missing read:
-   without it the screen cannot tell a paused schedule from a live one, and
-   *Pause* cannot be offered honestly. No subject is invented for them here.
-7. *Unscheduling is not pausing, and neither stops a run.* Unschedule removes
-   the expression and the scheduler job, so the definition has no recurrence
-   left. Pause would keep both and stop only the firing. Neither action cancels a
-   run in flight, and neither removes past runs or their archives. The screen
-   states all of it. A person who needs a running report stopped has no action
-   in this journey.
-8. *No preview and no validation on the screen.* The expression is validated by
-   the service when the write arrives, and the screen does not evaluate it. A
-   bad expression is refused by the service, and the screen shows the refusal.
-   A next-firing preview would need the scheduler's own evaluation, which no read
-   here provides.

-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A tenant administrator or market-risk owner names a report, binds the configurations it reads, reads the analytics the bound configuration carries, saves it, reads back exactly what was written, and leaves it on demand or hands it to the schedule journey. The analytics themselves are set on the one screen that manages them, which this journey links.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"I need a new report that runs our analytics over my portfolio, and I need to be
-sure it can actually run before I schedule it."
-
-The person has a question the existing reports do not answer: another analytic
-set, another portfolio, another party. They want a report definition they can run
-and, later, schedule. The second half of the sentence is the hard one. A report
-that runs nothing, or that runs an analytic whose input nothing produces, looks
-complete on the screen and fails on the grid. The person wants the screen to say
-what the definition needs before it leaves their hands, and to say plainly where
-it cannot: nothing today answers "what does this report need in order to run"
-beyond the configuration types its report type requires.
-
-The journey is done when a definition exists that reads back as the person wrote
-it: a name, a report type, five bound configurations, the analytics the bound
-configuration carries with their settings, and a portfolio scope. It has never
-run, and the front door already draws that state.
-
-The analytics are not chosen here. They belong to the run settings configuration
-the person binds, they are set on the one screen that manages them, and this
-journey reads them and links there.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-A tenant administrator or a market-risk owner runs this journey. The
-administrator creates reports for the tenant's parties; the market-risk owner
-creates the report the desk or the committee asks for. Both act inside one
-party, and the party of a new definition is the party of the session, not a
-choice.
-
-The trigger is a request for a report that does not exist yet. A regulator asks
-for exposure profiles the party does not produce, a committee wants the same
-numbers over a portfolio nobody configured, or a party joins the group and needs
-the reports its siblings already run. The person opens
-[[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]], finds
-no row that answers the question, and presses Create.
-
-This journey writes a definition and the bindings it makes, and creates no run.
-The analytic rows and their settings belong to the configuration and are written
-on Manage the analytics, which this journey links. Nothing in the application
-creates a report today: no BFF route serves reporting, and the definitions that
-exist were seeded. The screen this journey describes does not exist, and the
-operations below are the ones it would send.
-
-* Steps
-
-The journey is the standard steps UI, the one the system bootstrap journey uses.
-A step carries an id, a title for the rail, a lead sentence and a body, and the
-last one is final; the rail is drawn from the same list, so the rail and the
-steps cannot disagree
-([[id:6A63AAC7-4869-493A-97E7-55B919874784][Journey runtime]]). Going back is
-refused at the first step, and at a final step
-([[id:166B2D77-6D04-47D5-A651-5431E1F2E082][UX Language]], section *The rail*).
-
-The rail is fixed at eight steps: what it is, one step for each of the five
-configuration types it binds, the analytics the bound configuration carries, and
-the final review. The rail, the step numbering and the step foot are one list, so
-all three agree at every moment.
-
-The rail used to be computed from what the report runs: seven fixed steps, then
-one step for every analytic that was on in =display_order=, then the review. Those
-analytic steps are gone. Analytic management belongs to one screen,
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/][Manage the analytics]],
-and *What it runs* reads the set and links there. A rail that renumbers itself for
-a write made on another screen told the person nothing they could act on here.
-
-The five configuration types get one step each, in the order
-=report_type_configuration_types= states and the seeder writes: =conventions=,
-=pricing_engines=, =todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and
-=risk_report_config=. One step for all five said what each slot supplied and
-left the reader to work out what the choice decides. Four of the five steps
-therefore carry the same four parts: what binding a configuration of that type
-means, where its data lives, the picker for the configuration this report binds,
-and what the binding reaches and what it does not. The conventions step is the
-exception: it reads the set the bound configuration carries, the kinds that are
-bound and the ones that are not, and it links to the shared screen that owns the
-per-kind choice.
-
-1. *What it is.* The person types a =name= and a =description=, and chooses a
-   =report_type= from a combo box. The combo box reads
-   =ores_reporting_report_types_tbl=, and the type is a category that also names
-   the workflow which runs the report. One type is registered today: =risk=, the
-   full ORE risk analytics run, which names =report_execution_workflow=. More
-   types are expected, so the control is a combo box reading the table rather
-   than a fixed set of choices: a type added as a row must appear without a code
-   change. The name is unique within the party, so the screen refuses a name the
-   party already uses and says which row holds it. The definition is created
-   official unless the person clears =is_official=, and an official report never
-   reads a sandbox: its scope cannot name a sandbox portfolio or a virtual book.
-   The screen states that rule where the flag sits, because a person who clears
-   it is widening what the report reads. The step also asks for the
-   =concurrency_policy=, which decides the state a run is born in: skip, queue,
-   or fail.
-
-2. *The conventions it binds.* A convention is the set of market terms an
-   instrument is built on: the day count, the calendars, the payment frequency,
-   the index, and the other terms its instrument family fixes before a trade
-   exists. A =conventions= configuration is a reporting row of type
-   =conventions= whose detail lives with =ores.refdata=, so binding it decides
-   what every trade in the run means. The same trade read under two convention
-   sets gives two different numbers, and neither of them is a mistake.
-
-   The reporting model does not name one document per convention kind.
-   =ores_reporting_configurations_tbl= carries a name, a configuration type and
-   an owning component and no document column. The conventions document refdata
-   owns is one document for the party, read with
-   =refdata.v1.conventions_documents.get=, which takes a party and not a
-   configuration, and it holds one vector per convention kind. There is no
-   per-kind choice in a report: conventions are named convention sets, a system
-   holds few of them, and what a set holds is decided in authoring, which is its
-   own UX and is deferred.
-
-   The convention entities live in =projects/ores.refdata/modeling/= as
-   =ores.refdata.<instrument>_convention.org=. There are 25 curated kinds: 25
-   =ores_dq_*_conventions_artefact_tbl= tables and 25 vectors in the conventions
-   document agree. The folder holds 26 models because it also holds
-   =tenor_convention=, which has no curated artefact table.
-   =ores.refdata.bond_yield_convention.org=,
-   =ores.refdata.cds_convention.org= and
-   =ores.refdata.average_ois_convention.org= are three of the 25.
-   =doc/knowledge/journeys/conventions/= states what a convention is, and which
-   reference data lists it picks from.
-
-   The person chooses one convention set the party holds, from the candidates
-   =reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code= returns, and the
-   binding is written with =reporting.v1.report_configurations.put=. This step is
-   one page of sets: a row per set with its name, its purpose, the number of kinds
-   it covers and whether it is the one this report uses, and a radio that chooses
-   it. It draws no per-kind table and no alternative per kind, because what a set
-   holds is decided in authoring. One link leaves the page for that authoring UX,
-   and it is marked as not in this MR. The names, purposes and counts on the page
-   are a fixture: no table stores a set's name or purpose, nothing marks the
-   document a run reads for a kind, and the configuration carries no children.
-   [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/create-a-report/][Create a report]] draws the
-   page, and the story [[id:DE6C0BDA-D12A-4E31-AA86-C323F5A7E016][Name the
-   convention sets a report chooses]] holds the decision and the gaps.
-
-   The binding reaches every instrument family the set covers, on every run of
-   every definition that binds the configuration, and the day count and calendars
-   every analytic reads through it. It creates no convention and edits none, and
-   it names no market data: the reference data lists a convention picks from are
-   untouched.
-
-3. *The pricing engines it binds.* A pricing engine configuration is ORE's
-   =pricingengine.xml=. For each product it names the pricing model, the
-   numerical engine that evaluates the model, and the parameters the two take.
-   Binding it decides how a trade is priced, not what it is priced from: a
-   European swaption mapped to BlackBachelier and a Grid engine carries a
-   different number from the same swaption mapped to LGM and AMC. A product the
-   configuration carries no row for has no model in this run.
-
-   The data lives in =projects/ores.analytics/modeling/=: 
-   =ores.analytics.pricing_model_config.org= is the document,
-   =ores.analytics.pricing_model_product.org= is one row per pricing engine type
-   naming the model and the engine, and
-   =ores.analytics.pricing_model_product_parameter.org= holds the model, engine
-   and global parameters as name and value rows. The person picks one
-   configuration with =reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code=
-   and writes the binding with =reporting.v1.report_configurations.put=.
-
-   *No screen holds a pricing engine configuration.* The application has no route
-   that reads or edits one, and the step states that rather than drawing a link
-   that would not resolve.
-
-   The binding reaches every analytic that prices a trade, npv first and every
-   exposure figure built on it, and the parameters of every product in the
-   document. It does not choose the market data or the curves: a model fits to
-   the curves the run builds, and those belong to the two steps after this one.
-
-4. *The market data it binds.* A today's market configuration is ORE's
-   =todaysmarket.xml=. It holds the data a run prices against as up to
-   twenty-four collections, such as =DiscountingCurves=, =FxSpots= and
-   =SwaptionVolatilities=, each with its own ordered entries. It also holds named
-   configuration blocks, and a block selects one collection of each kind by id,
-   so a report names a coherent set of curves and volatilities instead of
-   restating them. Binding it decides which block each market role reads. The
-   role is ORE's own, pricing and simulation among them, and reporting holds the
-   binding and not the data it names.
-
-   The data lives in =projects/ores.analytics/modeling/=:
-   =ores.analytics.todays_market_collection.org= is one collection with its
-   identity, its kind and its entries;
-   =ores.analytics.todays_market_configuration.org= is one configuration block,
-   and =ores.analytics.todays_market_configuration_binding.org= is one collection
-   reference the block makes. The role a run binds is a row of
-   =ores.reporting.configuration_market_binding=, and the journey's own write for
-   it is =reporting.v1.configuration_market_bindings.put=. The person picks the
-   configuration with
-   =reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code=, and the binding
-   of the definition is written with =reporting.v1.report_configurations.put=.
-
-   *No screen holds a today's market configuration*, so the step states that.
-
-   The binding reaches every price the run produces, and the curves as they are
-   built, because the quotes a curve recipe names come from here. It holds
-   references by name and not prices: the recipe that turns a quote into a curve
-   is the next step's configuration. It does not fix a valuation date either; the
-   date the run reads is a setting of the run settings step.
-
-5. *The curve configuration it binds.* A curve configuration is ORE's
-   =curveconfig.xml=, which is the set of recipes a run builds its curves from. A
-   recipe names a curve, its definition, the segments it is built from, the
-   quotes that feed each segment, and how it is bootstrapped. The document also
-   writes the volatility and correlation sections that the option analytics read.
-   Binding it decides which recipes the run has: without the recipe the curve is
-   not built, whatever the market quotes.
-
-   The data lives in =projects/ores.refdata/modeling/=:
-   =ores.refdata.curve_configuration.org= is the document, its identity and the
-   sections it writes, and the curves themselves are rows of =curve_definition=,
-   with the segments and quotes hanging off those.
-   =ores.refdata.curve_configuration_section.org= is one row per section element
-   the document writes, empty or not, because =BaseCorrelations= and
-   =Correlations= appear empty in the corpus and the export writes them back. A
-   curve configuration is registered as a reporting configuration, which is how a
-   definition binds it.
-
-   *No screen holds a curve configuration*, so the step states that.
-
-   The binding reaches every analytic that discounts, projects or reads a
-   volatility, and it decides what the curves analytic writes, which is the one
-   place where a curve built the wrong way can be seen. It holds no quote, because
-   the quotes are entries of the market data configuration, and it builds nothing:
-   the run builds the curves, and this journey creates no run.
-
-6. *The run settings it binds.* A risk report configuration holds the ORE-level
-   run settings a party shares: the base currency, the observation model, the
-   number of threads, the market data type and date, and the ORE flags such as
-   =continue_on_error= and =imply_todays_fixings=. It also carries the VaR and
-   SIMM settings. Binding it decides how the run behaves rather than what it
-   reads: the currency the figures are stated in, how many threads price them,
-   and what happens to a trade that fails to price.
-
-   The data lives in =projects/ores.reporting/modeling/=:
-   =ores.reporting.risk_report_config.org= is one row per named configuration of
-   a party, and its name is also the name of the reporting configuration a
-   definition binds. =ores.reporting.configuration.org= is that named, reusable
-   configuration, whose kind comes from =configuration_type= by foreign key rather
-   than from a text code.
-
-   *No screen holds a risk report configuration*, so the step states that.
-
-   The configuration also carries the analytics the report runs and the portfolio
-   and book scope. **The scope lives here and not on the definition**, in
-   =ores_reporting_risk_report_config_portfolios_tbl= and
-   =ores_reporting_risk_report_config_books_tbl=, which is why the definition
-   chooses no portfolio: a definition binds a configuration, and the
-   configuration names the portfolio the run reads. Two definitions that bind one
-   configuration read one scope.
-
-   The binding reaches the behaviour of every run of every definition bound to
-   it, the analytics the next step changes, and the scope. It carries no market
-   data, no curve and no model. *No operation in this journey's set writes these
-   settings or the scope*: both come from the seeder, and the step reads them
-   rather than offering a choice.
-
-7. *What it runs.* These are the analytics of the run settings configuration
-   the previous step bound, not of the definition. A
-   =configuration_analytic= row hangs off that configuration, so every
-   definition bound to it runs the same set, and a set that must differ belongs
-   to a configuration of its own. The step reads the vocabulary with
-   =reporting.v1.analytic_types.list= and the set with
-   =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.list_by_configuration_id=, and it names
-   these fourteen analytic types, which are the whole vocabulary: =npv=,
-   =sensitivity=, =cashflow=, =curves=, =simulation=, =saccr=,
-   =parametricVar=, =portfolioDetails=, =creditcurves=, =pfe=, =calibration=,
-   =pnlExplain=, =historicalSimulationVar= and =xva=.
-
-   *The step is a reading and a link, not a second implementation.* It shows the
-   set the configuration currently has: the count that is on, the list with each
-   analytic's =display_order=, a one-line statement of what each produces, and
-   the rows that are on the configuration and off, kept apart from the types that
-   carry no row at all. It also shows the incompatibility state: when =pfe= is on
-   and =simulation= is off, the rule strip states that the set cannot run, both
-   rows are marked, and the save refuses the pair.
-
-   *The analytics are set on Manage the analytics.* That screen owns the whole
-   interaction: the switchboard of every type with the on/off control, the
-   =display_order= and a one-line summary; a step for each analytic that is on,
-   titled with its name, carrying what the analytic is, how it is calculated, and
-   every parameter with a control chosen for the shape of its value, a note on
-   what the parameter means and what a normal value looks like; and a final step
-   that reads the set back. An analytic that takes no parameter says so there. The
-   step links to it, and a build that omits the link would be asking a person to
-   leave the wizard with no way to find the screen that changes the set.
-
-   Turn one off and the write is =active= false, never a deletion: the row keeps
-   its =display_order= and its =configuration_analytic_parameter= rows and reads as
-   off, so a later reader can see the report used to produce it. *No control on
-   either screen deletes a row*. The shared screen asks first before it turns one
-   off, because the parameter values leave its rail with the step.
-
-   =pfe= reads a cube that =simulation= writes, so a report that enables =pfe=
-   without =simulation= cannot work. *This stays a state, not a blocked click*:
-   the rule strip on *What it runs* marks both the =pfe= row and the
-   =simulation= row, the save refuses the pair, and the shared screen refuses the
-   toggle and refuses to read such a set back. The statement is honest about where
-   the rule lives: it is enforced by the ACME seeder, in
-   =generate_risk_config_data.py=, function
-   =check_exposure_needs_simulation=, and *nothing in the reporting service
-   validates it when a definition is written*. A caller that does not use this
-   screen can write the combination today, and the run fails later.
-
-   The analytic rows hang off the configuration, and the configuration is
-   shared, so the step states which other definitions bind the same configuration
-   and would run the changed analytic set from their next run. This is the one
-   place in the journey where a person's local choice reaches rows they did not
-   open, and the step says so rather than leaving it in a note.
-
-8. [@8] *Review and save.* The final step states every value before the write: the
-   name, the description, the report type, the official flag, the five bindings,
-   the analytics with their =active= and =display_order= as the bound
-   configuration holds them, the parameter values, and the portfolio scope. The
-   analytics and their settings are read here and written on the shared screen;
-   this journey writes neither. On confirmation the screen sends
-   =reporting.v1.report_definitions.put= for the definition, after the binding
-   writes of the steps before it. The definition is written on
-   demand: =schedule_expression= is empty and =scheduler_job_id= is null. Its
-   =fsm_state_id= is null until first activation, =run_grant_id= is null until the
-   grant is created at admission, =pre_processing= is =execute=,
-   =prepared_input_key= is empty, =post_processing= is =execute=, and
-   =concurrency_policy= is the policy the person chose. Then the screen reads the
-   definition back with =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= and shows the stored
-   row rather than the values the person typed, so the new row reads beside the
-   party's other definitions. The definition is bitemporal, so an edit writes a new version and a
-   past run keeps the version it ran under.
-
-   It has never run. There is no =report_instance= for it, so the front door
-   draws it as never run, which is a state
-   [[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]]
-   already draws for the definitions the seed writes. =run_grant_id= is empty:
-   the grant every run acts under is created at admission, by whichever act needs
-   it first, scheduling or a person asking, so a definition that has never been
-   scheduled can still run on demand.
-
-   This step is final, so *Back is refused from it*, and the rail says so: the
-   mark beside the review carries the final flag, and the step offers no Back
-   ([[id:166B2D77-6D04-47D5-A651-5431E1F2E082][UX Language]], section *The
-   rail*). Once the review has stated every value and the definition is written,
-   there is no earlier state to return to. From here the person either stops, with
-   a definition they can run when they want, or goes on to
-   [[id:933649DD-1F86-4B40-99FD-1D4316D39A46][Choose when a report runs]] and
-   gives it a recurrence. This journey writes no schedule, and nothing here makes
-   the report produce anything: it creates the definition that a run or a
-   schedule then uses.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen on the standard steps UI: the rail the system bootstrap journey draws,
-with the step list as its only source. The rail is fixed at eight steps, and it
-does not move while the person works: *What it is*, *The conventions it binds*,
-*The pricing engines it binds*, *The market data it binds*, *The curve
-configuration it binds*, *The run settings it binds*, *What it runs*, then
-*Review and save*. The configuration steps follow the order
-=report_type_configuration_types= states and the seeder writes. The rail marks
-each entry done, current or ahead, and it knows position only: it cannot say how
-many items a save would refuse. The step foot carries Back unless going back is
-refused, which it is at the first step and at a final step
-([[id:6A63AAC7-4869-493A-97E7-55B919874784][Journey runtime]]); the review is
-final, so it draws no Back at all.
-
-A second screen holds the analytic interaction:
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/][Manage the analytics]].
-It is where the set is built, where every parameter is set, and where the pair
-=pfe= and =simulation= is refused. *What it runs* reads the set that screen
-leaves and links to it.
-
-The screen writes two kinds of row and reads each one back: the definition and
-its bindings. The analytic rows and the parameter rows are read and named, and
-written on the shared screen. Two of its answers are absences it must state
-rather than draw round. The first is the checklist: the screen can name the
-configuration types the report type requires, and it cannot name what else a run
-needs. The second is the analytic rule: the rule strip on *What it runs*, the
-marks on both rows and the refused save exist because the seeder enforces that
-pair, and no service check exists to point at. A third is where the configuration
-data lives: only conventions has a screen, and the other four are stated as
-missing. Each configuration step therefore carries its own explanation, its own
-picker, its own answer about the screen, and what the binding reaches.
-
-=?step=N= is numeric over the eight steps, and it is stable, because the rail does
-not move. =?pfe=without-simulation= opens the draft with the rule broken, so the
-rule strip on *What it runs* can be read without changing two rows by hand.
-Nothing here carries an analytic's step number, because an analytic has no step on
-this screen.
-
-#+caption: Create a report on the standard rail: what it is, one step for each of the five configurations it binds, the analytics the bound configuration carries, and review and save. The analytics step reads the set and links to the screen that manages it.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_create_a_report.png]]
-
-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/create-a-report/][prototype]] draws this
-journey on the standard steps UI, and
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/create-a-report.org][its design note]] says what
-it follows and what is fake. It belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/create-a-report/=.
-
-The analytics are not drawn there. They are set on
-[[file:../../prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/][Manage the
-analytics]], which the journey links and which owns the whole analytic
-interaction. Its [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics.org][design
-note]] says what it argues.
-
-The prototype must draw the rail the system bootstrap journey uses, with done,
-current and ahead marks and no Back on the final step, and it must be eight
-steps: what it is, one step for each of the five configuration types, the
-analytics the bound configuration carries, and the final review, all numbered from
-one list. It must draw one step for each of the five configuration types, each
-with what binding a configuration of that type means, where its data lives, the
-picker, and what the binding reaches. *What it runs* must be the read-only
-summary of the set the bound configuration carries: the count that is on, the list
-with their =display_order=, the rows kept off, the broken =pfe=/=simulation= pair
-as a visible state with the rule stated and the seeder named as where it lives,
-and the link to the shared screen. It must draw the scope read off the bound
-configuration, since no operation writes it, and a review that names the field
-values rather than counting them. It must label every drawn value a fixture,
-because no operation here creates a report and no service check exists for the
-analytic rule it refuses.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_definition= | The row this journey creates: =name=, =description=, =report_type=, =is_official=, =concurrency_policy=, =pre_processing=, =prepared_input_key=, =post_processing=, and the =fsm_state_id= and =run_grant_id= that stay empty until a run | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =report_configuration= | One row per configuration the definition binds, where the configuration type is the slot | [[id:7F2C8A41-6E93-4B57-A0D4-3C9E1B5D7826][ores.reporting.report_configuration]] |
-| =configuration= | The named, reusable configuration the party holds, and the component that owns its detail | =ores.reporting.configuration= |
-| =configuration_analytic= | The analytics the configuration runs: =analytic_type_code=, =display_order= and =active= | =ores.reporting.configuration_analytic= |
-| =configuration_analytic_parameter= | One setting of one analytic: =parameter_name=, =value= and its position | =ores.reporting.configuration_analytic_parameter= |
-| =analytic_type= | The vocabulary the picker offers | =ores.reporting.analytic_type= |
-| =report_type_configuration_type= | The configuration types a report type cannot start without, which is the checklist half the screen can show | =ores.reporting.report_type_configuration_type= |
-| =risk_report_config= | The run settings a party shares, and the portfolio and book scope the definition reads | =ores.reporting.risk_report_config= |
-| =party= | The owner of the definition, fixed from the session | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-| =portfolio= | The scope the report reads | [[id:282C87C1-11E1-42F0-BEE6-D6983A5F836B][ores.refdata.portfolio]] |
-
-The definition is the row the journey creates and the other rows are what it
-reaches: a binding names a configuration, the configuration owns the analytics,
-and each analytic owns its parameters. That chain is why *What it runs* says whose
-rows the analytics are, and why it links to the screen that changes them. A person
-who changes the analytic set of a shared configuration changes what every
-definition binding it runs, and no copy stands between them. It is also why the
-set on *What it runs* is a reading of
-=configuration_analytic.display_order= on the configuration the person bound, so
-the same report set up against another configuration reads a different set.
-
-The scope is two levels down that chain: =risk_report_config= holds it in
-=ores_reporting_risk_report_config_portfolios_tbl= and
-=ores_reporting_risk_report_config_books_tbl=, keyed by that row. The definition
-carries no portfolio field at all.
-
-Every row above carries =party_id= and is party-scoped by row-level security. The
-definition is bitemporal, so an edit writes a new version and a past run keeps
-the version it ran under. The analytic rows and their parameters are temporal
-too: turning an analytic off sets =active= false and writes a version, so the
-row stays readable.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| What it is | The configuration types the report type requires | =reporting.v1.report_type_configuration_types.list= | exists |
-| Every configuration step | The configurations of one type the party holds | =reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code= | exists |
-| Every configuration step | Every configuration the party holds | =reporting.v1.configurations.list= | exists |
-| Every configuration step | Bind one configuration in its slot | =reporting.v1.report_configurations.put= | exists |
-| What it runs | The analytic vocabulary the summary names | =reporting.v1.analytic_types.list= | exists |
-| What it runs | Read the analytics of the configuration | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.list_by_configuration_id= | exists |
-| What it runs | Read the settings of the analytics that are on | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytic_parameters.list_by_configuration_analytic_id= | exists |
-| Manage the analytics, the switchboard and each analytic step | Write the whole analytic set at once | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytics.put_many= | exists |
-| Manage the analytics, each analytic step | Write one setting of one analytic | =reporting.v1.configuration_analytic_parameters.put= | exists |
-| The market data it binds | Bind a market role to a today's market configuration | =reporting.v1.configuration_market_bindings.put= | exists |
-| Review and save | Write the definition | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.put= | exists |
-| Review and save | Read the definition back | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| The run settings it binds | Choose the portfolio the report reads | (no operation writes the portfolio scope) | missing |
-| The run settings it binds | Read what a portfolio scope is | (no operation reads =risk_report_config='s scope) | missing |
-| What it runs, the shared screen, and the save | Refuse =pfe= without =simulation= | (no service check; the rule lives in the ACME seeder) | missing |
-| What it is | Ask what else a run requires, beyond the configuration types | (no operation answers it) | missing |
-| (no step) | Create a report from the browser | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-This journey writes two things here: a definition and its bindings. A person
-creating the next report runs the same writes again. The definition write is the
-only one that creates the row the front door then lists; the binding writes
-attach what the definition reads. The analytic rows and their parameters are
-written on Manage the analytics, and *What it runs* reads them.
-=configuration_analytics.put_many= is the one write of the analytic set there:
-turning a type on writes its row with the default value of each parameter, and
-turning one off writes =active= false and nothing else.
-
-Nothing in this journey's set creates a configuration. The person chooses among
-the ones the party already holds, which is why a party that holds none of a
-configuration type cannot finish this journey, and why *What is missing* records
-that gap rather than the screen drawing a Create button.
-
-Two of these writes reach rows the person did not open. A binding is shared with
-every definition that binds the same configuration, and an analytic row belongs
-to the configuration rather than to the definition, so the shared screen changes
-the next run of every definition binding it. The journey states this and no
-operation warns about it. Each configuration step states how many definitions
-already bind the configuration the person picks, and *What it runs* repeats the
-count for the run settings the analytics came from.
-
-No BFF route serves this screen. The prototype adds one, for example
-=POST /api/reporting/reports= for the definition and its bindings,
-=GET /api/reporting/reports/<definition-id>= for the read-back, and
-=GET /api/reporting/report-types/<report-type>/configuration-types= for the
-checklist half the screen can show. The handler authenticates the caller's token
-and checks a report-definition write code, which does not exist yet.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *Nothing validates the rule between two analytics.* =pfe= reads a cube that
-   =simulation= writes. That rule lives in the ACME seeder,
-   =generate_risk_config_data.py=, function =check_exposure_needs_simulation=,
-   and it is a guard over the seed's own data, not a constraint on the database
-   and not a check in the reporting service. A definition written by any other
-   caller can enable =pfe= without =simulation=, and nothing refuses it. The run
-   then fails, later, on the grid. The two screens this journey describes can
-   refuse the pair, and they cannot make the refusal true for callers that do not
-   use them. A report also needs at least one analytic: a run with none produces
-   nothing, and nothing states that either.
-2. *No operation answers what a report needs in order to run.*
-   =reporting.v1.report_type_configuration_types.list= names the configuration
-   types a report type cannot start without, and that is all. Nothing names the
-   analytics a run must enable, the inputs each analytic reads, or the pairs that
-   cannot work together. A screen therefore cannot show the full checklist a
-   definition must satisfy, and it cannot answer the person's question "can it
-   actually run" before the run. It can only show what it bound.
-3. *No operation writes or reads the portfolio scope.* The scope lives on the
-   =risk_report_config= row, in
-   =ores_reporting_risk_report_config_portfolios_tbl= and
-   =ores_reporting_risk_report_config_books_tbl=, and no operation in this
-   journey's set touches either table. The scope a definition reads is the scope
-   of the configuration it binds, and that configuration is built by the seeder.
-   A person who needs a scope no configuration carries cannot state it here.
-4. *Nothing creates the run settings inside a =risk_report_config=.* The base
-   currency, the observation model, the VaR and SIMM settings and the threading
-   are columns of a row this journey cannot write. When the party holds no
-   configuration with the settings a new report needs, the journey stops.
-5. *The refusal to save =pfe= without =simulation= is the screen's own rule.*
-   Manage the analytics draws it as a refusal, and this journey's save refuses the
-   pair too. A build would have to keep that rule in both screens, since no service
-   check exists, and a second client would have to keep it again. Consolidating
-   the analytic interaction into one prototype removes the third copy, and it does
-   not remove the second: the save is still this journey's.
-6. *No BFF route serves reporting, and nothing in the application creates a
-   report today.* Every definition that exists was seeded. This journey's screen,
-   its review, its read-back and its refusals are new, and it has no row in any
-   build to attach to.
-7. *No write permission is named for creating a definition.* The reads in this
-   journey's set are gated by the reporting service's read codes. No code names
-   the right to create a definition or to change a shared configuration's
-   analytics, and a person who may write one and not the other cannot be told
-   apart. The tenant administrator holds =*= and reaches everything.
-8. *The analytic set has no draft behind it, and it is written from another
-    screen.* Turning an analytic on writes its =configuration_analytic= row on the
-    shared configuration at once, and a parameter typed on its step writes a
-    =configuration_analytic_parameter= row at once, because those are the
-    operations the journey's set holds. No operation stages an analytic set for
-    one definition, and no operation undoes the writes of a screen that was given
-    up. A person creating a report therefore changes rows other definitions read
-    before the definition is saved, and this journey cannot stage that change or
-    take it back.
-9. *This screen cannot tell whether the analytics were changed, or when.* The
-    link to the shared screen is a link: it carries no state and reports nothing
-    on return. A person who leaves the wizard, changes the set, and comes back sees
-    the new set on *What it runs*, and the review states it, but nothing says
-    whether that screen was opened at all, by whom, or how long ago. The same is
-    true of a set another person changed while this one was working.
-10. *No operation orders the summary, and =display_order= is not an identity.*
-    =configuration_analytic.display_order= orders the list on *What it runs* and
-    the steps on the shared screen, and turning one analytic off leaves the order
-    of the others alone. No route, link or operation in the application carries an
-    analytic's position: nothing outside the shared screen can point at "step 9"
-    and still be right after the next change. The shared screen offers
-    =?analytic=<code>= for that reason, and this journey offers nothing of the
-    kind.
-11. *The rail cannot say that the set it reads is not fit to run.* The runtime's
-    rail marks position only: done, current or ahead. A report whose bound
-    configuration cannot run looks exactly like a report whose configuration can,
-    so the state is carried by the rule strip on *What it runs*, by the marks on
-    two rows and by the refused save, and nowhere on the rail itself.

-#+title: User Journey: Find out why a run went wrong
-#+description: A person opens one run's errors and places every one of them by scope and subject, down to the trade, the analytic or the curve the engine named.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-+#+updated: 2026-10-17
-+#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A person opens one run's errors and places every one of them by scope and subject, down to the trade, the analytic or the curve the engine named.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"The numbers are wrong, or the run failed. Tell me which trade, which analytic
-and which curve." The person has a run whose answer they do not trust, and they
-want the run's own account of what went wrong. They want every error the run
-recorded, each one placed on the thing it names, and they want to see when two
-errors are about the same trade for two different reasons. The journey is done
-when the person can point at a trade, an analytic or a curve and say what the
-engine said about it.
-
-This is the journey that carries the error model. Every row it shows is an event
-the run wrote, and the screen's job is to place the row, not to explain it.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-Three actors read this screen. The engineer reads it to place a failure in the
-engine: which analytic, which curve, which trade. The market risk reader reads
-it because a number they must sign off is suspect, and needs to know whether the
-run's answer is complete. The tenant administrator reads it because a report
-they own has failed, and needs to know whether the cause is the report or the
-data behind it. All three read the same rows; the permissions decide who can.
-
-The trigger is doubt. A run completed while carrying errors, a run failed, or a
-number does not look right and somebody follows the number back to the run. The
-person arrives from a health row on
-[[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]], from
-a terminal panel on
-[[id:76431668-8656-4276-9F9B-F292FE45B2CA][Run a report and watch it finish]],
-or from the output screen of
-[[id:969C14D2-4280-4D7C-8F51-1D395B521C83][Read what a run produced]]. The
-journey ends when every error row has a home, or when the person knows that some
-rows name nothing below the run.
-
-This is a read-only journey. Errors are immutable, written once and never
-changed, and the screen creates nothing. A run's errors are read as a group,
-because one error rarely tells the story on its own.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Open the run's errors.* The person opens the errors from the run. The header
-   states the run, its definition, its state when it finished, when it completed
-   and when the errors were collected. An error carries =event_time=, the instant
-   the errors were collected from the run's output, and no actor: the run already
-   names who asked for it. The screen shows the collection time once, in the
-   header, and the rows share it.
-2. *Read the shape of the run before reading a row.* The summary counts the
-   errors by severity and by scope. Severities are exactly =error= and
-   =warning=. Scopes are exactly =Trade=, =Analytics=, =Curve=, =Configuration=
-   and =Report=. The counts are the first diagnosis, because the same report
-   produced two shapes. A clean run of it recorded eleven rows: eight
-   =Analytics= errors and three =Configuration= warnings. The run whose market
-   data was removed recorded twenty: one =Curve= error, sixteen =Trade= errors
-   across eight trades and two analytics, two =Analytics= errors and one
-   =Analytics= warning. The summary tells the person which shape they are
-   looking at, and so which question to ask.
-3. *Read a row.* Every row states a =severity=, a =scope_code=, a =message= and
-   a =subject= with a =subject_id=. The message is the engine's own words,
-   unaltered; the screen shows it as it is and does not translate it. The scope
-   is the engine's own group name, and it says what kind of thing the error is
-   about. The subject is the particular thing, and it names that thing in full
-   or names none. A row never names half a subject: a subject without an id, or
-   an id without a subject, is not a row the model admits.
-4. *Place the row by its subject.* The subject is a discriminator and a value
-   because the ids are of different kinds. A trade's id is a UUID. A curve's id
-   is a free-text name, for example =[IndexCurve(GBP-SONIA,Yield/GBP/GBP1D)]=.
-   The pair is not a database foreign key: the engine names its own trades and
-   curves, and neither is a key any table holds. The screen therefore treats the
-   subject as a label and a value to copy and filter by, not as a link that
-   always resolves. A person can ask for every error about one trade id, or one
-   curve name, and the screen answers with the rows that carry it.
-5. *See one trade fail twice.* This is the step the screen exists for. A trade
-   that will not build can fail in more than one analytic, and each failure is
-   its own row. Two rows then have the same scope, =Trade=, the same subject and
-   =subject_id=, the same trade UUID, and the same message,
-   =Cannot build all required curves! Building failed for:
-   ([IndexCurve(GBP-SONIA,Yield/GBP/GBP1D)])=. Only =detail= tells them apart:
-   one carries ={"exceptionType": "Error building trade for context
-   'analytic/PRICING'"}=, the other ={"exceptionType": "Error building trade for
-   context 'analytic/SA_CCR'"}=. The screen must show the detail beside the
-   message and must never de-duplicate rows by message, scope and subject. A
-   list that collapsed them would report one error where the run recorded two,
-   and it would hide the second analytic — which is the fact the engineer needs.
-6. *Follow the curve.* The curve error is the root the trade errors point at. It
-   carries scope =Curve=, severity =error=, subject =curve=, the subject id
-   =[IndexCurve(GBP-SONIA,Yield/GBP/GBP1D)]=, and the message =yield curve
-   building failed for curve(s) Yield/GBP/GBP1D on date 2026-10-15 while
-   processing Yield/GBP/GBP1D=. A person who filters by that curve name sees the
-   curve row and the trade rows that name the same curve in their messages. The
-   screen does not claim the trades caused the curve failure or the reverse; it
-   shows that the engine said both.
-7. *Read the analytic row.* An analytic error names the analytic as its subject,
-   for example =PRICING=, with the message =Portfolio does not contain any built
-   trades, context is 'analytic/PRICING'=. A warning can name the application
-   rather than a portfolio object, for example subject_id =OREApp::run()= with
-   the message =Error in ORE analytics: Failed to run analytics
-   PRICING,SA_CCR=. The two are both scope =Analytics= and they are not the same
-   kind of statement: one is about the analytic's portfolio, the other is the
-   application's summary of the run. The subject and the severity separate them.
-8. *Read the configuration warning.* A =Configuration= warning names an input
-   that belongs to no one trade, for example subject =configuration=, subject_id
-   =Counterparty=, message =Input configuration was not provided. The default
-   values will be used for all netting sets in the portfolio=. It is a warning:
-   the run continued with defaults, and a reader who signs the numbers off needs
-   to know the defaults were used. The screen does not present it as a trade
-   error because it names no trade.
-9. *Read the Report scope.* Some failures happen before the engine sees the run.
-   The model states a scope of =Report= for exactly that, because a run can fail
-   for a reason no engine saw. A =Report= row names no subject: the row names
-   the run itself. The screen shows it at the top of the list, stated as an error
-   about the run, and never as a row about an unnamed trade.
-10. *Understand what the rows can and cannot say.* The rows place a failure;
-    they do not explain it. The curve row says the curve would not build on a
-    date, and it cannot say that the market data for that date was removed. The
-    screen stops at what the engine said. A person who needs the cause follows
-    the curve name to the market data that should have built it, or follows the
-    run's step failure to the workflow, and both are outside this screen.
-11. *Leave, or go on.* The person opens the run's output to see what the archive
-    does contain, or returns to the front door to see whether the next run
-    cleared the errors. A failure that needs a reproduction continues in the
-    compute journeys, where the job behind the run is followed.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen. The run header, the summary by severity and scope, the subject
-filter, the row index and the expanded rows are panels of the same screen,
-because the person reads them as one answer. The screen is read-only: it creates
-nothing, changes nothing and destroys nothing.
-
-The row index is deliberately redundant with the expanded rows: the index is how
-a person sees that two rows are identical except for their detail, and the
-expanded rows are how they read the detail. The wireframe draws the two Trade
-rows one after the other, with the same scope, subject, subject id and message,
-and different detail. That is the design rule this screen must not lose.
-
-#+caption: Find out why a run went wrong: the summary by scope, the row index, and two Trade rows that only detail tells apart.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_find_out_why_a_run_went_wrong.png]]
-
-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong/][prototype]] argues this journey in three interpretations, and [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong.org][its design note]] says what each argues and what is fake. This journey is the design intent for the run's error screen, and its
-prototype belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong/=. The prototype must
-draw a run whose market data was removed, with its twenty rows: one =Curve=
-error, sixteen =Trade= errors across eight trades and two analytics, two
-=Analytics= errors and one =Analytics= warning. It must draw the two Trade rows
-with the same trade UUID and the same message and different =detail=, and make
-the difference visible without opening a row. It must also draw a clean run that
-still records eleven rows — eight =Analytics= errors and three =Configuration=
-warnings — so that "carrying errors" is not mistaken for "failed", and a run
-whose only rows are =Report= scope rows with no subject.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_error_event= | One error: =severity=, =scope_code=, =message=, =subject=, =subject_id=, =detail=, =event_time= and the run it belongs to | [[id:080B3871-8BAA-4AAA-A98F-3E79F4B83BAA][ores.reporting.report_error_event]] |
-| =report_error_scope= | The scope vocabulary the row's =scope_code= comes from, with the engine's own code for each | [[id:FF774B04-12E6-4BDF-B94C-222095651C4F][ores.reporting.report_error_scope]] |
-| =report_instance= | The run the errors belong to: its name, its state, its =completed_at= and its definition | [[id:9FCCF6C8-9C10-403B-BDA4-C3E28706BD67][ores.reporting.report_instance]] |
-| =report_definition= | The report whose run produced the errors, so a reader knows what was being computed | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the run and its errors | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-The error is the row. Its =report_instance_id= is the run, and a run's errors
-are the rows that name it: they are read as a group, never one error as the
-answer. The scope is a lookup on =scope_code=, so the screen reads the scope
-vocabulary once and labels every row from it. The subject is not a lookup and
-not a foreign key: it is a discriminator and a value, and the screen keeps the
-pair together.
-
-Every entity above carries =party_id= and is party-scoped by row-level security.
-The error event and the trigger event are immutable events; the error is written
-once when the run's output is read, and it is never edited afterwards. The run
-and the definition are bitemporal, so the definition the run used is the run's
-own record even after the definition changes.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Open the errors | Read the run | =reporting.v1.report_instances.get= | exists |
-| Open the errors | List the run's errors as a group | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id= | exists |
-| Open the errors | List the errors the party holds | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list= | exists |
-| Read a row | Read one error | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.get= | exists |
-| Read a row | Read many errors at once | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.get_many= | exists |
-| Read the scopes | List the scope vocabulary | =reporting.v1.report_error_scopes.list= | exists |
-| Read the scopes | Read one scope | =reporting.v1.report_error_scopes.get= | exists |
-| Read the scopes | Read many scopes at once | =reporting.v1.report_error_scopes.get_many= | exists |
-| Read the definition | Read the report behind the run | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Watch the errors | Learn that a run gained errors | =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.updated= | exists |
-| Watch the errors | Learn that an error row was written | (no event for =report_error_event=) | missing |
-| The failed step | Read why a run failed before the engine saw it | (no reporting read; the steps live in =ores.workflow=) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Read a run's errors from the browser | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-The error reads are generated from =report_error_event=, and the list by report
-instance is the one this journey uses. The scopes are a simple lookup. Every read
-is gated: =reporting::report_error_events:read= for the rows and
-=reporting::report_error_scopes:read= for the vocabulary, with
-=reporting::report_instances:read= for the run. The two error codes are held by
-no role below =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=, which hold =*=.
-
-The error model's own consequence is visible in the table. There is no read of
-=report_trigger_event=, so the screen cannot say who triggered the run; the
-run's =trigger_id= names the trigger event, and nothing resolves it. There is no
-event for an error row, so a screen showing a finished run finds new errors only
-by re-reading the list. And there is no read that says which workflow step
-failed, so a =Report= row says the run failed and not where.
-
-No BFF route serves this screen. The prototype adds one, for example
-=GET /api/reporting/runs/<run-id>/errors=, which returns the rows with their
-scope labels and the summary by severity and scope. The handler authenticates
-the caller's token and checks the error read codes.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *A route and a screen.* No BFF route serves reporting, and nothing in the web
-   application shows a report today. The errors screen, its summary and its
-   subject filter are new.
-2. *The error permissions sit too high.* =reporting::report_error_events:read=
-   and =reporting::report_error_scopes:read= are held by no role below
-   =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=, which hold =*=. The trading desk and the
-   market risk reader can run a report and cannot read its errors, so this
-   journey is closed to two of its three actors until a role below the tenant
-   administrator is granted the read. This is the group's most important
-   permission gap.
-3. *No aggregate read.* The summary by severity and scope is computed from the
-   rows. A run with twenty rows is fine; a screen that summarises errors across
-   runs has no grouped read and would page every row to count it.
-4. *No event for an error row.* The model writes errors once, and there is no
-   =report_error_event= change event. A screen open on a running run cannot be
-   told that errors arrived; it waits for the run's update and re-reads. That is
-   acceptable for a run that writes its errors before finalisation, and it is
-   not a general answer.
-5. *A trade id does not resolve to a trade.* The error names a trade UUID, and
-   the pair is deliberately not a database foreign key: the engine names its own
-   trades, and no table here holds that key. The screen can copy and filter the
-   id, and it cannot link to the trade. A resolver from the engine's trade id to
-   the platform's trade is the missing piece, and it is not in this model.
-6. *A curve id is free text.* =[IndexCurve(GBP-SONIA,Yield/GBP/GBP1D)]= is a
-   name the engine writes, not a row this platform owns. The screen can filter by
-   the exact string and cannot follow it to the market data curve that should
-   have built it. The market data journey is where that link belongs.
-7. *No actor on the error, and no read of the actor on the run.* The model is
-   right that an error carries no actor, because the run names who asked for it.
-   The run reaches that person through =trigger_id=, and no read of
-   =report_trigger_event= exists. The screen therefore cannot show who triggered
-   the failing run, which is the first question an operator asks.
-8. *A =Report= row does not name the step.* The model states =Report= for a
-   failure no engine saw, and it names no subject. It does not say which
-   workflow step failed. The steps live in =ores.workflow= and no reporting read
-   serves them, so the row says the run failed and not where.
-9. *The errors have no diagnosis.* The engine's message is the engine's own
-   words, and the platform holds no explanation of them. The screen must not
-   invent a cause; the engineer reads the message and the detail, and follows
-   the subject out of the screen.
