-#+title: User Journey: Look back over a report's history
-#+description: A person opens one report definition's run history, reads the runs newest first with each run's started and completed time, sees the last five fire times, opens any earlier run, and learns without losing their place that a newer run has arrived.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A person opens one report definition's run history, reads the runs newest first with each run's started and completed time, sees the last five fire times, opens any earlier run, and learns without losing their place that a newer run has arrived.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"What did this report produce over the last few weeks, and is what I am looking
-at the newest one?" The person has a report open. They want an earlier run, or
-they left a run open and need to know whether it is still current. They open the
-history of that one report definition and read its runs newest first. Every run
-carries the time it started and the time it completed, and the newest run is
-marked *latest*, so the second half of the question has one answer on the
-screen and not an inference.
-
-The journey is done when the person has either found the earlier run they came
-for, or has confirmed that the run in front of them is the newest one. A person
-who leaves the screen with a run still open is told when a newer run arrives,
-and the screen does not move under their hands to show it.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-Three actors read the same screen. A trading desk or a market risk reader has
-been reading a report and wants an earlier run: the one from the morning the
-trading desk first noticed the numbers move, or the run a colleague quoted. A
-reader who left a run open over lunch needs to know whether that run is still
-the newest one before they sign off. An engineer compares a good run against a
-bad one, to place the change between them.
-
-The trigger is a specific question about a specific report. The person arrives
-from the report, not from a global list of runs: the history is the history of
-one report definition, and its runs belong to that definition alone. The
-journey begins when the person opens the history of that definition and ends
-when they have read the run they came for, or have been told that a newer one
-has arrived.
-
-This is a read-only journey. It creates nothing, changes nothing and destroys
-nothing. It reads the one definition, the runs of that definition, the errors of
-the run the person opens, and it subscribes to the run change events so a run
-that arrives while the screen is open is signalled in place.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Open the history of the report.* The person is reading a report and asks for
-   its history. The screen is the history of one report definition: a header
-   that names the definition, the party that owns it, its report type, its
-   schedule expression and its owner, and below it the runs of that definition.
-   The header is what makes the scope unmistakable: a person reading a run row
-   can see that the row belongs to *this* report and no other. There is no route
-   to a list of runs across the tenant in this journey, and the screen does not
-   offer one.
-2. *Read the runs newest first, and the trend above them.* The runs are ordered
-   by =started_at=, descending, so the first row is the newest run the definition
-   produced. Every row states two timestamps and labels them: *Started* and
-   *Completed*. Above the list the screen plots the series: a line of the
-   report's exposure across the runs, oldest to newest, with the latest run's
-   point marked and named, because a history is a change over time and a line is
-   the form for one. The value axis states the range it spans, and the exact
-   numbers are in a table under the plot. The screen has a plot vocabulary and a
-   stated rule that chooses between its forms: a donut for one whole in few
-   parts, stacked bars for several wholes each split the same way, grouped bars
-   for two series over the same categories, and a scatter for two measures
-   against each other. That rule draws the latest run's problems by scope as a
-   donut, the same problems across the runs as stacked bars, the errors against
-   the warnings as grouped bars, and the time a run took against the positions it
-   placed as a scatter. A run whose figure the errors left partial is drawn
-   hollow and dashed, carries the same =partial= marking its row carries, and the
-   caption names what its errors exclude; a run that failed produced no figure at
-   all, so the line breaks at it instead of drawing a zero. A report whose
-   history holds one run has no trend on the screen, and the panel says why
-   rather than plotting a point.
-   =started_at= is shown because it is the only time a run in flight has, and
-   because it is the field the order and the latest marker use; a failed run
-   has a start and a finish, and a run that is still going has a start alone.
-   =completed_at= is shown because it answers when the output was ready, and it
-   is the difference a person reads when they ask why the report was late. A run
-   that has not completed states a dash in *Completed* and does not state a
-   guessed time.
-3. *See which run is latest.* The newest run carries the word *latest* in the
-   first cell of its row, in the accent tone, and the marker follows
-   =started_at= exactly as the order does. Two timestamps on a row could leave a
-   reader asking which one makes the run newest, so the screen states the rule
-   once, beside the timestamps: the newest run is the run that started last. The
-   marker must never be inferred from colour alone, from position alone, or from
-   the completion time.
-4. *See the previous fire times.* Above the runs, the screen states the last
-   five fire times of the definition, each with its date and its time. The date
-   is what lets a person tell a report that fires every hour from one that fires
-   once a day, and a gap in the five shows a window the definition did not run
-   in. The five are *derived from the runs that exist*, and the screen says so,
-   because no read of =report_trigger_event= exists: a firing that produced no
-   run is not in the list, and the screen cannot say whether that window was
-   missing, skipped by the concurrency policy, or refused. That sentence is part
-   of the panel and not fine print.
-5. *Open any historical run.* Every row opens its run, whichever way the run
-   ended. A run that failed opens with its state, its times and its errors. A
-   run that completed while carrying errors opens the same way, and the errors
-   are part of the answer rather than a warning on the way in. A run that is
-   still going opens with its start time and no completion. Opening a run keeps
-   the history visible, so the person can compare it against the rows around it
-   without going back.
-6. *Leave a run open while a new run arrives.* A report that fires on a schedule
-   produces runs while the screen is open. When the change notification for a
-   new run of this definition arrives, =Refresh= draws the eye and a notice —
-   not a modal — says that the run the person has open is no longer the latest,
-   names the new run's start time, and offers a way to it. The screen does not
-   navigate on its own and does not take focus. A person who is reading a
-   number keeps their place, and a person who wants the new run takes it with
-   one press.
-7. *Reload, and see what changed.* When the person reloads, the runs newer than
-   the previous load are marked for three seconds, so the rows that appeared
-   while they were away are the rows their eye lands on. The first load marks
-   nothing, because nothing arrived. A person can turn the marking off, and the
-   choice is theirs rather than the screen's.
-8. *Leave, or go on.* The person opens what the run produced, or reads why it
-   went wrong, or goes back to the report. Those are the group's other
-   journeys: [[id:969C14D2-4280-4D7C-8F51-1D395B521C83][Read what a run
-   produced]] and [[id:F58B0FB5-3FD8-4BEB-982E-E54D284C0539][Find out why a run
-   went wrong]]. The history itself creates nothing, and a reader without a
-   write permission sees the same rows.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen. The definition header, the previous fire times, the run list and the
-open run are panels of that screen, because the person reads them as one answer
-about one report. The screen is read-only. Every run row carries its two
-timestamps, its health word and its error count, so no row needs opening to be
-told apart from its neighbours; opening a run adds the detail the row cannot
-carry.
-
-#+caption: Look back over a report's history: the last five fire times derived from runs, the runs newest first with started and completed times, the latest run marked, an earlier run open, and the notice that a newer run has arrived.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_look_back_over_a_reports_history.png]]
-
-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/look-back-over-a-reports-history/][prototype]] argues this journey in three interpretations, and [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/look-back-over-a-reports-history.org][its design note]] says what each argues and what is fake. This journey is the design intent for a report's history, and its prototype belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/look-back-over-a-reports-history/=, with hyphens
-because the inventory gate reads the directory name as a link.
-
-The prototype must draw three structural readings of the same history: a list of
-runs with the selected run read below it, a timeline that shows the rhythm of the
-schedule, and a comparison of the latest run against one earlier run. In all three
-it plots the series above the runs: a line of exposure with the latest run marked
-and named, the range of its value axis stated, its exact numbers in a table beneath
-it, and the =partial= marking on every point a run's errors left incomplete. In all
-three, every run states its started and completed time, the newest run is marked
-*latest*, the last five fire times are visible with the sentence that they are
-derived from runs, and any run can be opened. The prototype must also simulate
-the arrival of a new run, because a static page cannot receive an event, and
-must then follow the Recency pattern of the
-[[id:00BA1689-B060-4BD8-BC46-67034D663B7F][UX]] standard: the refresh control
-draws the eye, a notice says the open run is no longer the latest, the page
-neither navigates nor takes focus, and a reload marks the new rows for three
-seconds unless the person has turned the marking off.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_definition= | The header: name, party, report type, schedule expression, scheduler job and owner. The history is of one definition, so the definition is the scope of every row | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =report_instance= | One row of the history: state, =started_at=, =completed_at=, =output_message= and =output_storage_key=. The order, the latest marker and both timestamps come from here | [[id:9FCCF6C8-9C10-403B-BDA4-C3E28706BD67][ores.reporting.report_instance]] |
-| =report_error_event= | The errors of the run the person opens: severity, scope, message and subject | [[id:080B3871-8BAA-4AAA-A98F-3E79F4B83BAA][ores.reporting.report_error_event]] |
-| =report_instance_kind= | The kind of run an earlier one was, so a person comparing two runs knows that one of them stopped early | [[id:79A42255-AACC-43BA-B876-60D421F6DBD0][ores.reporting.report_instance_kind]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the definition and of every run: the party code and name in the header | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-The definition is the scope and the run is the row. The runs of the definition
-are the =report_instance= rows whose =definition_id= is its id, ordered by
-=started_at= descending; the newest is the first of them. Two runs that started
-in the same second have no stored tie-break, so the order needs the run's id as
-a second key, and *What is missing* states it. The fire times are the
-=started_at= values of the last five of those runs, and they are labelled as
-derived from runs rather than read from the firings. Neither the latest run, the
-fire times nor the error count is a stored field: the screen derives all three,
-and *What is missing* states the reads that would spare it.
-
-=party_id= is on every one of these entities and every read is party-scoped by
-row-level security. The definition and the run are bitemporal, so the header
-shows the definition as it is now, while each run carries the state and the
-output it recorded then.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Open the history | Read the one definition the history is of | =reporting.v1.report_instances.get= | exists |
-| Read the runs | List the runs of the definition | =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= | exists |
-| Open any run | Read one run, including a failed one or one carrying errors | =reporting.v1.report_instances.get= | exists |
-| Read the run's errors | List the errors of the run the person opened | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id= | exists |
-| Leave a run open | Learn that a new run of this definition was created | =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.created= | exists |
-| Reload the history | Learn that a run changed, which is how a running run becomes a completed one | =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.updated= | exists |
-| See the previous fire times | Read when the schedule fired, whether or not a run survived | (no read of =report_trigger_event= over NATS) | missing |
-| Say when the next run is due | Read the scheduler job behind the definition's =scheduler_job_id= | (no scheduler read) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Read one definition with its runs in one answer | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-The two run reads are gated by =reporting::report_instances:read=, and the error
-read by =reporting::report_error_events:read=. The error read is held by no role
-below =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=, so a trading desk can open a run that
-carries errors and cannot read the errors behind it until a role below those two
-is granted the read. That is the permission gap [[id:F58B0FB5-3FD8-4BEB-982E-E54D284C0539][Find out why a run went wrong]] states in full.
-
-=reporting.v1.report_instances_events.created= is the real signal behind step 6,
-and =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.updated= is the real signal behind a
-row that changes state in place. The screen uses them and does not poll. No event
-exists for =report_trigger_event=, so a firing that produced no run sends nothing
-at all, and the one signal this journey most needs is the one it cannot subscribe
-to.
-
-No BFF route serves this screen. The prototype adds one, for example
-=GET /api/reporting/reports/<definition-id>/runs=, which reads the definition,
-its runs in one page and the error counts for the runs shown, and returns the
-health words and the five fire times already derived. The handler authenticates
-the caller's token and checks the run read code, and the row-level policy narrows
-the reads to the session's party.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *No read of =report_trigger_event=, so a firing that produced no run is
-   invisible.* The five previous fire times are the runs that exist, ordered by
-   =started_at=, and they are not the firings. A firing whose run was skipped by
-   the definition's concurrency policy, =skip=, =queue= or =fail=, recorded
-   nothing the screen can read. A firing the scheduler refused recorded nothing
-   either. Both leave a gap in the five, and the screen cannot tell a quiet
-   window from a firing that happened and produced no run. *This is the central
-   gap of this journey*: the question "did this report run every hour
-   yesterday?" has no answer on a screen that can only read runs. A read of the
-   trigger events over NATS would close it, and [[id:933649DD-1F86-4B40-99FD-1D4316D39A46][Choose when a report runs]] states the same gap from the scheduling end.
-2. *No read of the scheduler job, so the screen cannot say when the next fire is
-   due.* The definition stores =scheduler_job_id= and the job holds the
-   recurrence, its =is_active= flag and its next due time. The screen can repeat
-   the cron expression and cannot say when it will next fire, so "the next one
-   should be at 08:00" stays the reader's own arithmetic.
-3. *No BFF route serves reporting.* No route serves this screen either, and
-   nothing in the web application shows a report today. The history panel, its
-   fire-time strip and its recency behaviour are all new.
-4. *No read returns a definition with its runs.* The definition and its runs are
-   two reads, and the history is a join the screen performs. A definition with
-   two years of runs is a list of runs the browser filters by
-   =definition_id=, and the list is paged without the filter the screen needs.
-   A read of the runs of one definition, newest first, is the missing read.
-5. *No read counts errors for a set of runs.* The screen reads the errors of the
-   run the person opens, and the row's error count needs a count per run. A page
-   of fifteen runs is fifteen error reads after the run list.
-6. *The order has no stored tie-break.* "Newest first" is =started_at=
-   descending, and two runs that started in the same second have no order
-   between them. The latest marker and the first row must agree, so the read
-   needs a stable second key or the server needs to state the latest run itself.
-7. *The previous load is not on the server.* The recency rule marks the rows that
-   are new since the last load, and the server does not hold what this person
-   last saw. The screen keeps that in the browser, so the marking is a property
-   of one tab and is lost on a new one. Nothing in this set states the last load
-   for a person.
-8. *A run carries no trigger.* A run records that it started and no field says
-   what started it: a firing, a person pressing run now, or an upstream
-   workflow. The history can show that an unscheduled run appeared and cannot say
-   why, because the answer is the trigger event the screen cannot read.

-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A person opens one finished run and reads what it produced: the system's output message, the engine's output archive, the exported ORE package, and the errors that came with it.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"What did this run actually produce?" The person has a run in front of them,
-usually the latest one of a report they care about, and wants the file or the
-package that came out of it. They want to know where the engine's output landed,
-what the system said when the run ended, and what else the run left behind.
-The journey is done when they can take the output away, or say why there is no
-output to take.
-
-The person is not asking what the numbers mean. Reading the CSV artefacts is
-reading a report; this journey is about the run's own products: the archive, the
-package the engine read, and the record of what the run said.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-The trading desk and the market risk function read this journey. The desk takes
-the output of a Headline Position run to a meeting, and the market risk function
-takes the same output for sign-off and for the file it keeps. Both act inside
-their party, and they arrive from a run's row on
-[[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]] or
-from the run page of
-[[id:76431668-8656-4276-9F9B-F292FE45B2CA][Run a report and watch it finish]].
-
-The trigger is a run that has finished, or a person asking whether it has
-produced anything yet. The journey starts when the person opens the run's
-outputs and ends when they have the archive, or the package, or the reason
-neither exists.
-
-This is a read-only journey. It downloads what the run already wrote; it does
-not run, rerun or edit anything.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Open the run.* The person opens the run from its row, or the screen opens it
-   after a run completes. The header states the run's name, the definition it
-   came from, its kind, its state, and when it started and completed. A person
-   who has just finished
-   [[id:76431668-8656-4276-9F9B-F292FE45B2CA][Run a report and watch it finish]]
-   arrives with the run already in front of them.
-2. *Read what the system said.* The run carries an =output_message=, the
-   system's own sentence about the run. A completed run states exactly
-   =Report execution completed.= The screen shows that sentence as it is, and it
-   does not paraphrase it into a friendlier one. The message is the run's whole
-   account of itself when nothing went wrong, and it is the first thing a person
-   reads when they ask what happened.
-3. *Read where the output is.* A completed run carries an =output_storage_key=,
-   the storage key of its output archive, of the form
-   =reporting/runs/<instance-id>/output.tar.gz=. The screen shows the key and
-   offers the archive. The key is the answer to "where did it land": it names
-   the run's own directory in storage, so a person can quote it, find it with a
-   storage tool, or hand it to another reader. The screen does not pretend to
-   list the files inside the archive, because nothing lists them — see
-   *What is missing*.
-4. *Drill down from the run's figures to one trade.* The run's figures are an
-   aggregate: one NPV for the run, or one per book. Beneath them the screen
-   shows the per-trade table, one row per trade, because the run produced that
-   detail: the engine writes =npv.csv= into the run's archive, and its columns
-   are =TradeId=, =TradeType=, =Maturity=, =MaturityTime=, =NPV=,
-   =NpvCurrency=, =NPV(Base)=, =BaseCurrency=, =Notional=,
-   =NotionalCurrency=, =Notional(Base)=, =NettingSet= and =CounterParty=.
-   Each row states that trade's NPV, its base-currency NPV, its notional and
-   its counterparty. Opening a row shows that trade's result, and, where the
-   run recorded an error against the trade, that error. A trade in the result
-   is the trading trade with that id, so a row leads to the trade itself:
-   =trading.v1.trades.get= is what resolves the id to the trade. Nothing parses
-   the archive yet, so no screen can serve these rows as data — see
-   *What is missing*.
-5. *Read the results by book.* A run's results have a third reading beside the
-   aggregate figures and the one-row-per-trade table: the book tree. The tree has
-   four levels. A portfolio is the top level. A portfolio nests under another
-   portfolio, so a sub-portfolio is a level of its own. A book hangs off a
-   portfolio. A trade is booked to a book, so the trade is the bottom level.
-   The person opens the tree of the run's portfolios and books, sees each node's
-   name, its trade count and its aggregate NPV, and expands a level to read the
-   books inside it. Each node aggregates what sits below it: a book's figure is
-   the sum of its trades, and a portfolio's figure is the sum of its books.
-   Selecting a node filters the per-trade table to that subtree, so a person
-   drills from the group portfolio to a book and then to one row. A trade that is
-   booked to no book is a real state, and the tree shows it. That trade has no
-   =book_id= on =ores_trading_trade_bookings_tbl=, so it cannot sit under a book,
-   and the screen draws it as an unbooked node rather than dropping it. The
-   hierarchy is the schema's. =ores_refdata_portfolios_tbl= carries
-   =parent_portfolio_id=, so portfolios nest. =ores_refdata_books_tbl= carries
-   =parent_portfolio_id=, so a book hangs off a portfolio.
-   =ores_trading_trade_bookings_tbl= carries =trade_id= and =book_id=, so a trade
-   is booked to a book. The tree on the prototype is a fixture, for two reasons
-   the journey states in *What is missing*: the archive carries no book column,
-   and no operation returns the run's results grouped by book.
-   The screen also plots these numbers, and the plot is chosen to fit the analytic
-   that produced them: NPV by book is horizontal bars, sorted and drawn from a
-   zero rule; Delta and Gamma by book are that same bar form in two charts,
-   because a Greek is a different unit from an NPV; the change against a previous
-   run is a signed bar chart of its own; and the run's NPV across the runs of the
-   same definition is a line, with the current run and the baseline marked, which
-   is what makes the comparison legible. The screen has a plot vocabulary wider
-   than bars and lines — a donut for one whole in few parts, stacked bars for
-   several wholes each split the same way, grouped bars for two series over the
-   same categories, and a scatter for two measures against each other — and it
-   states the rule that chooses between them, so a later screen applies the same
-   rule rather than guessing: each book's share of the run and the run's problems
-   by scope are donuts, Delta against Gamma is grouped bars, and a book's Gamma
-   against its Delta is a scatter. Selecting a node of the book tree
-   narrows the bars to that subtree exactly as it narrows the table. Every plot
-   states its title, its unit, a text alternative and a one-line reason for its
-   form, and keeps its exact numbers in the table beside it. A figure that is not
-   a magnitude to compare — positions priced, books, counterparties — is a table
-   answer, and the screen draws no plot of it.
-6. *Read the errors that came with the output.* Output and errors are not
-   alternatives. A run that completed while carrying errors produced its
-   archive and recorded its errors, and a reader who takes the archive must know
-   what the run said was wrong. The outputs screen therefore carries the error
-   summary: the count, the severities and the scopes. A reader who wants the
-   detail follows
-   [[id:F58B0FB5-3FD8-4BEB-982E-E54D284C0539][Find out why a run went wrong]].
-   The archive is still the answer to "what did this run produce", and the errors
-   are the answer to "what is missing from it".
-7. *Read a partial result.* A run can complete, write its archive, and still
-   not hold the whole answer. The engine may fail to build some trades, so
-   =npv.csv= carries no row for them and every total read from that file leaves
-   them out. A configured analytic may skip positions it could price, so those
-   positions carry an NPV and no Delta. Both facts are rows of the run, read by
-   =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id=, and both are
-   already recorded before the person opens the screen. The screen must say so
-   before the numbers are trusted, and not in a panel a person may close.
-   - A banner above the results states that the results are partial and why: how
-     many trades the engine could not build, how many positions carry an NPV and
-     no Delta, and that the totals below exclude them. The banner names the count
-     of error rows and offers the way to see them, the same way the summary of a
-     completed run that carries errors does.
-   - The aggregate figures keep their number and carry a marker and a footnote.
-     The figure is not hidden and not replaced: a person who needs the total gets
-     it, and a person who would take it for the whole answer is told otherwise on
-     the figure itself.
-   - A plot of a partial result is marked too. A bar or a point drawn from a
-     figure the errors left incomplete carries the same =partial= marker the
-     figure carries, is drawn dashed or hollow, and its caption names what the
-     figure excludes. A plot never presents a floor as the whole answer.
-   - A book whose trades include a failed one is marked, and it states that its
-     figure excludes the failed trades. A portfolio above it states that it
-     inherits the exclusion, because its figure is the sum of its books and it
-     must not include a book that lost trades in silence.
-   - The per-trade table draws each failed trade as a row with its =TradeId=, its
-     =TradeType=, its =Notional= and its =CounterParty=, with =NPV= and
-     =NPV(Base)= empty, and with an =error= tag. Opening the row shows the error
-     the run recorded. A trade the engine could not build writes no row into
-     =npv.csv=, so its price cells are empty by nature and not by omission, and
-     the screen says so.
-   A completed run whose totals are incomplete is the ordinary case this step
-   exists for. The message =Report execution completed.= is true and says nothing
-   about it.
-8. *Read the exported ORE package.* Pre-processing produces the engine's input,
-   and the step that prepares it is =ore.v1.ops.prepare_ore_package=. The
-   package is the engine's input, and it is what a person would run locally to
-   reproduce the output. The screen states
-   the package the run produced and offers it where the run has one. A run whose
-   definition substitutes pre-processing resolves a prepared input instead, and
-   the package it resubmits is named by the definition's =prepared_input_key=.
-   The two are different objects, and the screen says which one this run used.
-9. *A run still in flight.* Output does not exist until retrieval. The run's
-   =output_storage_key= is set only once the run's results have been retrieved,
-   so a running run states that no output is available yet and that the panel
-   will fill when the run completes. It does not draw an empty archive, which
-   would read as a run that produced nothing.
-10. *A run that failed.* A failed run has no archive and no package to hand over.
-   The screen says there is nothing to take, states that the run failed, and
-   sends the reader to the run's errors. The empty answer is explained, not
-   dressed as an empty folder.
-11. *Compare the run with a previous run.* A run's figures answer what the
-    books were worth; they do not answer what changed. The person chooses a
-    previous completed run of the same definition on the result panel, or turns
-    the comparison off. The panel names the baseline by its run instance id and
-    its start time, and never by a report number. Each aggregate figure, each
-    book row, each tree node and the total row then carries its change and its
-    percentage against that run. Both sides are the actual figures of two runs and
-    the change is subtraction: no figure is multiplied by a constant to stand in
-    for another run, because a per-metric multiplier moves every book by the same
-    percentage and the change is then fiction. A stress scenario is not a run of
-    this report, and yesterday's official close belongs to a different run, so
-    neither is offered as a baseline. When either run in the comparison carried
-    errors, the change is partial: a total over the trades that survived cannot be
-    compared as if it were the whole answer. The badge carries a =partial= marker
-    and the screen says so once in words, with what the current run's errors leave
-    out. The book tree's selected node drives both sides, so selecting a book
-    compares that book across the two runs. Reading an earlier run's figures needs
-    the same parsed result the current run needs, so the comparison waits on the
-    same missing read twice; =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= is the existing
-    read that finds the earlier runs of the definition.
-12. *Take it away, or leave.* The person copies the storage key, downloads the
-    archive through the route the screen provides, or follows the error screen.
-    The run remains the record: its outputs do not expire with the screen, and a
-    person who comes back later reads the same key.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen. The run header, the output panel, the errors summary and the ORE
-package panel are panels of that screen, because they are one answer: what this
-run produced and what it said about it. The screen is read-only: it creates
-nothing, changes nothing and destroys nothing.
-
-The outputs panel is deliberately thin. It names the archive, offers it, and
-says that its contents are not listed, because no operation lists them. The
-wireframe shows the three states a person meets: a completed run with an archive,
-a run in flight with no output yet, and a failed run with nothing to take.
-
-#+caption: Read what a run produced: the output message, the archive's storage key, the exported ORE package, and the states where there is nothing to take.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_read_what_a_run_produced.png]]
-
-The book tree sits with the figures and the per-trade rows, because it is a
-third reading of the same result. It draws the run's portfolios and books with a
-trade count and an aggregate NPV at each node, an unbooked node for the trades
-that have no booking, and a selected node that filters the per-trade rows to its
-subtree.
-
-The result panel also carries the comparison: the control that chooses a previous
-run of the definition, the change badge under each figure, the change columns on
-the book tree and the by-book table, and the total row. The plots sit under the
-book tree and above the by-book table they take their numbers from: bars for NPV,
-for Delta and for Gamma across the books in view, a signed bar chart of the change
-when the comparison is on, and a line of NPV across the runs of the definition
-with the current run and the baseline marked. A plot whose figure the errors left
-partial carries the same =partial= marking the figure carries, with its caption
-naming what the figure excludes, because a bar of a floor must not read as a bar
-of the whole answer. When either side of the
-comparison carried errors the badge and the panel mark every change as partial,
-because a change between one incomplete figure and one complete figure is not the
-change the two runs would show.
-
-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/read-what-a-run-produced/][prototype]] argues this journey in three interpretations, and [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/read-what-a-run-produced.org][its design note]] says what each argues and what is fake. This journey is the design intent for the run's outputs screen, and
-its prototype belongs at =doc/prototypes/reporting/read-what-a-run-produced/=.
-The prototype must draw a completed run with an archive and a package; a
-completed run carrying errors, where the archive and the error summary sit
-together; a run in flight with no output yet; and a failed run with nothing to
-take. It must also draw the archive panel without a file list, and say in the
-panel why the list is absent. It must draw the drill-down too: the run's figures
-as an aggregate with the per-trade table under them, one row per trade, and the
-error a row carries where the run recorded one against that trade. Because no
-operation parses the archive, the prototype labels the rows a fixture on the
-panel that draws them. It must draw the book tree in all three interpretations,
-in each one's own shape: the run's portfolios and books with a trade count and an
-aggregate NPV at each node, an unbooked node for the trades with no booking, and
-a selected node that filters the per-trade rows. Because the archive carries no
-book column and no operation returns a result grouped by book, the prototype
-labels the tree a fixture and says on the panel how a built screen would join it.
-It must draw the partial case too, in all three interpretations: a completed run
-whose results carry errors, with the banner above the figures, the marker and the
-footnote on the figures, the marked books and portfolios, and the row of every
-trade the engine could not build. Because a person must be able to find that case
-on purpose, the prototype selects it by a fixture chip and by =?scenario= on the
-URL. It must draw the comparison too, on the result panel: a control that chooses
-a previous completed run of the same definition or no comparison, every aggregate
-figure, book row, tree node and the total row carrying its change and percentage
-against that run, the baseline named by its instance id and start time, and the
-=partial= marking on the change when either side carried errors. The page opens
-with the previous run chosen and =?baseline=none= turns the comparison off.
-Because an earlier run's
-figures need the same parsed result the current run needs, the changes are a
-fixture like the figures, and the panel says so.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_instance= | The run: state, =completed_at=, =output_message= and =output_storage_key= | [[id:9FCCF6C8-9C10-403B-BDA4-C3E28706BD67][ores.reporting.report_instance]] |
-| =report_definition= | The definition behind the run: its name, its schedule, and the =prepared_input_key= a substituting run resolves | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =report_instance_kind= | The kind of run, so a reader knows what this run set out to do | [[id:79A42255-AACC-43BA-B876-60D421F6DBD0][ores.reporting.report_instance_kind]] |
-| =report_error_event= | The errors the run recorded beside its output: severity, scope and message | [[id:080B3871-8BAA-4AAA-A98F-3E79F4B83BAA][ores.reporting.report_error_event]] |
-| =report_error_scope= | The vocabulary that names what each error is about | [[id:FF774B04-12E6-4BDF-B94C-222095651C4F][ores.reporting.report_error_scope]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the run and the archive | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-
-The run is the row and the archive is its =output_storage_key=. The package is
-not a column: it is the object the pre-processing step prepared, and the screen
-reaches it through the definition's =prepared_input_key= when the run
-substituted pre-processing. The errors are rows of the run, read as a group,
-and the summary counts them by severity and by scope.
-
-Every entity above carries =party_id= and is party-scoped by row-level security.
-The run and the definition are bitemporal, so the name and the definition the
-run started with are the run's own; editing the definition today does not rename
-the output of a run from last week.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Open the run | Read the run | =reporting.v1.report_instances.get= | exists |
-| Open the run | Read the run's definition | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Open the run | Read the kind of run | =reporting.v1.report_instance_kinds.get= | exists |
-| Read the output location | Read the archive key the run recorded | carried by =reporting.v1.report_instances.get= | exists |
-| Drill down to one trade | Read a run's per-trade results | (no operation parses the archive) | missing |
-| Drill down to one trade | Read the trade a result row names | =trading.v1.trades.get= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | List the run's portfolios | =refdata.v1.portfolios.list= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read one portfolio, and its =parent_portfolio_id= | =refdata.v1.portfolios.get= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read many portfolios | =refdata.v1.portfolios.get_many= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | List the books under a portfolio | =refdata.v1.books.list_by_parent_portfolio_id= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | List the books | =refdata.v1.books.list= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read one book, and its =parent_portfolio_id= | =refdata.v1.books.get= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read many books | =refdata.v1.books.get_many= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | List the trades' bookings, and so each trade's =book_id= | =trading.v1.trade_bookings.list= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read one booking | =trading.v1.trade_bookings.get= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read many bookings | =trading.v1.trade_bookings.get_many= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | List the trades that were booked | =trading.v1.trades.list= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | List the runs of a definition, to reach the run | =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= | exists |
-| Read the results by book | Read a run's results already grouped by book | (no operation returns results grouped by book) | missing |
-| Read the results by book | List the portfolios under a portfolio in one read | (no =refdata.v1.portfolios.list_by_parent_portfolio_id=; the tree is assembled from =portfolios.list=) | missing |
-| Read the errors | List the run's errors | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id= | exists |
-| Read a partial result | Read the errors that make a completed run's results partial | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id= | exists |
-| Read a partial result | Read the per-trade rows, to draw the trades that carry no price | (no operation parses the archive) | missing |
-| Compare with a previous run | List the earlier completed runs of the same definition | =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= | exists |
-| Compare with a previous run | Read the baseline run's figures, book rows and total | (no operation parses the archive) | missing |
-| Read the errors | Read one error | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.get= | exists |
-| Read the errors | Read the scope vocabulary | =reporting.v1.report_error_scopes.list= | exists |
-| Read the package | Prepare the ORE package the engine reads | =ore.v1.ops.prepare_ore_package= | exists |
-| Watch for output | Learn that the run completed and its output landed | =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.updated= | exists |
-| Take the archive | List the files inside the run's archive | (no operation lists an archive's contents) | missing |
-| Take the archive | Read or stream the archive's bytes | (no reporting operation serves the archive) | missing |
-| Take the package | Read the exported ORE package, or list its files | (no operation in the set returns it) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Read a run's outputs from the browser | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-The output message and the storage key are fields of the run, so the read that
-opens the run already answers "where did it land". A per-trade result names a
-=TradeId=, and the trade with that id is =trading='s trade, so
-=trading.v1.trades.get= resolves the row to the trade itself. The per-trade read
-is the one that is missing: =ores_compute_results_tbl= carries the archive's
-=output_uri=, its =outcome= and its =error_message=, and it carries no parsed
-rows. No operation parses the archive. The errors are a list by
-report instance. The package is an operation of the ORE component, and no
-reporting read returns it. The archive's own bytes are behind storage, not
-reporting: the run names the key and the screen needs a route that can fetch the
-object it names.
-
-The book tree is assembled from reads that exist: =refdata.v1.portfolios.list=
-for the portfolios and their =parent_portfolio_id=,
-=refdata.v1.books.list_by_parent_portfolio_id= for the books under a portfolio,
-and =trading.v1.trade_bookings.list= for each trade's =book_id=. The two that do
-not exist are the read of a result grouped by book and
-=portfolios.list_by_parent_portfolio_id=, and both are in *What is missing*.
-
-The comparison adds one existing read and no new one: =report_instances.list=
-returns the runs of a definition, and the baseline is the earlier completed one
-among them. Reading the baseline's figures needs the parsed result this journey
-already needs, so a comparison is one read the platform has and two parsed
-results it does not.
-
-The reads are gated by =reporting::report_instances:read= and
-=reporting::report_definitions:read=, and the errors by
-=reporting::report_error_events:read= and =reporting::report_error_scopes:read=.
-The error codes are held by no role below =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=.
-
-No BFF route serves this screen. The prototype adds one, for example
-=GET /api/reporting/runs/<run-id>/outputs=, which returns the run's output
-message, its storage key, the package it used and the error summary, and a
-second route that streams the archive by its key. The handler authenticates the
-caller's token and checks the read codes above.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *A route and a screen.* No BFF route serves reporting, and nothing in the web
-   application shows a report today. The run's outputs screen is new.
-2. *No file list for the archive.* The run names one archive,
-   =reporting/runs/<instance-id>/output.tar.gz=, and no operation lists the
-   files inside it. A person who wants one CSV must download the archive and
-   open it. A read of the archive's entries is the missing piece, and the
-   screen states the absence rather than showing an empty list.
-3. *No read of the archive itself.* Reporting states the key; no reporting
-   operation returns the bytes. The download is a BFF and storage concern, and
-   it is not designed here. The screen can quote the key today and cannot hand
-   the object over without that route.
-4. *No read of the exported ORE package.* =ore.v1.ops.prepare_ore_package= is
-   the step that prepares the package, and no operation in the set returns it or
-   lists its contents. A person who wants to reproduce the run locally has the
-   same problem as with the output archive: they need the object, and the
-   journey can only name where it came from.
-5. *No operation parses the archive.* Per-trade results are real: the engine
-   writes =npv.csv= into the run's archive, one row per trade with its NPV, its
-   base-currency NPV, its notional and its counterparty. What is missing is the
-   read. =ores_compute_results_tbl= holds the run's =output_uri=, its =outcome=
-   and its =error_message=: it points at the archive and carries no parsed rows.
-   No operation parses =reporting/runs/<instance-id>/output.tar.gz=, and none
-   serves the rows inside it, so trade-level results need a result store or an
-   archive read before a screen can serve them. The result store that would
-   ingest the archive is designed on
-   [[id:D697A04C-387C-451E-AC90-1989FCDFCAB9][Report post-processing]] and is
-   not built, so there are no report rows to query and "what did this run
-   produce" is still answered by an archive rather than by a table. The
-   prototype draws the per-trade table as a stated fixture for that reason.
-6. *No read returns a result grouped by book.* The run's archive carries no book
-   column. =npv.csv='s columns are exactly =TradeId=, =TradeType=, =Maturity=,
-   =MaturityTime=, =NPV=, =NpvCurrency=, =NPV(Base)=, =BaseCurrency=,
-   =Notional=, =NotionalCurrency=, =Notional(Base)=, =NettingSet= and
-   =CounterParty=, so a row of the file names a trade and never a book.
-   Attributing a result to a book needs the join from =TradeId= to
-   =trade_bookings.book_id=, through =trading.v1.trade_bookings.list=, and no
-   operation returns results already grouped by book. The booking is real and
-   stored; the grouped read is the missing piece. The book tree therefore needs
-   the per-trade read above *and* this join before a screen can serve it, and the
-   prototype draws every node's trade count and NPV as a fixture.
-7. *No =portfolios.list_by_parent_portfolio_id=.* Portfolios nest through
-   =parent_portfolio_id= on =ores_refdata_portfolios_tbl=, and there is no read
-   that returns the portfolios under a portfolio. A client assembles the
-   portfolio tree from =refdata.v1.portfolios.list=, which carries
-   =parent_portfolio_id=, and pays for it with a full list of the party's
-   portfolios per level. =refdata.v1.books.list_by_parent_portfolio_id= exists
-   for books, so the book level needs no such workaround; the portfolio level
-   does.
-8. *The run does not name the job that produced the archive.* =report_instance=
-   carries no batch or workunit id, so the screen cannot link this output to the
-   compute job whose =output_uri= it came from. The key is on the run; the
-   lineage to the grid is not.
-9. *The error permissions sit too high.* =reporting::report_error_events:read=
-   and =reporting::report_error_scopes:read= are held by no role below
-   =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=, which hold =*=. A trading desk can open the
-   archive and cannot read the errors that say what is missing from it, which is
-   the one warning the outputs screen exists to give.
-10. *The package a substituting run used is named on the definition, not the
-    run.* A run that resolves a prepared input leaves the definition to state
-    =prepared_input_key=, and a later edit to the definition changes what the
-    screen reports for an earlier run. The definition keeps its history, and the
-    run does not name the version of the definition it used, so the screen has no
-    key to the prepared input the run actually read.
-
-11. *No artefacts page, and no icon to open it with.* The screen offers an
-    =Artefacts= link beside each package, the input package and the output
-    archive, because the package is a container of files and a reader who wants
-    to look inside it expects to leave the screen for somewhere that lists them.
-    Two things are missing behind that link. There is no artefacts page and no
-    route serves one, so the link is the requirement on the platform rather than
-    a working destination. And the icon set carries no box, package or archive
-    glyph: the sixty-eight Fluent icons in the application have a folder and
-    nothing nearer, so the prototype draws a folder and the catalogue needs a
-    package icon before the real screen can use a fitting one.

-#+title: User Journey: Run a report and watch it finish
-#+description: A person runs one report definition on demand, then follows the run through the pipeline's phases to a terminal state and reads when it completed and what it said.
-#+type: user_journey
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :knowledge:user_journey:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-#+startup: inlineimages
-
-This page documents a [[id:F44766FA-1E9C-416F-849A-E131101B2ECA][user journey]]: A person runs one report definition on demand, then follows the run through the pipeline's phases to a terminal state and reads when it completed and what it said.
-
-A user journey describes what one person is trying to do, before anything is
-built. It is a design document that outlives any sprint, so it names the
-screens, the entity fields each screen shows, and the operations and messages
-each step needs.
-
-* Goal
-
-"Run this report now, and tell me when it is done." The person has a report in
-mind and a reason to want it before the schedule would produce it: a position
-changed, a number is needed for a meeting, or yesterday's run failed and the
-answer is wanted today. They press one button, watch the run reach a terminal
-state, and read when it completed and what the system said about it. The journey
-is done when the person can say the run finished and whether it finished clean.
-
-The person is not asking to configure the report. The scope, the analytics and
-the schedule are the definition's; running it takes the definition as it stands
-and makes one run of it.
-
-* Actor and trigger
-
-The trading desk and the market risk function run this journey. The trading
-desk runs Headline Position for a book during the day; the market risk function
-runs it for sign-off, and runs the deeper risk reports when a number moves. Both
-act inside their party, and the definition they run is one of the rows on
-[[id:891DE3CB-2374-4FD9-B7FB-D8892F5174A1][See the reports a party runs]]. A
-tenant administrator can run any definition of their tenant, because the
-administrator holds the tenant's permissions in full, but the journey is the
-same screen whatever the role.
-
-The trigger is impatience with the schedule or the failure of the last run. The
-person opens a definition that is on-demand, or one that is scheduled but whose
-next run is too late, and presses *Run now*. The journey starts at that press
-and ends when the run is terminal and the person has read its completion time
-and its output message.
-
-This journey writes. A press creates a report instance, records a trigger and
-starts the workflow that runs the pipeline. The run's state, its start time, its
-completion time and its output are written by the reporting service and the
-workflow steps, never by the person. The person states one thing: which
-definition to run.
-
-* Steps
-
-1. *Choose the definition.* The person reaches the definition from the reporting
-   front door, or by name. The system shows one definition's summary: its name,
-   its report type, the schedule it carries, the health of its latest run, and
-   the scope the run will read. The scope is the book or the portfolio the
-   definition's configuration selects, and it is the part a person checks before
-   pressing, because a report run against the wrong book is a correct answer to
-   the wrong question. The summary also states how the run will be configured:
-   whether pre-processing executes or resolves a prepared input, and whether
-   post-processing executes or is ignored. A run of the Sample bundle smoke test
-   resolves a prepared input and ignores the results; a run of Headline Position
-   does both.
-2. *Press Run now.* The system asks the person to confirm the run, restating the
-   definition, its scope and the run configuration, because a run costs compute
-   and writes rows. On confirmation the screen sends one request to the
-   reporting service: =reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance=, naming the
-   definition. The service records the trigger, creates the run and starts the
-   workflow; it answers with the run it created.
-3. *Read the run that was created.* The system switches to the run's own page.
-   The header states the run's name, the definition it came from, its kind, its
-   state and when it started. The state is *running* from the moment the
-   workflow begins. The trigger the press wrote is a =report_trigger_event=, and
-   the run records it in =trigger_id=; the type is =on-demand=, which separates
-   this run from the ones the scheduler fires.
-4. *Read the pipeline the run will walk.* The system draws the six phases in
-   their fixed order — Pre-processing, Submission, Execution, Retrieval,
-   Post-processing, Finalisation — and under them the seven workflow steps that
-   the definition's run configuration selects. For a definition that executes
-   both substitutable phases the steps are =gather_trades=,
-   =gather_market_data=, =assemble_bundle=, =prepare_ore_package=,
-   =submit_compute=, =collect_compute_results= and =finalise_report=. A
-   definition that substitutes pre-processing starts at
-   =resolve_prepared_input=; one that ignores post-processing uses
-   =ignore_compute_results=; a run that cannot finish uses =fail_report=.
-   Execution is drawn differently from the rest, because it happens on a worker
-   node and no ORE Studio service performs it: the services submit the work and
-   wait.
-5. *Understand what the screen can and cannot say about progress.* The run's own
-   state and times are reporting's. The step-by-step position is in
-   =ores.workflow=, and no reporting read serves it. The screen therefore draws
-   the steps the run will take and marks the run as *running*; it does not point
-   at the step in flight, and it must not fake a moving bar. The phases are
-   marked as reported only when the run reaches its terminal state. The screen
-   says why it cannot say more, and *What is missing* names the read that would
-   close the gap.
-6. *Wait, and be told.* A run can outlast the person's patience and the
-   screen's session. The screen subscribes to =report_instances_events.updated=
-   and to =report_instances_events.created=, so the run's row changes state and
-   time in place while the page is open. A person who leaves and comes back
-   reads the same run by id and gets the state it has reached. The question
-   "when is it done" is answered by the run's =completed_at=, not by the
-   screen's timer.
-7. *Read the terminal state.* The run is terminal when it has completed or
-   failed. A completed run carries =completed_at= and an =output_message=, for
-   example exactly =Report execution completed.=; it may also carry
-   =output_storage_key=, the storage key of its output archive, of the form
-   =reporting/runs/<instance-id>/output.tar.gz=. The screen states how long the
-   run took, from =started_at= to =completed_at=, and reads the output message
-   as the system's own sentence about the run.
-8. *A run that completed while carrying errors.* Completion is not the same as
-   clean. A run that records errors still completed, and that is normal and
-   expected: the engine finished, wrote its report, and said in its own log that
-   a trade would not build. The terminal panel states *completed while carrying
-   errors*, gives the count and the worst severity, and links to
-   [[id:F58B0FB5-3FD8-4BEB-982E-E54D284C0539][Find out why a run went wrong]].
-   The person does not read the run as failed, and the screen does not hide the
-   errors behind the green word.
-9. *A run that failed.* A failed run has no output archive to read. The screen
-   states *failed* and links to the run's errors, which include the errors the
-   engine wrote and the ones the model states itself under the =Report= scope
-   when a run fails for a reason no engine saw. A run that failed before the
-   engine ran is still a run with errors in one table, which is the point of
-   reading a run's errors as a group.
-10. *Leave, or go on.* The person opens what the run produced
-    ([[id:969C14D2-4280-4D7C-8F51-1D395B521C83][Read what a run produced]]), or
-    reads why it went wrong. The definition is still there, and its row on the
-    front door now shows this run as its latest.
-
-* Screens and wireframes
-
-One screen. The definition summary, the run action, the run header, the phase
-ladder and the terminal panel are panels of that screen. The confirmation is a
-dialog on the same screen, because it restates the run the person is about to
-create and nothing more.
-
-The screen writes exactly once. The press sends one trigger request; every other
-message on it is a read or a subscription. The phase ladder is a plan derived
-from the definition, not a progress read, and the wireframe draws it as such.
-
-#+caption: Run a report and watch it finish: the definition summary, the run action, the seven steps the run will walk, and the terminal panel with the output message.
-#+attr_html: :width 100%
-[[proj:doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/wireframe_run_a_report_and_watch_it_finish.png]]
-
-* Prototype
-
-The [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish/][prototype]] argues this journey in three interpretations, and [[file:../../prototypes/reporting/run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish.org][its design note]] says what each argues and what is fake. This journey is the design intent for the run screen, and its
-prototype belongs at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish/=. The prototype must
-draw the confirmation dialog before the write; the run in flight with the phase
-ladder and no step marked current; the terminal state *completed clean* with
-=Report execution completed.= and the time it took; the terminal state
-*completed while carrying errors* with the count beside it; and the terminal
-state *failed* with no archive. It must also draw a run whose definition
-substitutes pre-processing, so the four-step chain is visible next to the
-seven-step one.
-
-* Entities composed
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Entity | What it contributes | Model |
-|--------+---------------------+-------|
-| =report_definition= | The definition the person runs: name, report type, schedule expression, concurrency policy and the run configuration | [[id:FB4A11C5-07EA-4923-B8AC-65F46EBA517C][ores.reporting.report_definition]] |
-| =report_configuration= | The scope and analytics the definition binds, and the market data date the run reads | [[id:7F2C8A41-6E93-4B57-A0D4-3C9E1B5D7826][ores.reporting.report_configuration]] |
-| =portfolio= | The portfolio the scope names, when the definition's scope is a portfolio | [[id:282C87C1-11E1-42F0-BEE6-D6983A5F836B][ores.refdata.portfolio]] |
-| =book= | The book the scope names, when the definition's scope is a book | [[id:5A63B4D1-0F55-468B-B734-A5DC37B26DC4][ores.refdata.book]] |
-| =party= | The owner of the definition and the run | [[id:8F3A1C2D-4B5E-4A6C-8F9D-2E3F4A5B6C7D][ores.refdata.party]] |
-| =report_instance= | The run: state, =started_at=, =completed_at=, =output_message= and =output_storage_key= | [[id:9FCCF6C8-9C10-403B-BDA4-C3E28706BD67][ores.reporting.report_instance]] |
-| =report_instance_kind= | The kind of run the press created | [[id:79A42255-AACC-43BA-B876-60D421F6DBD0][ores.reporting.report_instance_kind]] |
-| =report_trigger_event= | The firing the press records: the definition, the trigger type, who triggered it and when | [[id:47E6903C-DFA7-4D2F-B044-C1C74428F719][ores.reporting.report_trigger_event]] |
-| =report_trigger_type= | The vocabulary the trigger's type comes from, where =on-demand= sits apart from =scheduled= | [[id:5E202386-A853-4F09-8D3A-026ECE6DAD4D][ores.reporting.report_trigger_type]] |
-
-The definition is read before the press and never edited by it. The run is the
-record of what the press caused: the service writes its state, its times and its
-output, and the person's screen reads them. The trigger event is immutable: it
-is written once when the press is accepted and never changed, so the record of
-who asked for a run survives any later edit to the run.
-
-Every entity above carries =party_id= and is party-scoped by row-level security.
-The definition and the run are bitemporal, so the run keeps the shape it started
-with even if the definition is edited while it runs. The trigger event is an
-immutable event, and it is the fact the screen could use to say which run the
-press produced, if a read served it.
-
-* Operations and messages
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Step | Operation | Subject | Status |
-|------+-----------+---------+--------|
-| Choose the definition | Read the definition being run | =reporting.v1.report_definitions.get= | exists |
-| Choose the definition | Read the definition's configuration and scope | (no read of =report_configuration= is named in this set) | missing |
-| Press Run now | Trigger a run of one definition | =reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance= | exists |
-| Read the run | Read the run that was created | =reporting.v1.report_instances.get= | exists |
-| Read the run | List the runs of the definition | =reporting.v1.report_instances.list= | exists |
-| Wait, and be told | Learn that the run changed | =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.updated= | exists |
-| Wait, and be told | Learn that the run was created | =reporting.v1.report_instances_events.created= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Follow the pre-processing steps | =reporting.v1.ops.gather_trades=, =gather_market_data=, =assemble_bundle= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Prepare the ORE package the engine reads | =ore.v1.ops.prepare_ore_package= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Submit the work to the compute grid | =compute.v1.ops.submit_compute= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Collect the engine's result | =reporting.v1.ops.collect_compute_results= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Close the run | =reporting.v1.ops.finalise_report= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Resolve a prepared input instead of gathering | =reporting.v1.ops.resolve_prepared_input= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Record that results exist without ingesting them | =reporting.v1.ops.ignore_compute_results= | exists |
-| Read the pipeline | Close a run that could not finish | =reporting.v1.ops.fail_report= | exists |
-| Terminal state | Read the run's errors | =reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id= | exists |
-| Progress | Read which step the run is on | (no reporting read; the steps live in =ores.workflow=) | missing |
-| The trigger | Read the trigger event the press wrote | (no read of =report_trigger_event= over NATS) | missing |
-| The screen itself | Trigger a run and follow it from the browser | (no BFF route) | missing |
-
-The workflow steps are invoked by the workflow engine, not by the screen. They
-are listed because the journey follows them and the phase ladder draws them; the
-screen's one write is the trigger. The trigger request is gated by
-=reporting::report_instances:write=, and the run reads by
-=reporting::report_instances:read=. The step commands are the workflow engine's
-and carry the workflow instance and the step's own inputs.
-
-The run events are the canonical change events for =report_instance=. They carry
-the subject and the key, so a subscriber can tell a run it is showing from one
-it is not. No event exists for a step completion, and that is the gap in step 5.
-
-No BFF route serves this screen. The prototype adds one, for example
-=POST /api/reporting/reports/<definition-id>/runs= for the press and
-=GET /api/reporting/runs/<run-id>= for the follow, and it keeps the event
-subscription on the server rather than exposing the bus to the browser.
-
-* What is missing
-
-1. *A route and a screen.* No BFF route serves reporting, and nothing in the web
-   application shows a report today. The definition summary, the confirmation,
-   the run page and its terminal panel are all new.
-2. *No per-step progress.* The reporting service states the run's state and its
-   times. The step the workflow is on lives in =ores.workflow=, and no reporting
-   read serves it. The phase ladder therefore marks the plan and the run's
-   state, and it cannot point at the step in flight. A read that carries the
-   workflow instance's current step, exposed beside the run, is the missing
-   piece.
-3. *The run does not name its workflow instance.* =report_instance= carries
-   =trigger_id=, =fsm_state_id=, the times and the output, and no field for the
-   workflow instance that runs it. Even with the step progress available in
-   =ores.workflow=, the screen has no key to reach it from the run. The
-   workflow instance id is carried in the run's start message, so the run needs
-   to keep it.
-4. *The trigger is written and unreadable.* The press records a
-   =report_trigger_event= with the definition, the trigger type, the person and
-   the time, and there is no read of it over NATS. The run's =trigger_id= names
-   it, and nothing resolves that id to a row. The screen can say a run was
-   triggered on demand because the trigger's type is known when it is written;
-   it cannot show the trigger's own record.
-5. *No cancellation.* A press creates a run, and no operation stops one. A run
-   that was started by mistake, or one that is waiting on a worker node, has to
-   be waited out. The journey offers no stop action rather than an action that
-   would be refused.
-6. *The error permissions sit too high.* =reporting::report_error_events:read=
-   and =reporting::report_error_scopes:read= are held by no role below
-   =TenantAdmin= and =SuperAdmin=, which hold =*=. A trading desk that runs a
-   report cannot read the errors that say it completed carrying problems. The
-   terminal panel's count and its link need that read.
-7. *The concurrency policy is the definition's and the answer is the service's.*
-   The definition carries =concurrency_policy= and the screen does not evaluate
-   it. What the person sees when a run is refused is whatever the trigger reply
-   says, and the reply's shape for a refusal is not part of this journey. The
-   screen must show the service's answer, not invent a queue position.
-8. *The scope is held in a configuration with no named read.* The definition
-   binds a =report_configuration= that holds the book and portfolio scope and
-   the market data date. No operation in the reporting set reads that entity, so
-   the confirmation cannot show the scope from a read the journey can cite. The
-   scope panel waits on that read, and the run itself still gathers its trades
-   and market data because the inputs a run needs are gathered by the run.
