-#+title: Change what a report runs prototype
-#+description: A three panel wizard over the definition and the configurations it binds: the analytics of the bound configuration read as a summary, then what a change to that set reaches, with the analytic interaction handed to its own prototype.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                             |
-|---------------+---------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:change-what-a-report-runs/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                              |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]            |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues how a person reads what a report runs, and it answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_change_what_a_report_runs.org][Change
-what a report runs]]. The screen is a wizard of three panels titled =What this
-report runs=: the definition and the configurations it binds, the analytics the
-bound run settings configuration carries, and what a change to that set reaches.
-
-It draws no analytic control. [[file:manage-the-analytics.org][Manage the
-analytics]] owns the analytic interaction — the switchboard, a step per analytic,
-every parameter, the refused pair, the read-back — and step 2 summarises the set
-and links there. The switchboard, the nested list-detail-effect flow and the
-three variants that read its detail screen are gone from this page; that layout
-question moved with the screen it belonged to.
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, and the page states which parts of the set
-it cannot show, which rules the server does not enforce, and which editors are
-deferred.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The wizard's three panels
-
-1. *The definition and the configurations it binds.* The definition's name, type
-   and party, then the five configuration types with what each supplies and where
-   its data lives. A conventions configuration is a named convention set, so its
-   row shows the set chosen below, and below the table sits the one page of sets
-   the report chooses between: a row each with its name, its purpose, the kinds it
-   covers and whether this report uses it, a radio to bind one, and one link out
-   to the authoring UX marked as not in this MR. It draws no per-kind row. The
-   other four types have no screen in the application, and they are stated as
-   missing, never drawn as working. The panel also names the other definitions
-   bound to the shared configuration, because the analytics belong to it and not
-   to the definition that was opened.
-2. *The analytics.* A read-only summary of the set the bound configuration
-   carries: the count that is on, every row with its =display_order= and a
-   one-line statement of what it produces, the rows kept off with the note that
-   they keep their order and their parameters, and the rule strip when =pfe= is
-   on without =simulation=. Then the link to Manage the analytics.
-3. *What a change reaches.* What the change reaches and does not reach, the runs
-   that stop being comparable, that past runs keep their configuration, and where
-   the write happens.
-
-The panels are deep-linked with =?step=1|2|3=, and step is part of every URL the
-page writes.
-
-** The analytics are read here, and set elsewhere
-
-The analytics belong to the run settings configuration, not to the definition, so
-the same set is what four definitions run. Two prototypes were drawing that set:
-this one with a switchboard and a nested flow, and
-[[file:create-a-report.org][Create a report]] with a switchboard and a rail
-step per analytic. The same fourteen types had two vocabularies for the same three
-states — on, off, and no row — and the parameters of an analytic were drawn
-twice.
-
-The product owner asked for one screen to own analytic management. This page
-keeps the wizard over the definition and the configurations, and it keeps one
-panel that answers the question the journey asks: *what does this report run, and
-what changes if I change it?* Every control leaves the page. Step 2 states the set
-and the incompatibility, and links to the screen that changes it.
-
-What the consolidation costs:
-
-- *A step out of the wizard.* Reading the set and changing it are now two places.
-  The person returns to step 2 when the shared screen is done, and this page
-  cannot say whether it was opened or what changed while it was.
-- *No parameter control on the summary.* The values are not on this page at all,
-  so a person who wants to check one setting leaves the wizard. That is
-  deliberate: a read-only summary that also drew the settings would be the second
-  implementation again.
-- *The three variants move.* They read the per-analytic step, so the open layout
-  question travels to the shared prototype with the screen it belongs to. This
-  page has no =?variant=.
-
-The state it keeps is the one this journey is about: which rows are on, in which
-order, which rows were kept off rather than deleted, and whether the pair
-=pfe= and =simulation= can run.
-
-** The toggle writes =active=, and never deletes
-
-This page states the rule even though it does not draw the control: turning an
-analytic off is a write of =active = false=. The row keeps its =display_order= and
-its =configuration_analytic_parameter= rows, and reads as off, so the history
-shows the report used to produce it. A type the configuration never carried reads
-as "no row" on the summary, and the shared screen offers it as a type to add.
-**No control anywhere removes a row.**
-
-** The incompatibility is a state, not a sentence**
-
-=pfe= reads a cube that =simulation= writes, so =pfe= on without =simulation=
-cannot work. Step 2 marks the pair in red on the summary, with a tag on each side
-naming what is broken, and it names the rule: it lives in the ACME seeder, in
-=generate_risk_config_data.py=, function =check_exposure_needs_simulation=, and in
-no service, so the write would be accepted and the run would fail later. The
-refusal of the write itself belongs to Manage the analytics, which will not write
-either row of the pair while it is broken.
-
-** What is deferred**
-
-=simulation= and =pfe= need purpose-built editors for the cube, the shift and the
-time grid. Manage the analytics draws those settings as plain fields and labels
-each one a deferred editor on the parameter itself. This page says so once and
-names the screen, rather than drawing the fields a second time.
-
-** What the change reaches, and what it does not**
-
-A run keeps the configuration it ran with, with its outputs and its errors. The
-configuration is shared, so a change reaches every definition bound to it,
-including the three the person did not open. Nothing reaches the definition's
-schedule, its processing phases, its concurrency policy or its other four
-configurations.
-
-** The runs that stop being comparable**
-
-The results screen compares a run with a previous run of the same definition. A
-run made after a change did not produce the same measures, so the comparison
-between it and an older run is not a comparison, and step 3 says that plainly. It
-places each run by its own start time against the definition's version history and
-marks the placement an inference, because **no operation says which configuration
-version a run used** and the analytics are not on the definition. The results
-screen marks a comparison partial where a side carried errors; it cannot mark this
-case at all.
-
-** What is fake**
-
-The definition, the five bindings, the eight analytic rows, the convention sets
-with their names, purposes, descriptions and kind counts, the runs, the versions
-and the clock are fixtures. Nothing reads a server and the page sends nothing.
-The rules are not fixtures: =active = false= is how the model turns an analytic
-off, and =pfe= without =simulation= is a rule the seeder enforces and no service
-does. The convention sets are a fixture for a reason the page states: no table
-stores a set's name or purpose, nothing marks the document a run reads for a
-kind, and the conventions configuration carries no children. Authoring a set is
-deferred to its own work, so the link out on that page opens nothing.
-
-** Where the code lives**
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/change-what-a-report-runs/=. Three files, plain HTML,
-CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step. The stepper is this page's
-own; the standard steps UI belongs to Manage the analytics, because this journey
-is three panels about one definition rather than a walk through a set.
-
-** The verdict**
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review.
-
-** What it does not settle**
-
-Which runs a change reached. Until an operation names the configuration version
-behind a run, every placement on this page is an inference, and a build can only
-repeat that inference. The parameter's allowed values are unsettled too: no
-operation in the journey's set reads the value domain, so the shared screen draws
-a select only where its fixture knows the enumeration and a text field where it
-does not. The four configuration types without a screen are unsettled in the plain
-sense: nothing shows them, so step 1 can only say where the data lives. And it does
-not settle what a wizard should do when one of its steps is finished on another
-screen.
-
-* See also

-#+title: Choose when a report runs prototype
-#+description: Three structural variants of scheduling a report, on a throwaway page that states the missing scheduler read, the absent pause operation and the absent time zone.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                             |
-|---------------+---------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:choose-when-a-report-runs/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                              |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]            |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues where scheduling lives: on the report, in a schedule list,
-or on a calendar. It carries three structural variants switched with =?variant=,
-and it answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_choose_when_a_report_runs.org][Choose when a report runs]].
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, and the page says plainly which parts of a
-scheduler it cannot show.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-A schedule is one field on a report definition, but "what runs tomorrow morning"
-is a question about the whole set. Those two readings want different screens, and
-the open question is which one earns the space.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | On the report | Scheduling is a field group on the report: a cadence and a time, edited in place, with the next fire times under it. |
-| =B= | A schedule list | One row per schedule, scanned and edited together, so the whole week is answerable in one view. |
-| =C= | A calendar | A weekly grid of when reports fire, each report in its slots, so clashes and quiet nights are visible before they happen. |
-
-All three carry the same four actions beside a schedule, and none of them folds
-one action into another.
-
-** The four actions are four
-
-Run now starts one run at once and changes no schedule: it sends
-=reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance=. Pause keeps the schedule and stops it
-firing. Play starts it firing again on the same expression. Unschedule removes the
-schedule, so the definition becomes on demand: it sends
-=reporting.v1.ops.unschedule_report_definitions=.
-
-Pause and Unschedule are the pair people confuse, so the page says what separates
-them. A paused schedule keeps its expression and its scheduler job, and firing
-starts again after Play. An unscheduled definition keeps neither, so there is
-nothing to resume. **Pause and Play have no operation.** The scheduler job carries
-=is_active= in =ores_scheduler_job_definitions_tbl=, so the data can express a
-paused schedule and nothing exposes it to a reporting screen. The paused row the
-page draws, and the Pause and Play buttons, are a fixture, and the amber note says
-so.
-
-** What the page refuses to invent
-
-Three operations exist: =reporting.v1.ops.trigger_report_instance=,
-=reporting.v1.ops.schedule_report_definitions= and
-=reporting.v1.ops.unschedule_report_definitions=, and a definition carries a
-schedule expression. **There is no pause or play operation, no read or write of a
-scheduler job from this screen, and no time zone on the schedule.** The calendar
-variant shows an installation clock and says the times are derived from the
-expression, and the note says a built screen could not show a job's state, its
-last firing or its next due time. A scheduler dashboard drawn as though the
-server served it would be a lie a reviewer could not see.
-
-** What a schedule does and does not reach
-
-A schedule sets when the run starts. It does not change the report's inputs, its
-portfolio or its outputs. Run now starts one run and leaves the schedule alone.
-Pause stops the firing and keeps the schedule, and Unschedule removes it. None of
-the four touches a run already produced or cancels a run in flight. Only a tenant
-administrator may schedule, and only for
-reports their own party owns; every other role reads the cadence and nothing more.
-The page states the party constraint rather than hiding it behind a disabled
-button.
-
-** What is fake
-
-The cadences, the next fire times, the reports and the paused schedule are mock.
-Nothing reads a server, and the application has no reporting UI today. Pause and
-Play have no operation, so the paused row and those two buttons are a fixture. The
-next fire times are computed from the expression in the page, which is what a
-person is actually judging when they set a cadence.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/choose-when-a-report-runs/=. Three files, plain HTML,
-CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-The time zone, which the schedule does not carry at all. Until it does, a
-calendar that draws a local week is drawing a promise the server cannot keep.
-
-* See also
-
-- [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]] — the group, and the axis this prototype turns on.
-- [[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/reporting.org][Reporting journeys]] — the five journeys these answer to.

-#+title: Create a report prototype
-#+description: Creating a report on the standard steps UI: seven fixed steps, the analytics the bound configuration carries read only on step 7, and a final review, on a throwaway page that hands analytic management to its own prototype and states the missing scope write, the absent service check behind the pfe rule, and the four configuration types with no screen.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                             |
-|---------------+---------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:create-a-report/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                              |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]            |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype draws the act of creating a report on the standard steps UI, the
-one the system bootstrap journey uses. Eight steps: what the report is, one step
-for each of the five configuration types it binds, the analytics the bound run
-settings configuration carries, and the final review. It answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_create_a_report.org][Create a report]].
-
-Step 7 is the *entry point* to the analytics, not a second implementation of
-them. It reads the set the bound configuration holds — the count that is on, the
-list with their =display_order=, the rows kept off, and the incompatibility state
-when =pfe= is on without =simulation= — and it links to
-[[file:manage-the-analytics.org][Manage the analytics]], which owns the
-interaction. Its rail carries no analytic step, and it has no switchboard.
-
-The shape is decided, so the page carries one reading and no structural
-switcher. It used to argue three variants of the same content, and it used to
-draw a switchboard and a step per analytic; *Why the rail is fixed at eight*
-records what replaced them and what the consolidation costs.
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, and the page says plainly which parts of
-the definition it cannot write.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question the screen answers
-
-Creating a report is not one write. It is a definition, five configuration
-bindings, and a scope, and none of them sits in the same table. The person has to
-hold all of it while answering one question: *can this report actually run?* The
-journey is the way of asking it one step at a time. One step for all five
-configurations answered "what does this slot supply" and left "what does binding
-it decide" to the reader, so the page gives each configuration its own step and
-its own argument.
-
-The analytics are the other half of that question. They are not the definition's
-rows, they are the bound configuration's, and another screen manages them; so
-step 7 reads them and says whose they are, and the person who wants to change
-them has one place to go.
-
-** The standard steps UI, and where it is copied from
-
-The steps UI is not invented here. The rail, its marks and the step foot are
-copied from =doc/prototypes/setup/first-run/prototype.css= and
-=doc/prototypes/setup/first-run/prototype.js=, which copy =JourneyPage.tsx= and
-the journey runtime:
-
-- =.journey=, a grid of =14rem 1fr= with the rail left, and its 820px collapse;
-- =.railnav ol= and =.railentry= with its =.done=, =.current= and =.ahead=
-  states;
-- =.railmark= with the same three states, a tick once a step is behind the
-  person and its number otherwise;
-- =.stepfoot= with =.ml-auto= for the primary action.
-
-The rail is drawn from one list, so the rail, the step numbering and the step
-foot cannot disagree, as the runtime requires. A step is data: an id, a title, a
-lead sentence, a body and a final flag
-([[file:../../knowledge/ui/ux_language.org][UX Language]], sections *The rail*
-and *A step's body*). Going back is refused at the first step and at a step that
-is final. The review is final, so it draws no Back, and its rail entry carries a
-*final* tag so the rail says so too.
-
-The standard rail knows position only: done, current or ahead. It cannot say how
-many items a save would refuse, because the runtime never asks it to.
-
-** The rail, and why it is fixed at eight
-
-| Position | Step | What it draws |
-|----------+------+---------------|
-| 1 | What it is | The name, the description, the report type as a combo box over the type table, =is_official=, and the concurrency policy. |
-| 2 | The conventions it binds | One page of named convention sets: a row per set with its name, its purpose, the kinds it covers and whether this report uses it, a radio to choose one, and one link out to the authoring UX. |
-| 3 | The pricing engines it binds | The same four parts for =pricing_engines=, with no screen stated plainly. |
-| 4 | The market data it binds | The same four parts for =todays_market=, with no screen stated plainly. |
-| 5 | The curve configuration it binds | The same four parts for =curve_configuration=, with no screen stated plainly. |
-| 6 | The run settings it binds | The same four parts for =risk_report_config=, plus the portfolio and book scope the configuration carries. |
-| 7 | What it runs | The analytics the bound configuration carries, read only: the count on, every row with its =display_order= and a one-line summary, the rows kept off, the rule strip, and the link to Manage the analytics. |
-| 8 | Review and save | Every field value, the five bindings, the analytics and their settings as the configuration holds them, the scope, then =report_definitions.put= and the row read back. |
-
-The five configuration steps follow the order =report_type_configuration_types=
-states and the seeder writes: =conventions=, =pricing_engines=,
-=todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and =risk_report_config=. Each carries the
-same four parts, so two of them can be read side by side.
-
-The rail was computed from what the report runs: seven fixed steps, one step per
-analytic that was on in =display_order=, then the review. That made a report with
-every analytic on draw twenty-two entries, and it made this page the second place
-that configured an analytic. Both are gone. The rail is now eight steps and it
-does not move, and the analytic steps live where the analytic controls live.
-
-** Why the rail is fixed at eight
-
-The product owner asked for one prototype to own analytic management. Two
-prototypes were answering the same question in two designs: this one with a
-switchboard and a rail step per analytic, and
-[[file:change-what-a-report-runs.org][Change what a report runs]] with a
-switchboard and a nested list-detail-effect flow. The same fourteen types had two
-vocabularies for the same three states — on, off, and no row — and the parameters
-of an analytic were drawn twice.
-
-The consolidation is a deletion on this page:
-
-- the analytic steps leave the rail, so the rail no longer renumbers and the deep
-  links no longer have to survive a moving number;
-- the switchboard, the on/off control, the confirmation and the parameter
-  controls leave the page, so nothing here writes a =configuration_analytic= or a
-  =configuration_analytic_parameter= row;
-- step 7 becomes a reading and a link.
-
-What it costs is a step out of the journey. A person who wants to change the set
-while creating a report leaves the wizard, changes the set on the shared screen,
-and comes back to step 7 with the set it now holds. The page cannot say whether
-that screen was opened, and the review cannot warn about a change made in another
-tab. The alternative was two screens owning the same rows, which is worse.
-
-** Deep links
-
-=?step=N= is numeric over the eight steps, and it is stable, because the rail
-does not move. =?pfe=without-simulation= opens the draft with the rule broken, so
-the rule strip on step 7 can be read without changing two rows by hand. Neither
-this page nor anything outside it carries an analytic's step number: an analytic
-has no step here any more.
-
-** The analytics belong to the configuration, not the definition
-
-The picker offers the fourteen analytic types: =npv=, =sensitivity=,
-=cashflow=, =curves=, =simulation=, =saccr=, =parametricVar=,
-=portfolioDetails=, =creditcurves=, =pfe=, =calibration=, =pnlExplain=,
-=historicalSimulationVar= and =xva=. Each carries an =active= flag and a
-=display_order=, and turning one off sets =active= false rather than deleting the
-row.
-
-The rows hang off the configuration, and the configuration is shared, so the set
-a person reads on step 7 is the set other definitions also run. The page says so
-on step 7 and again in the review. *What it runs* is step 7, after the run
-settings step that carries the analytic rows, so the person changes a set they
-have just chosen — on the screen that owns it.
-
-** One step for each of the five configurations
-
-A definition binds configurations of exactly five types: =conventions=,
-=pricing_engines=, =todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and
-=risk_report_config=. Four of them own a step that carries the same four parts, so
-a reader comparing two of them compares like with like. Conventions is the
-exception and is described at the end of this section.
-
-1. *What binding it means.* The argument, in plain words and grounded in the
-   type's own model, because the five do not decide the same thing. Binding
-   =conventions= decides what a trade means: the day count, the calendars, the
-   payment frequency and the index every trade is read with. Binding
-   =pricing_engines= decides how a trade is priced: the model and the engine of
-   each product. Binding =todays_market= decides what it is priced from, and
-   which configuration block each market role reads. Binding
-   =curve_configuration= decides which recipes the run has, because without the
-   recipe the curve is not built whatever the market quotes. Binding
-   =risk_report_config= decides how the run behaves, and it carries the analytics
-   and the scope.
-2. *Where the data lives.* The model files, named, so the argument can be
-   checked: =projects/ores.refdata/modeling/= for the convention entities and the
-   curve configuration, =projects/ores.analytics/modeling/= for the pricing
-   models and today's market, =projects/ores.reporting/modeling/= for the run
-   settings. Each step names its own tables and says which one holds which part.
-3. *The picker.* One combo box over the configurations of that type the party
-   holds, from =configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code=, with the count of
-   definitions already bound to the one chosen.
-4. *What it reaches, and what it does not.* Two lists. The reach is what changes
-   in the next run of every definition binding the configuration; the limit is
-   what the binding leaves alone, such as the market data a pricing engine
-   configuration does not name, or the quotes a curve configuration does not
-   hold.
-
-Each step also states the screen that holds the type's data. *Only conventions
-has one*, at =PATHS.conventions=, =/refdata/conventions=. =pricing_engines=,
-=todays_market=, =curve_configuration= and =risk_report_config= have no screen in
-the application, and their steps say so rather than drawing a link that would not
-resolve.
-
-** The conventions step is one page of named sets
-
-Conventions are named convention sets. A set carries a name, a purpose and a
-description, and it covers some of the 26 convention kinds. A system holds few of
-them, and each one is clearly named and clearly purposed, so the report's whole
-conventions UX is a choice: one row per set, a radio to bind one, and one link
-out for the person who finds that no set fits.
-
-The step draws nothing else. There is no per-kind table, no alternative per kind
-for a person to weigh, no provenance card and no migration state. Those belong to
-authoring a set, which is a separate UX: it is not in this MR, the link to it is
-marked as such, and it opens nothing. The story *Name the convention sets a
-report chooses* holds the decision and the gaps.
-
-Every name, purpose, description and kind count in the list is a fixture, and the
-page says so. No table carries a name or a purpose column for a set, nothing marks
-the document a run reads for a kind, and the conventions configuration carries no
-children, so the list stands in for those columns until the story lands.
-
-** The scope is read off the configuration
-
-The scope is not a field of the definition. It is a column of the
-=risk_report_config= in the slot, held in that row's portfolio and book junction
-tables, and no operation in the journey's set writes it. *The run settings it
-binds* — step 6 — therefore reads the scope off the bound configuration and states
-which configuration carries it, rather than offering a portfolio to choose. The
-step says why the definition chooses no portfolio: the scope lives on the
-configuration, and two definitions that bind one configuration read one scope.
-The configurations and their scopes on this page are the seeder's.
-
-** The review names the field values
-
-The final step states values rather than counting them: the definition's fifteen
-fields including the ones that stay empty (=fsm_state_id=, =schedule_expression=,
-=scheduler_job_id=, =run_grant_id=, =prepared_input_key=), one binding row per
-configuration type, the analytic rows with their =active= and =display_order=,
-and the parameter rows with their values. The analytics and their settings are
-drawn as the bound configuration holds them and marked as read here and written
-on the shared screen: this page writes neither. The save is refused while an item
-is open, because the definition would read back unlike the review. After the
-save, the read-back panel states the stored row, that the definition is on
-demand, and that it has never run.
-
-** What is deferred
-
-The complex editors for =simulation= and =pfe= — the cube, the shift and the time
-grid — are drawn as plain fields on Manage the analytics, and that page labels
-each one a deferred editor. This page says only that they are deferred and names
-the screen that draws them. Authoring a convention set is deferred too, and to its
-own work: this page draws the choice between sets and the link to that UX, and it
-draws no way to name a set, state its purpose or choose the kinds it holds.
-Likewise the scope: a person who needs a portfolio no
-configuration carries cannot state it here, because no operation writes the
-scope, and that is a gap the journey records rather than this page invents round.
-
-** What the page refuses to invent
-
-No BFF route serves reporting, and nothing in the application creates a report
-today. No operation writes or reads the portfolio scope or the run settings
-inside a =risk_report_config=. Nothing answers what a report needs in order to
-run beyond the configuration types its report type requires. Four of the five
-configuration types have no screen, and the prototype states that instead of
-drawing a route. Nothing stages an analytic set for one definition, so step 7 is
-a view over rows already written to a shared configuration, and the page says so
-instead of pretending the draft is private. The operations named are the
-journey's own; no subject is invented for the gaps.
-
-** What is fake
-
-Every value is a fixture: the party, the configurations and their binding counts,
-the scopes, the analytic settings, the identifier the save would return, and the
-convention sets with their names, purposes, descriptions and kind counts.
-Nothing reads a server and nothing is written. =?pfe=without-simulation= opens
-the draft with the rule broken, so the state can be read without changing two
-rows by hand. =?step=N= lands on a step.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/create-a-report/=. Three files, plain HTML, CSS and
-JavaScript, no framework, no modules, no fetch, and no build step. The rail is
-=rail()=, and every navigation reads that one function.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Whether a person should be able to create an analytic set, a configuration or a
-scope from this screen at all, or only choose among the ones the party already
-holds. The journey answers "choose", because nothing here can write those rows; a
-build that wants to answer "create" needs operations this journey does not have.
-It also does not settle what the rail should show about a set that cannot run: the
-standard rail marks position, not readiness, so the state is carried by the rule
-strip on step 7 and by the review's refusal, and nowhere on the rail itself. And
-it does not settle how a wizard should feel when one of its steps is completed on
-another screen.
-
-* See also

-/* Create a report. Self-contained: published by the site build through its
- * existing css project, so there is no import to wire.
- *
- * The design tokens are the application's own, copied from
- * projects/ores.web/packages/web/src/styles.css, so the screen reads in the
- * colours the real one uses. The prototype's own chrome -- the banner and the
- * foot bar -- is deliberately unlike the design on trial.

-/* Create a report. Self-contained: plain JavaScript, mock data, no framework,
- * no build step, and nothing that outlives the page.
- *
- * See doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_create_a_report.org.
- *
- * The shape is decided: this screen is the standard steps UI, the one the
- * system bootstrap journey uses. The rail, its done/current/ahead marks and the
- * step foot are copied from doc/prototypes/setup/first-run/, which copies
- * JourneyPage.tsx.
- *
- * The rail is computed from the draft, not written out. Seven fixed steps, one
- * step per analytic that is on, in display_order, and the final review:
- *
- *   1  What it is                  the name, the description, the report type,
- *                                  is_official, and the concurrency policy
- *   2  The conventions it binds    the named convention sets the party holds,
- *   3  The pricing engines it binds  one row each with a radio, and a link out
- *   4  The market data it binds      to the authoring UX. No per-kind table.
- *   5  The curve configuration it binds
- *   6  The run settings it binds     the other four are pickers, because binding
- *                                  a configuration means something different for
- *                                  each type
- *   7  What it runs                the fourteen analytic types, one row each:
- *                                  the switch, the order and a one-line summary.
- *                                  The index of the analytic steps that follow.
- *   then one step per analytic that is on, in display_order, each titled with
- *        the analytic's name and carrying what it is, how it is calculated and
- *        every parameter with a control chosen for its shape.
- *   final  Review and save        every field value, the bindings, the analytics
- *                                  with their settings, then report_definitions.put
- *                                  and the read-back. It is final, so it draws no
- *                                  Back.
- *
- * Turning an analytic on is how one is added: it writes the row with its default
- * settings and its step appears in the rail, renumbering the steps after it.
- * Turning one off asks first, sets active false, and removes the step. The rail,
- * the step numbering and the foot bar are one list, so they agree at every
- * moment.
- *
- * Four of the five configuration steps carry the same four parts: what binding
- * a configuration of that type means, where its data lives, the picker for the
- * configuration this report binds, and what the binding reaches and does not.
- * The conventions step is the exception: it is one page of named convention
- * sets, and choosing one with the radio is the whole of the binding. It draws
- * no per-kind row, because what a set holds is decided in authoring, which has
- * its own UX and is not in this MR.
- *
- * Deep links: ?step=N is numeric over the current rail, and ?analytic=<code>
- * resolves to that analytic's step whatever its number. Navigation rewrites both,
- * so a reload lands on the same step. ?pfe=without-simulation opens the draft
- * with the rule broken.
- *
- * Three absences the copy never hides:
- *
- *  - the portfolio scope is a column of the bound risk report config and no
- *    operation in this journey's set writes it, so the step reads the scope
- *    off the configuration rather than offering a choice;
- *  - pfe reads a cube simulation writes, and the rule that pairs them lives in
- *    the ACME seeder (generate_risk_config_data.py,
- *    check_exposure_needs_simulation) and not in the reporting service, so the
- *    refusal on this page is the screen's own rule;
- *  - no screen exists for four of the five configuration types. Only
- *    conventions has a route, PATHS.conventions = /refdata/conventions.
- *
- * Nothing here sends a message. The operations named are the journey's own. */

-#+title: Find out why a run went wrong prototype
-#+description: Three structural variants of a run's errors, rendering twenty-one real rows including one trade that failed in two analytics.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:

-| Item          | Where                                                |
-|---------------+------------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                                 |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]               |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues the sharpest question of the five: whether errors are a
-place you go, a panel beside the run, or a ledger across runs. It carries three
-structural variants switched with =?variant=, and it answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_find_out_why_a_run_went_wrong.org][Find out why a run went wrong]].
-
-It is throwaway. The rows are mock, copied from a real run whose market data was
-removed.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-An error is not an entity a person manages. It is a fact about a run, and the
-person reading it arrived from somewhere: a failure they were told about, a
-number they do not believe, or a party-wide question about what is broken. Which
-of those the screen is built for decides its shape.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | A tab on the run | Errors are one tab of the run, beside the outputs and the timeline, with the count on the tab. You go there deliberately. |
-| =B= | A panel beside the run | The run stays visible and the errors sit beside it, filterable, so a failure is read against the run it belongs to. |
-| =C= | A ledger across runs | The errors are the screen, all runs together, grouped by scope and subject, with the run as a column. For "what is broken across my party right now". |
-
-** The rows
-
-The page renders twenty-one rows from one run: nineteen errors and two warnings,
-across one =Curve=, sixteen =Trade=, three =Analytics= and one =Configuration=
-row. The scopes are exactly the vocabulary the server holds: =Trade=,
-=Analytics=, =Curve=, =Configuration=, =Report=. The severities are exactly
-=error= and =warning=.
-
-** The row that makes this prototype worth having
-
-One trade failed in both =PRICING= and =SA_CCR=. The engine wrote the same
-scope, the same subject, the same trade UUID and the same message twice, and only
-=detail= tells the two apart. The page draws both rows, side by side and
-visibly, with a pair marker and a plain sentence that the two differ only in
-detail. A screen that collapses them loses a fact.
-
-** What the errors are not
-
-Immutable and read as a group. There is no edit, no delete and no acknowledge,
-and the page draws none of them. The run names who asked and when; an error
-carries =event_time= and no actor.
-
-** What is fake
-
-The rows, the run and the party are mock. Nothing reads a server, no operation
-serves a run's errors to a browser today, and the application has no reporting UI.
-The error model itself is real: the scopes, the severities, the subject and
-subject id pair, and the immutability are what the server enforces.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong/=. Three files, plain
-HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review. The
-requirement it settles whatever else changes is that two rows differing only in
-=detail= must both be visible.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Whether a person can reach a trade or an analytic from its error. The subject is
-a discriminator and a value, not a foreign key, so a link to the trade is a
-screen concern the server does not yet answer.
-
-* See also
-
-- [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]] — the group, and the axis this prototype turns on.
-- [[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/reporting.org][Reporting journeys]] — the five journeys these answer to.

-/* Reporting: find out why a run went wrong. Throwaway prototype:
- * self-contained, plain JavaScript, mock data, no framework, no build step,
- * and nothing that outlives the page.
- *
- * See doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_find_out_why_a_run_went_wrong.org.
- *
- * The question this page exists for: are a run's errors a place you go, a
- * property of the run you are already looking at, or a ledger across the
- * party's runs? Three answers, switched by ?variant=A|B|C:
- *
- *   A  one tab of the run, beside the outputs and the timeline. The count is
- *      on the tab. You go there deliberately.
- *   B  a panel beside the run. The run stays visible, the rows are filterable
- *      by scope and severity, and a failure is read against its run.
- *   C  a ledger across runs. The screen is the rows themselves, grouped by
- *      scope and then by subject, with the run as a column.
- *
- * Every row is a fixture. The twenty-one rows of the first run are copied from
- * a real run of SA-CCR Exposure whose market data had been removed; the other
- * two runs of the same report are fixtures too. Nothing here reads a server:
- * no operation and no BFF route serves a run's errors to a browser today, and
- * no reporting screen exists in the application.
- *
- * The error model is the spine of the page and every variant obeys it: a row
- * carries severity, scope_code, message and a subject with a subject_id, or it
- * names no subject at all; the subject is a discriminator plus a value and is
- * treated as a value, never as a link; a row carries event_time and no actor;
- * and no row is ever merged with another. Two rows of one trade with one
- * message are told apart by detail alone, and that difference is drawn. */
-

-    'use strict';
-
-    /* The scope vocabulary, in the order the engine's words read best: the
-       curve a trade needed, the trade, the analytic, the input, the run. The
-       membership is exactly these five and a row never invents a sixth. */
-    var ORDER = ['Curve', 'Trade', 'Analytics', 'Configuration', 'Report'];
-
-    var SCOPE_NOTE = {

-#+title: Reporting prototypes
-#+description: The prototypes that answer to the reporting journeys: what each argues, and the three interpretations every one of them offers.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:index:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-* Summary
-
-The reports a party runs, what each produced, what went wrong, and when the next
-one starts. Seven journeys describe that work, and there is no reporting surface
-in the application at all today, so nothing here has prior art to copy.
-
-10 prototypes answer to this group: one per journey, and one that two of them
-hand the analytics to. Each is a static page under =doc/prototypes/=, opens with
-no build and no session, and reads mock data only. The table below opens each one
-and says what it argues. Where a prototype carries a Gemini review, the last
-column opens it.
-
-The conventions have no prototype of their own. They are named convention sets,
-and the report chooses one: Create a report and Change what a report runs each
-carry that choice on one page. Authoring a set is its own UX, addressed outside
-this work, and the prototype that used to argue a per-kind interaction inside the
-reporting group has been retired.
-
-[[file:../index.org][Prototypes]] is the top page and the only inventory.
-
-* One decision, an axis for each journey
-
-The journeys are not a screen plan. Reading them one to one would give nine
-screens for one job, and nobody would build it that way.
-
-The decision this set exists to inform is what the reporting surface is, and how
-many screens own it. Each prototype offers three structural variants of its own
-journey, and each turns on the question that journey actually poses rather than
-one frame forced onto all nine. Forcing a single axis was tried first and it
-broke down: the question a catalogue asks is not the question a result asks.
-
-What is shared is the method. Three variants, one switcher, the same chrome, and
-the same rule that the variants disagree about structure and not colour.
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Prototype | The axis its three variants turn on |
-|-----------+-------------------------------------|
-| See the reports a party runs | What the front door is: the catalogue of reports, a ledger of runs, or only what needs a human. |
-| Run a report and watch it finish | Where waiting happens: a strip that reports itself while you work, a dedicated view you stay in, or a queue you watch together. |
-| Read what a run produced | What the result is: the numbers and the trade rows under them, the archive of files, or a sentence about the numbers. |
-| See a report's results by counterparty | How a result is read by counterparty: a ranked list of names, a tree through the group each one nests under, or a map of how concentrated the run is. |
-| Find out why a run went wrong | Whether errors are a place you go, a panel beside the run, or a ledger across runs. |
-| Choose when a report runs | Where scheduling lives: on the report, in a schedule list, or on a calendar. |
-
-The prototypes are not meant to be read as one design with nine parts. They are
-nine answers to nine different questions, drawn in one voice so that the
-answers can be compared.
-
-* The prototypes
-
-#+ATTR_HTML: :class hug-leading
-| Prototype | What it argues | Open it | Review |
-|-----------+----------------+---------+--------|
-| [[file:see-the-reports-a-party-runs.org][See the reports a party runs]] | The front door of reporting: which reports this party runs and how each one last went, with a run that completed while carrying errors told apart from a clean one without opening it. | [[file:see-the-reports-a-party-runs/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish.org][Run a report and watch it finish]] | A run is six phases and seven workflow steps, and the person waiting needs to know when to stop waiting. The three variants disagree about whether watching is a place you go or a strip that reports itself while you work. | [[file:run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:read-what-a-run-produced.org][Read what a run produced]] | What "the result" is: the numbers with the per-trade rows beneath them, the archive, or a sentence about the numbers. The drill-down runs from a run's figures to one trade's NPV and its error. The result also rolls up as a book tree: a portfolio, a nested sub-portfolio, a book, and a trade, with a trade booked to no book shown as an unbooked node. The gap is stated rather than drawn round, because no operation lists the files inside a run's archive, none parses them, and none returns a result grouped by book. It also plots the result in the form each set of numbers asks for, from a stated vocabulary and a stated rule that picks between them: sorted bars of NPV, Delta and Gamma by book, a donut of each book's share of the run and a donut of the run's problems by scope, grouped bars of Delta against Gamma, a scatter of Gamma against Delta, stacked bars of the problems of the two runs the comparison pairs, a signed bar chart of the change against the baseline, and a line of NPV across the runs of the definition with the current run and the baseline marked. A plot whose figure the errors left partial carries the same partial marking the figure carries, a donut draws the excluded part as a hatched slice named excluded, and a count with no magnitude to compare stays a table. | [[file:read-what-a-run-produced/][prototype]] | [[file:read-what-a-run-produced/review/][review]] |
-| [[file:see-a-reports-results-by-counterparty.org][See a report's results by counterparty]] | One run read by counterparty rather than by book, which is the question a credit reader or a limit conversation starts with. It ranks names by their aggregate NPV, notional, trade count and exposure, keeps a group above its members because counterparties nest through the parent, opens one name to its trades, netting sets and errors, and draws a counterparty with no result and a trade naming no counterparty as stated cases. The gap is stated on the page, because nothing parses the run's archive and npv.csv names the counterparty instead of identifying it by id. | [[file:see-a-reports-results-by-counterparty/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong.org][Find out why a run went wrong]] | The sharpest question of them: are errors a place you go, a panel beside the run, or a ledger across runs. It renders twenty real error rows, including one trade failing in two analytics with the same message. | [[file:find-out-why-a-run-went-wrong/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:choose-when-a-report-runs.org][Choose when a report runs]] | Where scheduling lives: on the report, in a schedule list, or on a calendar. It keeps run now, pause, play and unschedule apart, and states that the schedule has no time zone, that no scheduler read exists for this screen, and that pause and play have no operation. | [[file:choose-when-a-report-runs/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:look-back-over-a-reports-history.org][Look back over a report's history]] | The runs of one report newest first, each with its timestamp, the newest marked latest, the last five fire times, and a notice when the run being read stops being the newest. A trend line of the report's exposure sits above the list, with the latest run's point marked and named, every point a run's errors left partial drawn hollow and dashed, and a run that produced no figure breaking the line. Beside it sits the page's plot vocabulary and the rule that picks a form: a donut of the latest run's problems by scope, stacked bars of the problems by scope across the runs, grouped bars of the errors against the warnings, and a scatter of how long a run took against how many positions it placed. | [[file:look-back-over-a-reports-history/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:create-a-report.org][Create a report]] | Creating a report on the standard steps UI: seven fixed steps (what it is, one step for each of the five configurations it binds, and the analytics that configuration carries), then a final review that states every value and reads the row back. Step 7 is the entry point to the analytics and not a second implementation of them: it reads the set the bound configuration holds, with the count that is on, the display order, the rows kept off and the incompatibility state, and it hands the work to Manage the analytics. Step 2 is one page of named convention sets: a row per set with its name, its purpose, the kinds it covers and whether this report uses it, a radio to choose the set the report binds, and one link out to the convention authoring UX marked as not in this MR. It draws no per-kind table, and every name, purpose and count in it is a fixture, because no table stores a set's name or purpose, nothing marks the document a run reads for a kind, and the conventions configuration carries no children. | [[file:create-a-report/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:change-what-a-report-runs.org][Change what a report runs]] | A wizard over three panels: the definition and the configurations it binds, with where each one's data lives, then the analytics of the bound configuration as a read-only summary, then what a change to that set reaches. It draws no analytic control: the switchboard and the add-analytic flow are gone, and step 2 hands the analytics to Manage the analytics and states what the change reaches. A conventions configuration is a named convention set, so its row shows the set chosen on the card below, and that card is the same one page of sets the create flow draws: name, purpose, kinds covered, whether this report uses it, a radio to bind one, and one link out to authoring marked as not in this MR. Incompatibility is a visible state, so pfe without simulation is marked and the rule is named. | [[file:change-what-a-report-runs/][prototype]] | none |
-| [[file:manage-the-analytics.org][Manage the analytics]] | The one prototype that owns the analytic interaction of a run settings configuration: a switchboard of the fourteen types with the on/off control, the =display_order= and a one-line summary, a rail step for each analytic that is on in =display_order=, and a final step that reads the set back. Turning one off asks first and sets =active= false rather than deleting the row. pfe without simulation is a state with both rows marked, the refused toggle and a final step that refuses to read the set back. Three readings of the per-analytic step behind =?variant=A|B|C=: a document, two columns, and a guided walk one parameter at a time. | [[file:manage-the-analytics/][prototype]] | none |
-
-* What none of them settle
-
-Whether the seven journeys become one area, one screen, or two. That is the
-decision this set exists to inform, and it is taken after the review rather than
-here. Each prototype argues one journey; the area they share is drawn only far
-enough to judge the journey inside it.
-
-Two things are settled. Analytic management has one screen: Create a report and
-Change what a report runs used to draw the same switchboard, the same parameters
-and the same incompatibility state, in two vocabularies for the same three
-states — on, off, and a type with no row. Both now read the set and link to
-Manage the analytics, which owns it.
-
-And the conventions are chosen, not assembled. A convention set carries a name, a
-purpose and a description, a system holds few of them, and a report binds one by
-choosing it. Authoring a set is its own UX, deferred to its own work, so no
-prototype here draws a per-kind table, an alternative per kind, a provenance card
-or a migration state.
-
-* Adding a prototype
-
-Follow [[file:../index.org][Prototypes]], which has the one way. A prototype here
-is a static page, never a route in =ores.web=, and it carries a design note at
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/<name>.org= that this page links.
-
-* See also
-

-:PROPERTIES:
-:ID: 43729172-bbe6-491e-aba5-fbfba78a6861
-:END:
-#+title: Look back over a report's history prototype
-#+description: Three structural variants of one report's run history, the trend plot across its runs, the last five fire times, the latest marked, and the arrival of a newer run using the Recency pattern.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                                |
-|---------------+------------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:look-back-over-a-reports-history/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                                 |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]               |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues what a report's history is, and what happens to the person
-reading it when a newer run arrives. It carries three structural variants
-switched with =?variant=, and it answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_look_back_over_a_reports_history.org][Look back over a report's history]].
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, every value is mock, and the arrival of a
-new run is simulated by a button because a static page cannot receive an event.
-
-The history is also plotted, and the page states the plot vocabulary it draws
-from and the rule that picks a form: a donut for one whole in few parts, stacked
-bars for several wholes each split the same way, grouped bars for two series over
-the same categories, a scatter for two measures against each other, and a line
-for a change over time. The trend line stays, and beside it sit a donut of the
-latest run's problems by scope, stacked bars of the problems by scope across the
-runs, grouped bars of the errors against the warnings each run recorded, and a
-scatter of how long a run took against how many positions it placed.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-A run list is easy. The hard part is that the list is alive: a scheduled report
-produces a new run while somebody is reading an old one, and the screen has to
-say so without taking the page away from them. The second question is what "the
-history" is measured in, because the firings and the runs are not the same set.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | A run list | A table of runs newest first, the latest pinned and marked, each row with its started and completed time, and a selected run read below. |
-| =B= | A timeline | Runs down a vertical timeline with their timestamps, the current one expanded inline, so the rhythm of the schedule is visible at a glance. |
-| =C= | A comparison | The latest run beside one selected earlier run, with the differences stated, for the person asking what changed between them. |
-
-** Five fire times, and what they are really counting
-
-The panel shows the last five fire times, because a person needs to tell an
-hourly report from a daily one and to notice a window where nothing ran. Each
-time is derived from a run, and that is stated, because it is not the same thing
-as a firing. A firing that produced no run, because the concurrency policy
-skipped it or the trigger was refused, leaves no trace the screen can read.
-
-The page goes further and points at a gap. The five runs it draws are 59 minutes
-50 seconds apart except across one window where no run started, and the panel
-says so rather than smoothing the timestamps into a tidy cadence. That is what
-the honest version of this panel looks like.
-
-** The newest run is marked, and stays marked
-
-Every run carries its started and completed time to the second, and the newest is
-marked =LATEST= in a column of its own, so it is found without reading timestamps
-in order. A run that completed while carrying errors reads differently from a
-clean one at a glance.
-
-** The trend: exposure across the runs, and why it is a line
-
-A history is a series, so the page plots it. One card sits under the fire times
-and above the run list, and it carries a line of the report's SA-CCR exposure
-across every run the page holds, oldest to newest.
-
-The form is chosen by the shape of the numbers, not by decoration: a run-by-run
-series is a change over time, and a change over time is a line. The latest run's
-point is marked and named, so the line's direction has a subject; when the newest
-run is still in flight and has no figure yet, the mark falls on the newest run
-that has one, the label says so, and the caption says why the newest run is a
-break in the line rather than a point. The day boundaries are drawn as labelled
-markers, so an hourly axis keeps readable clock ticks; and the value axis states
-the range it spans instead of starting at zero, because a line of levels drawn
-from zero would flatten a series this narrow.
-
-The form of every plot on this page follows one rule, and the rule is written on
-the page beside the plots so the next person does not guess:
-
-| The numbers are | Form | The rule that chooses it |
-|-----------------+------+--------------------------|
-| One whole, few parts | Donut | One whole in not more than about six parts becomes a donut. A seventh part and the ones after it join one =other= slice, and the hole carries the total. Each part states its percentage and its value in the legend beside the slice, never on it. |
-| One whole, many parts, or parts that must be compared precisely | Horizontal bars | A pie of fifteen parts is unreadable and its angles cannot be compared. |
-| Many wholes, each split the same way | Stacked bars | One bar per whole, one segment per part, the same colour for the same part in every bar. |
-| Two series over the same categories | Grouped bars | Side by side, because a stack would make the second series a length from the end of the first. |
-| Two measures against each other | Scatter | So an outlier is visible as a point away from the rest. |
-| A change over time | Line | A change over time is a line, and a single point is not a trend. |
-| A contribution that sums to a total | Waterfall | No figure on this page is a contribution to a known total, so none is drawn as one. |
-| Exact and few | Table only | A handful of exact numbers stays a table, and nothing on this page replaces it. |
-
-What that rule draws on this page:
-
-| Numbers | Form | Why |
-|---------+------+-----|
-| SA-CCR exposure across the runs of one definition | A line, latest point marked and named | The runs of one report in order are a change over time |
-| The latest run's problems, by the scope of each | A donut, with the count in the hole and each scope's count and share in the legend | One whole in a few parts. When the latest run carries nothing, the whole is the runs of the window divided by how each ended, which is still one whole in at most four parts. |
-| The problems of each run, by scope | Stacked bars, one bar per run, one segment per scope | Several wholes, each split the same way, so the comparison is not lost inside one pie |
-| Errors against warnings, run by run | Grouped bars | Two series over the same runs and the same unit, compared side by side |
-| How long a run took against how many positions it placed | A scatter, both axes from zero | Two measures against each other, so a slow run that placed few is a distance on the plot |
-| The state of each run: completed, carrying errors, failed, in flight | A donut of the window's runs, and the run table | A state is a word, so it is a part of the window rather than a measure |
-| A report with one run | No trend | One point states no direction |
-
-A run that completed carrying errors wrote an exposure over the trades it
-placed, so its point is drawn hollow with its segment dashed, the card carries
-the same =partial= tag the run rows carry, and the caption names the runs and
-says what the errors leave out. A run that failed wrote no archive and has no
-exposure at all: the line breaks at it rather than drawing a zero, because a
-failure is not a value of zero. The exact numbers are in the table under the
-plot, one row per run, with each row's state and its =partial= mark, so the plot
-never replaces what a reader checks. The plot is inline SVG written in the
-prototype's own script: a prototype opens from =file://= with no build, no CDN
-and no network, so no chart library is loaded or copied in.
-
-A donut never hides a part the errors left out. The latest run's donut hatches
-the positions the run did not place as a slice of its own, labelled =excluded= and
-stated in the legend with its count, so the pie is the whole population the window
-priced and not a quietly smaller set. Its hole carries the two counts together,
-and the caption says which is which. A run that completed clean leaves no such
-slice, because it left nothing out.
-
-The scenario =results-with-errors=, reachable with =?scenario= set to that value,
-draws the latest run as a run that completed carrying what its errors left out: it
-adds three error rows and four unplaced positions to the fixture, the exposure
-point goes hollow and dashed, the donut's hatched slice appears, and the run's
-health changes to *completed with errors*. It arranges the run's own fixtures and
-changes no run; the page says so in a banner that carries no dismiss, because a
-partial figure a reader may put away is a figure a reader will take as whole.
-
-The exposure figure itself is a fixture, like the runs: it is what a run's
-archive says once something parses it, and nothing parses it today. The amber
-note on the page says so.
-
-** When the run being read stops being the latest
-
-This is the part the prototype exists for. The pattern is the one the record
-screen standard calls Recency, and the page follows it exactly:
-
-- The change signal is `reporting.v1.report_instances_events.created`, which the
-  screen listens to. It does not poll.
-- When a run arrives, Refresh draws the eye.
-- Rows newer than the previous load are marked for three seconds after a reload.
-  The first load marks nothing, and a person can turn the marking off.
-- A notice, not a modal, states that the run being read is no longer the latest,
-  names the new run's time, and offers a way to it. It does not navigate on its
-  own and does not steal focus.
-
-The arrival is simulated with a button in the bar, and the page says so, because
-nothing on a page opened from a file can receive an event.
-
-** What is fake
-
-Everything. The report, its party, its schedule, the twelve runs, their times,
-their durations, their errors, and the exposure each run carries are mock, so
-every point on the trend is a fixture. No service is read, there is no reporting
-BFF route, and the application has no reporting UI.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/look-back-over-a-reports-history/=. Three files, plain
-HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review. The
-part that must survive whichever variant wins is the notice: a person reading a
-superseded run is told, quietly, and is not thrown at the new one.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Whether a history belongs to a report definition or to a report type. This page
-argues a definition, because that is what the runs belong to and what the
-schedule is attached to. If a reader thinks in report types across parties, the
-page is answering a narrower question than they are asking.
-
-* See also
-

-    /* ------------------------------------------------ the form of a plot */
-    /* The vocabulary is the ordinary one, and the rule that picks a form is
-       written down here so the page states it rather than a reader guessing.
-       One whole in few parts is a donut; one whole in many parts, or parts
-       that must be compared precisely, is horizontal bars; many wholes each
-       split the same way are stacked bars; two series over the same
-       categories are grouped bars; two measures against each other are a
-       scatter; a change over time is a line; a contribution that sums to a
-       total is a waterfall; and a handful of exact numbers stays a table. */
-
-    var FORMS = [
-        {
-            id: 'donut',
-            name: 'Donut',
-            shape: 'One whole, few parts',
-            rule: 'One whole in not more than about six parts becomes a donut. A seventh part and the ones ' +
-                'after it join one \'other\' slice, and the hole carries the total. Each part states its ' +
-                'percentage and its value in the legend beside the slice, never on it.'
-        },
-        {
-            id: 'bars',
-            name: 'Horizontal bars',
-            shape: 'One whole, many parts, or exact comparison',
-            rule: 'One whole in more than about six parts, or parts that must be compared precisely, is ' +
-                'horizontal bars: a pie of fifteen parts is unreadable and its angles cannot be compared.'
-        },
-        {
-            id: 'stacked',
-            name: 'Stacked bar',
-            shape: 'Many wholes, each split the same way',
-            rule: 'More than one whole, each decomposing by the same categories, is a stacked bar: one bar ' +
-                'per whole and one segment per part.'
-        },
-        {
-            id: 'grouped',
-            name: 'Grouped bar',
-            shape: 'Two series over the same categories',
-            rule: 'Two series that share the same categories and the same unit are grouped bars, side by ' +
-                'side, so two things are compared rather than one stacked on the other.'
-        },
-        {
-            id: 'scatter',
-            name: 'Scatter',
-            shape: 'Two measures against each other',
-            rule: 'Two measures plotted against each other are a scatter, so an outlier is visible as a ' +
-                'point away from the rest.'
-        },
-        {
-            id: 'line',
-            name: 'Line',
-            shape: 'A change over time',
-            rule: 'A change over time is a line, and a single point is not a trend.'
-        },
-        {
-            id: 'waterfall',
-            name: 'Waterfall',
-            shape: 'A contribution that sums to a total',
-            rule: 'A contribution that adds up to a total is a waterfall. No figure on this page is a ' +

-:PROPERTIES:
