-#+title: Manage the analytics prototype
-#+description: The one prototype that owns the analytic interaction of a run settings configuration: a switchboard of the fourteen types, a rail step for each analytic that is on in display_order, a final step that reads the set back, and three readings of the per-analytic step behind ?variant=A|B|C.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                             |
-|---------------+---------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:manage-the-analytics/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                              |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]            |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype owns the whole analytic interaction of a run settings
-configuration: the switchboard, a step for each analytic that is on, and a final
-step that reads the set back. It is the one screen that manages analytics, and
-two prototypes that used to draw the same interaction hand the work here:
-
-- [[file:create-a-report/][Create a report]] reads the set on its step 7 and links here;
-- [[file:change-what-a-report-runs/][Change what a report runs]] reads the set on its
-  step 2 and links here.
-
-The analytics belong to the bound run settings configuration, not to a
-definition. A =configuration_analytic= row hangs off that configuration, so a
-change here reaches every definition bound to it, and a set that must differ
-belongs to a configuration of its own. The page says so on every step.
-
-The screen is the standard steps UI, the one the system bootstrap journey uses.
-The layout of the per-analytic step is the one open question, so the page carries
-three readings of that step and of nothing else, behind =?variant=A|B|C=.
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, and it states which parts of the
-interaction no operation supports.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question the screen answers
-
-A run produces a set of measures, and six tables hold that set: the
-=configuration_analytic= rows, their =configuration_analytic_parameter= rows, the
-type vocabulary, the configuration itself, the definitions bound to it, and the
-parameters each analytic accepts. The person has one question — *is this the set
-this report should produce?* — and the screen answers it one analytic at a time.
-
-Configuring an analytic inline in a list is too busy, and the settings of one
-analytic deserve room. A wizard opened from a row removes the settings from the
-rail, so the person cannot walk back to them. One step per analytic that is on
-keeps both: the settings are a step, and the rail shows the whole set in the
-configuration's own order.
-
-** The standard steps UI, and where it is copied from
-
-The steps UI is not invented here. The rail, its marks and the step foot are
-copied from =doc/prototypes/setup/first-run/prototype.css= and
-=doc/prototypes/setup/first-run/prototype.js=, which copy =JourneyPage.tsx= and
-the journey runtime:
-
-- =.journey=, a grid of =14rem 1fr= with the rail left, and its 820px collapse;
-- =.railnav ol= and =.railentry= with its =.done=, =.current= and =.ahead=
-  states;
-- =.railmark= with the same three states, a tick once a step is behind the
-  person and its number otherwise;
-- =.stepfoot= with =.ml-auto= for the primary action.
-
-The rail is drawn from one computed list, so the rail, the step numbering and the
-step foot cannot disagree, as the runtime requires. A step is data: an id, a
-title, a lead sentence, a body and a final flag
-([[file:../../knowledge/ui/ux_language.org][UX Language]], sections *The rail*
-and *A step's body*). Going back is refused at the first step and at a step that
-is final. The last step is final, so it draws no Back, and its rail entry carries
-a *final* tag so the rail says so too.
-
-** The rail shape
-
-| Position | Step | What it draws |
-|----------+------+---------------|
-| 1 | The switchboard | The fourteen analytic types, one row each: the on/off control, the =display_order=, a one-line statement of what the type produces, and the state the row is in. A type the configuration carries no row for says so and offers to add it. The rule strip. |
-| 2 to 1 + n | One per analytic that is on, in =display_order= | Titled with the analytic's name. What it is, how it is calculated, every parameter with a control chosen for its shape and a note on what it means and what a normal value is, the reach, and the control that offers to turn it off. An analytic with no parameter says so. |
-| last | What the analytics are now | The set as it now reads, the rows kept off, every parameter value, what a write would be, the definitions that read it, and the way back to the report. It is =final=. |
-
-The rail is computed from state. Turning an analytic on adds its step and
-renumbers the ones after it; turning one off removes it and renumbers them again.
-Nothing stores a step number. A configuration that carries all fourteen draws a
-rail of sixteen entries, so the column sticks to the top of the page and scrolls
-inside itself, the entries are denser, a divider opens the analytic run and
-another opens the final step, and a caption above the rail states its shape:
-"the switchboard, 6 analytics in display order, and what the analytics are now ·
-8 steps".
-
-The standard rail knows position only: done, current or ahead. It cannot say how
-many analytics a write would refuse, so the rule strip and the refused toggle
-carry that state instead.
-
-** Deep links over a rail that moves
-
-=?step=N= is numeric over the *current* rail, which is what makes it readable and
-also what makes it unstable: the number of a step moves whenever an analytic
-before it is turned on or off. So the page also accepts =?analytic=<code>=, which
-resolves to that analytic's step whatever its number, and it writes both into the
-URL as the person navigates. A reload therefore lands on the same step. An
-analytic that is off has no step, so that link lands on the switchboard with the
-row marked and the reason stated, rather than on a step that does not exist.
-
-Three more parameters open a state without a click: =?variant=A|B|C= chooses the
-reading of the analytic step, =?guide=N= opens the setting variant C is showing,
-=?pfe=without-simulation= opens the broken pair, and =?refuse=<code>= opens the
-refusal a switch draws. =?from=create-a-report|change-what-a-report-runs= decides
-where *Return to the report* goes, so the page returns to the screen that opened
-it.
-
-** The switch is the add, and off is active false
-
-- Turning a type on writes its =configuration_analytic= row at the next
-  =display_order= with the default value of every parameter, and gives it a step.
-  A row that exists and is off is turned back on with the settings it kept.
-- Turning one off *asks first*, in the row and on the analytic's own step.
-  Because the settings leave the rail with the step, the confirmation says so,
-  and it states the write: =active = false=. The row keeps its =display_order=
-  and its parameter rows, so a later reader can see the configuration used to
-  produce it.
-- **No control on the page deletes a row.** The switch is the only control that
-  removes something from the rail, and it removes the step, not the row.
-
-** pfe without simulation is a state, and the toggle is refused
-
-=pfe= reads a cube that =simulation= writes, so =pfe= on without =simulation=
-cannot work. The page draws that as a state:
-
-- the rule strip names the rule, states where it lives and marks the set as one
-  that cannot run, with the write that repairs it beside it;
-- both rows of the pair are marked, each with the half of the rule that applies
-  to it;
-- **the toggle is refused.** A switch that would leave =pfe= on without
-  =simulation= draws a refusal where it stands, with the rule and the repair, and
-  writes nothing. In the broken state the pair's switches are refused until the
-  pair is repaired, and the repair — *Turn simulation on* — is offered beside
-  them;
-- the final step **refuses to read the set back**. Reading it back would state a
-  configuration as complete that would fail in the run.
-
-The rule lives in the ACME seeder, in =generate_risk_config_data.py= at
-=check_exposure_needs_simulation=, and in no service: nothing validates it when a
-configuration is written. The page refuses what the server would accept, and it
-says that is what it is doing.
-
-Refusing the toggle is a decision with a cost, and it is the one place where this
-page is stricter than the prototype it replaces, which let =pfe= on and showed
-the break. A person who wants the broken pair cannot build it here, so it must
-arrive from elsewhere — the seeder, or another client — and the page still draws
-it. That is the trade: no state this screen can reach is a state that cannot run,
-and a broken set written elsewhere is still visible and still repairable.
-
-** Three readings of the analytic step
-
-=?variant=A|B|C= changes the per-analytic step and nothing else. The switchboard
-and the rail are identical across the three, so the comparison is of one screen.
-
-- *A, document.* The explanation as a short page, with the parameters in one
-  column below it, each with its control and its note.
-- *B, two columns.* Explanation and calculation left, settings and reach right,
-  so a person reads and sets at the same time.
-- *C, guided.* One parameter at a time with the explanation beside it, a list of
-  the settings left, and a summary at the end that states every value with a
-  control back to it. An analytic with no parameter goes straight to the summary.
-
-Variant C holds a cursor, and =?guide=N= is that cursor in the URL, so a reload
-lands on the same setting.
-
-** The final step reads the set back
-
-The last step states what the set is now, and it names the rows rather than
-counting them: each active analytic with its =display_order=, its name and its
-number of parameter rows; the rows kept off with their order; every parameter
-value with its position. Then it states what a write would be —
-=configuration_analytics.put_many= for the set and
-=configuration_analytic_parameters.put= for one setting — and the four definitions
-that read it. The table is read with
-=configuration_analytics.list_by_configuration_id= and
-=configuration_analytic_parameters.list_by_configuration_analytic_id=.
-
-It offers to return to the report, and the return goes to the prototype that
-opened the page. Nothing is written.
-
-** The deferred editors
-
-=simulation= and =pfe= each need a purpose-built editor: one for the cube, one
-for the shift and one for the time grid. The page draws those settings as plain
-fields and labels each one a *deferred editor* on the parameter itself, and it
-says so again on the analytic step. A plain field is not the design, and the page
-never presents it as one.
-
-** What the page refuses to invent
-
-No BFF route serves reporting, so the page reads nothing. No operation returns
-the value domain of a parameter, so a select is drawn only where the fixture
-knows the enumeration and a text field where it does not. No operation writes the
-portfolio scope or the run settings inside a =risk_report_config=, so the scope
-is read off the configuration and never offered as a choice
-(=reporting.v1.configurations.list= and
-=reporting.v1.configurations.list_by_configuration_type_code= name the
-configurations the party holds; none is created here). Nothing states what a run
-needs beyond the configuration types its report type requires. The subjects named
-are the reporting service's own, and no subject is invented for a gap.
-
-** What is fake
-
-Every value is a fixture: the party, the configuration, its scope, the four
-definitions bound to it, the analytic rows and every parameter value. Nothing
-reads a server and nothing is written. The page labels itself a fixture at the
-top, in the step captions and in the prototype's own bar.
-
-Two statements on it are not fixture, and the page keeps them apart from the
-mock: an analytic is turned off by setting =active= to false rather than by
-deleting the row, and =pfe= cannot run without =simulation=.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/manage-the-analytics/=. Three files, plain HTML, CSS
-and JavaScript, no framework, no modules, no fetch, and no build step. The rail
-is computed in =rail()=, and every navigation reads that one function.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-- *Which of the three readings is right.* That is the question the variants
-  exist to answer, and this note does not answer it.
-- *Whether a person should be able to create a configuration from here.* The
-  page offers the party's own configurations and creates none, because no
-  operation in this journey's set writes a configuration.
-- *What the rail should say about a step that is not fit to run.* The standard
-  rail marks position, not readiness, so a broken pair and a sound one look alike
-  on the rail itself. A build that wants the rail to carry that state needs a
-  primitive the runtime does not have.
-
-* See also
-

- *

- *                                                       here
- *
- * The rail is computed from state: a switchboard step, then one step per
- * analytic that is on in display_order, then a final step that reads the set
- * back and offers the way out. Turning an analytic on adds its step and
- * renumbers the ones after it; turning one off removes it and asks first,
- * because its parameter values go with it.
- *
- * The analytics belong to the bind run settings configuration, not to a
- * definition. Every step says so.
- *

- *
- *   ?step=N                               numeric over the current rail
- *   ?analytic=<code>                      that analytic's step, whatever its number
- *   ?variant=A|B|C                        which reading of the analytic step
- *   ?guide=N                              the setting variant C is showing
- *   ?pfe=without-simulation               open the broken pair
- *   ?from=create-a-report|change-what-a-report-runs

-#+title: Read what a run produced prototype
-#+description: Three structural variants of a run's result, the plots that fit each number, a comparison against a previous run of the same definition, and the archive listing drawn as a stated fixture.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                             |
-|---------------+---------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:read-what-a-run-produced/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | [[file:read-what-a-run-produced/review/][the review]] |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]            |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues what "the result" of a run is, and how much of it belongs
-on the screen before a person goes looking for a file. It carries three
-structural variants switched with =?variant=, and it answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_read_what_a_run_produced.org][Read what a run produced]].
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, and the archive manifest it draws is a
-fixture, said so on the page. So is the book tree: the run's archive carries no
-book column, so a node's trade count and NPV are drawn rather than read.
-
-One scenario sits beside the six runs: =results-with-errors= takes the completed
-run that carries eleven problems and draws the connection between the errors and
-the results, so the results say they are partial.
-
-The result panel also compares. A completed run carries a control that chooses a
-previous run of the same definition, or no run, and every figure, every book row,
-every tree node and the total row then carries its change against that baseline.
-The page opens with the previous run chosen, so a reviewer meets the comparison
-without hunting for it, and =?baseline=none= turns it off.
-
-The result is also plotted, in variant =A=, in the form each set of numbers
-asks for, from a stated vocabulary and a stated rule rather than bars and lines
-alone: bars for NPV and for each Greek across books, a donut for each book's share
-of the run and a donut for the run's problems by scope, grouped bars for Delta
-against Gamma, a scatter of each book's Gamma against its Delta, stacked bars for
-the problems of the two runs the comparison pairs, a signed bar chart for the
-change against the baseline, and a line of NPV across the runs of the same
-definition. Every plot carries a caption saying why that form, keeps its exact
-numbers in the table or the legend beside it, and carries the =partial= marking
-when the errors made the figure it draws partial; a donut draws the excluded part
-as a hatched slice of its own.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-A run produces an output message, an archive in storage, and a set of files
-inside that archive. Which of those is the thing a person came for? The three
-variants answer differently, and the difference decides how much of the screen is
-numbers and how much is files.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | Figures first | The numbers are the screen: headline figures, then a results table, with the archive as a modest footer action. |
-| =B= | Artefact first | The screen is a manifest of what the run produced: the archive, the files inside it with row counts and sizes, and a download per file. The numbers are a preview of one selected file. |
-| =C= | Narrative first | A short written summary of what the run did and what it means, with the figures embedded and the files at the end, for a reader who wants the sentence before the spreadsheet. |
-
-** Two things the page refuses to fake quietly
-
-The run carries an =output_storage_key= of the form
-=reporting/runs/<instance-id>/output.tar.gz=, and the page shows that shape
-rather than a friendly invented name.
-
-Neither the file list nor the two downloads exist. **No operation lists the files
-inside a run's archive**, and there is no archive download and no ORE package
-download as operations either. Variant =B= draws a manifest and labels it a
-fixture on the panel itself, so the gap is visible rather than designed around.
-That is the honest shape of this journey today.
-
-** The drill-down: from the run's figures to one trade
-
-A run's result is not only an aggregate. The engine writes =npv.csv= into the
-archive, and that file carries one row per trade, with the columns =TradeId=,
-=TradeType=, =Maturity=, =MaturityTime=, =NPV=, =NpvCurrency=, =NPV(Base)=,
-=BaseCurrency=, =Notional=, =NotionalCurrency=, =Notional(Base)=,
-=NettingSet= and =CounterParty=. The page uses them, so a person can get from
-the run's total to the trade that made it.
-
-Each variant carries the drill-down in the shape it already argues. =A= puts the
-per-trade table under the aggregate figures and keeps both. =B= offers the rows
-when =npv.csv= is selected in the manifest, instead of a handful of preview
-lines. =C= links from the prose to the table rather than reproducing the
-figures in a sentence.
-
-A row shows six columns: =TradeId=, =TradeType=, =NPV=, =NPV(Base)=,
-=Notional= and =CounterParty=. Opening a row answers with that trade's result,
-and, where the run recorded an error against that =TradeId=, the error itself.
-The page reuses the run's own error fixtures for this, so a trade that failed
-is reachable and shows why: the table covers a good number and a bad one.
-
-A trade in the result is the trading trade with that id, so the row leads to the
-trade. =trading.v1.trades.get= is what resolves the id.
-
-The table is a fixture, and the panel that draws it says so. **No operation
-parses the archive.** =ores_compute_results_tbl= carries the archive's location
-and an outcome, not parsed rows. A built screen cannot serve these rows
-until a result store or an archive read exists, and the page draws the gap
-rather than hiding it.
-
-** The book tree: portfolio, sub-portfolio, book, trade
-
-A run's results have a third reading beside the figures and the trade rows: the
-hierarchy the trades sit in. The page draws it as a tree with four levels. A
-portfolio is the top, a portfolio nests under another portfolio, a book hangs off
-a portfolio, and a trade is booked to a book. Each node states its name, its
-trade count and its aggregate NPV, and a node expands to show the books under it.
-
-The roll-up is arithmetic, not a label. A book's figure is the sum of its trades
-and a portfolio's figure is the sum of its books, and the page computes a
-portfolio from its children every time it draws, so a parent that disagrees with
-its children cannot appear. The root is the group portfolio: for Headline
-Position, 18,204 trades and USD 88,402,114, which is also the run's NPV figure.
-That 18,204 is the run's population, and the per-trade table draws 8 of those
-rows. The page says so on the tree's footer rather than implying the tree sums
-those eight rows. The footer also states how the leaves are counted: the run's
-own figure counts ten books, the fixture groups the same trades into ten book
-nodes, unbooked among them, and a trade the engine could not build writes no
-NPV row, so every priced trade sits in exactly one node and the root still adds
-up to the run. An earlier fixture counted 24 books, and that figure was
-corrected for that reason.
-
-A trade booked to no book is a real state, so the tree draws an =Unbooked= node
-at the portfolio level and gives it a trade count and an NPV like any other node.
-Dropping those trades would make the tree's total smaller than the run's and
-would hide a population that a desk has to reconcile.
-
-Selecting a node filters the per-trade table to its subtree, and each variant
-carries that in its own shape. =A= moves the aggregate figures onto the selected
-node: its NPV, its trade count, its share of the run, and how many books sit
-under it. =B= treats the tree as a lens over npv.csv, so choosing a book narrows
-the rows read out of that file while the manifest stays the whole archive. =C=
-names the largest book in the prose and links into the tree.
-
-Two gaps make every node a fixture, and the panel says both.
-
-- *The archive carries no book column.* =npv.csv='s columns are exactly
-  =TradeId=, =TradeType=, =Maturity=, =MaturityTime=, =NPV=, =NpvCurrency=,
-  =NPV(Base)=, =BaseCurrency=, =Notional=, =NotionalCurrency=, =Notional(Base)=,
-  =NettingSet= and =CounterParty=. A built screen needs the join from =TradeId=
-  to =trade_bookings.book_id= through =trading.v1.trade_bookings.list=, and no
-  operation returns results already grouped by book.
-- *No operation parses the archive*, so no node has a figure behind it either.
-  The tree is drawn from the page's own fixture, like the figures and the rows.
-
-The portfolio level has a third limit, and the tree footer states it: there is no
-=portfolios.list_by_parent_portfolio_id=, so a client assembles the portfolio tree
-from =portfolios.list=, which carries =parent_portfolio_id=.
-
-** The figures come from the analytics the configuration names
-
-A report's numbers are not free choice. Its report configuration names a set of
-analytics, and those are what the report produces. Headline Position runs =npv=
-and =sensitivity=, so the run this prototype draws shows an NPV, a Delta and a
-Gamma, and says so on the screen: the figures are the output of those two
-analytics and no others.
-
-The archive follows the same rule. A run that runs only =npv= and =sensitivity=
-does not write =cashflow.csv= or =saccr.csv=, so the manifest holds neither, and
-a second fixture run on a report that does run =saccr= shows NPV and exposure
-instead of Delta and Gamma. A reader can watch the analytic set change the
-figures.
-
-** A run can complete and still carry errors
-
-The page draws one run that completed clean and one that completed carrying
-eleven rows, eight =Analytics= errors and three =Configuration= warnings. The
-second warns before the figures are trusted, and offers the way to see why.
-
-** The scenario: results that carry errors
-
-The eleventh-row run is not enough on its own. A reader can read the notice, then
-read USD 88,402,114 under it and take the total for the whole answer, because
-nothing on the figures, the book tree or the trade table says otherwise. The
-scenario =results-with-errors= draws the connection, and a reviewer finds it by
-its chip beside the run chips, or by the query parameter =scenario= set to
-=results-with-errors=.
-
-It exercises five things, in all three variants:
-
-- A banner above the results states that they are partial and why: the engine
-  could not build three trades, 412 positions carry an NPV and no Delta, and the
-  totals below exclude them. It names the count of error rows and offers the way
-  to see them, as the completed-with-errors notice does, and it carries no
-  dismiss.
-- The aggregate figures keep their number and carry a =partial= marker and a
-  footnote, so nobody reads a total as the whole answer.
-- A book whose trades include a failed one is marked and states that its figure
-  excludes the failed trades; a portfolio above it states that it inherits the
-  exclusion, because its figure is the sum of its books.
-- The per-trade table draws each failed trade as a row with its =TradeId=, its
-  =TradeType=, its =Notional=, its =CounterParty=, an empty =NPV= and =NPV(Base)=,
-  and an =error= tag. Opening the row shows the error recorded. A trade the
-  engine could not build writes no row into =npv.csv=, so the price cells are
-  empty by nature, and the panel says so.
-- The scenario's chip is labelled, and the amber note states that the scenario is
-  a fixture like the rest of the page.
-
-Why a completed run's totals can be incomplete: =Report execution completed.=
-is the system's sentence about the run, and it is true. It says the run ended and
-retrieval finished. It says nothing about what the engine could not build. The
-archive holds a row per trade it priced, so a trade it could not build is absent
-rather than zero, and every total read from that file is a total over the trades
-that survived. The sensitivity analytic skips positions it cannot shift, so a
-Delta total covers fewer positions than the NPV beside it. Both facts are rows of
-the run, read by
-=reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id=, and no operation
-is invented for the scenario. What the scenario cannot show honestly is the join
-from a failed trade to its own error: the two =SENSITIVITY= rows are recorded
-against the analytic, and the panel says so rather than implying a per-trade key
-the model does not store.
-
-** The comparison: what changed since the last run
-
-A run's numbers answer "what is it worth now". They do not answer "what changed",
-and the second question is the one a desk asks every morning. The result panel
-therefore compares the run in view with a previous run of the same definition.
-The control offers no comparison and every completed earlier instance of the
-definition, and it prints the chosen baseline's instance id and start time beside
-the control. The page opens with the previous run chosen; =?baseline=none= turns
-the comparison off, and a run whose definition has no earlier completed instance
-says so rather than offering an empty list.
-
-Every figure keeps its value and gains the change and the percentage against the
-baseline. The by-book table gains an =NPV change= column and a =Change= column on
-every row, and a total row that carries the same change as the difference of the
-two totals and as the sum of the ten book changes. The tree gains a change column,
-so a book compares with that book and a portfolio with that portfolio, and the
-selected node drives both sides: select GBP Rates and the figures and the tree row
-describe GBP Rates in both runs. The tile is the review's pattern, kept: a label,
-the value, a note under it, and the change badge.
-
-The two sides are two fixtures. The page draws two Headline Position runs of the
-same definition: 17 October at USD 88,402,114 of NPV, USD 1,846,818 of Delta,
-USD 52,350 of Gamma over 18,204 positions in 10 books; and 16 October at
-USD 87,219,062, USD 1,818,348, USD 51,510 over 18,162 positions in the same 10
-books. Ten books, ten different changes:
-
-| Book | NPV change (USD) | Change |
-|------+------------------+--------|
-| GBP Rates | +1,400,000 | +3.5% |
-| EUR Rates | -785,716 | -2.7% |
-| USD Rates | +779,902 | +6.4% |
-| FX Options | -97,238 | -2.3% |
-| Inflation | +134,086 | +13.6% |
-| Equity | -42,030 | -13.9% |
-| Liquidity Buffer Bonds | -171,000 | -42.5% |
-| Group FX Hedges | +58,284 | +30.7% |
-| Group Intercompany Loans | +10,086 | +9.3% |
-| Unbooked | -103,322 | -87.6% |
-| Total | +1,183,052 | +1.4% |
-
-The total is the difference of the two totals, and it is also the sum of the ten
-rows, because every number is a fixture figure of one run and the change is
-subtraction. The books do not move together, which is the point: a per-metric
-multiplier would make every row move by the same percentage and the change would
-be fiction.
-
-When either run in the comparison carried errors the change is partial, because
-a total over the trades that survived is not the whole answer. The badge carries
-a =partial= marker and the panel says so once in words, with the count of problems
-and what the current run's errors leave out. The =results-with-errors= scenario is
-the deliberate case: it marks the current run's changes as partial and names the
-three unbuildable trades and the 412 positions with an NPV and no Delta. The code
-marks a baseline that carries errors the same way, though this fixture's baseline
-completed clean, so the baseline branch is not exercised by a screenshot.
-
-** The plots, the vocabulary, and the rule that chooses a form
-
-A run's result is numbers in tables, and a reader can answer some questions from
-them faster as a picture. Variant =A= therefore plots the result, and the form of
-each plot follows the shape of the numbers rather than decorating them. Bars and
-lines alone were too narrow a vocabulary: parts of one whole, several wholes each
-split the same way, two series over one set of categories and two measures plotted
-against each other are four ordinary questions that neither a bar nor a line
-answers.
-
-The rule below is written on the page as well, in the panel that draws the plots,
-so a reader of the prototype meets it where the plots are and not only here.
-
-| The numbers are | Form | The rule that chooses it |
-|-----------------+------+--------------------------|
-| One whole, few parts | Donut | One whole in not more than about six parts becomes a donut. A seventh part and the ones after it join one =other= slice with its own legend row, and the hole carries the total. Each part states its percentage and its value in the legend beside the slice, never on it. |
-| One whole, many parts, or parts that must be compared precisely | Horizontal bars | One whole in more than about six parts, or parts that must be compared precisely, is horizontal bars. A pie of fifteen books is unreadable and its angles cannot be compared. |
-| Many wholes, each split the same way | Stacked bars | More than one whole, each decomposing by the same categories, is a stacked bar: one bar per whole and one segment per part. One whole is a donut; several wholes are stacked bars. |
-| Two series over the same categories | Grouped bars | Two series that share the same categories and the same unit are grouped bars, side by side, so two things are compared rather than one stacked on the other. |
-| Two measures against each other | Scatter | Two measures plotted against each other are a scatter, so an outlier is visible as a point away from the rest rather than as two numbers a reader has to find. |
-| A change over time | Line | A change over time is a line, and a single point is not a trend. |
-| A contribution that sums to a total | Waterfall | A contribution that adds up to a total is a waterfall, so the parts and the total are one reading. |
-| Exact and few | Table only | A handful of exact numbers stays a table, and nothing on this page replaces it: a chart of three figures is harder to check than the three figures. |
-
-What that rule draws on the page:
-
-| Numbers | Form | Why, and where it appears |
-|---------+------+---------------------------|
-| NPV by book | Horizontal bars, sorted largest first, signed, from a zero rule | A magnitude compared across categories is what bars compare, and the selection of the book tree narrows it. |
-| Each book's share of the run's NPV | Donut, with the total in the hole and the share in the legend | One whole, five or six parts: the books that make up the run. Beyond the sixth, the smallest join one =other= slice, so the rim never crowds. |
-| Delta and Gamma by book | The same bar form, twice | Each Greek is a magnitude across the same books, and two charts keep the two units apart. |
-| Delta against Gamma, by book | Grouped bars | The two Greeks share the books and the unit, so they are compared side by side rather than stacked: a stack would make Gamma a length from the end of Delta. |
-| A book's Gamma against its Delta | Scatter, one point per book, both axes log decades | Two measures against each other, so a book away from the line the rest make is a distance and not a row to find. The logs are stated because the books span two orders of magnitude. |
-| The change against the baseline, by book | Bars of their own, signed, from a zero rule that is the point of no change | A change and a level are different magnitudes on different scales, so the change is its own chart and not a second series stacked into the level chart. |
-| The run's problems by scope | Donut, with the count in the hole and the scope's count and share in the legend | One whole, two parts on the fixture run: the problems the run recorded, divided by scope. |
-| The run's problems by scope, across the runs the comparison pairs | Stacked bars | Two wholes, each split the same way, so one bar per run and one segment per scope in the same colour. |
-| NPV across the runs of the definition | A line, with the current run marked and named and the baseline marked | The runs of one definition in order are a change over time, and the line is what makes the delta control legible. |
-| Positions priced, books, counterparties | No plot | A count with no magnitude to compare is a figure, not a chart: a bar of it would be a bar of nothing. |
-| One book, on its own | No plot | A chart of one bar states nothing a sentence cannot. |
-| A run with one completed instance | No trend | One point is not a trend: a line through it would state a direction the data does not have. |
-| Anything that sums to a known total | Not drawn as a waterfall | No figure on this page is a contribution to a known total. The waterfall row of the rule is written and exercised nowhere, because inventing a total to reach would be the invention. |
-
-Every pie is a donut, never a solid disc: the hole carries the total, where a
-reader looks for it, and the slices keep the rim. Every donut carries its
-percentages and its values in the legend, never on the arc, because an angle is a
-bad place to read a number. Every plot carries a title, its unit, an
-=aria-label= that lists the values a screen reader would otherwise read off the
-bars, and a one-line caption that says what it shows and why that form was
-chosen, for example *one whole, five parts*. The exact values stay in text: the
-by-book table under the plots carries every bar's figure, the trend carries a
-table of the runs it plots, and every legend states the value beside its
-percentage. A plot never replaces the figures a reader checks.
-
-Four rules keep the drawing honest.
-
-- *A bar starts at zero.* Every bar is drawn from the zero rule, so a negative
-  book reads as a bar on the other side of it. A line of levels cannot start at
-  zero without flattening the series, so it states the range of its axis in a
-  tick and in the caption: the NPV line runs from USD 83.2 m to USD 89.3 m and
-  says so rather than truncating silently. The scatter states both axes as log
-  decades for the same reason, in the axis title and in the caption.
-- *Colour comes from the tokens, one colour per book and one per scope, and the
-  same across every plot on the page.* A book keeps its colour in the donut, in
-  the grouped bars and in the scatter; a scope keeps its colour in the donut and
-  in the stacked bars, and the scope with the most rows takes the first token so
-  the heaviest part is the one the eye reaches first. The accent is spent on
-  controls and never on data, and the one place a token is spent on something
-  that is not a category is the hatched exclusion, which is the bad token because
-  an exclusion is not a category.
-- *A partial result is never plotted as if it were whole.* A run that carried
-  errors wrote a figure over the trades that survived, so a bar or a point drawn
-  from one is a floor. The plot carries the same =partial= tag the figures carry,
-  the mark itself is dashed or hollow, and the caption names what the figure
-  leaves out. For a donut the excluded part is its own hatched slice, labelled
-  =excluded= with its own legend row, so the whole of the pie is not silently
-  smaller than the run: the share donut hatches the trades the engine could not
-  build, and the problem donut hatches them beside the recorded rows, which is
-  why its hole carries both counts.
-- *Nothing is drawn that the run did not produce.* A run whose configuration
-  names =npv= and =saccr= has no Greek, so it has no grouped bar and no scatter of
-  one, and the page says which analytic set decided that.
-
-The book tree selection drives the plots exactly as it drives the table: choosing
-a node narrows the bars, the donut and the Greeks to the books under it, and
-choosing a single book removes them in favour of the tile and the table row. The
-comparison drives them too: with a baseline in view the change chart appears, the
-stacked bars pair the two runs, and the trend marks the baseline's point; with
-=?baseline=none= the chart is gone and only the current run is marked on the line.
-
-Every plot is inline SVG written in the prototype's own script. A prototype opens
-from =file://= with no build, no CDN and no network, so no chart library is
-loaded and none is copied in.
-
-** What is fake
-
-The figures, the file names, the row counts, the sizes, the archive key, the book
-and portfolio nodes, and every trade row are mock. So are the plots: each mark is
-drawn from the same fixtures the tables carry, and the run series behind the
-trend is a fixture like the two runs it contains. Nothing reads a server. The
-file names are real ORE output names — =npv.csv=, =saccr.csv=,
-=pricingstats.csv=, =log_structured.json= and the rest — because an invented set
-would hide the shape of the thing being judged. The book and portfolio names are
-free text in the seed, so they are the kind of name a real party writes.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/read-what-a-run-produced/=. Three files, plain HTML,
-CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step.
-
-** The verdict
-
-No verdict yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and has not been
-taken up.
-
-The review is the generated Gemini file, kept as it was produced in
-[[file:read-what-a-run-produced/review/gemini-dashboard.html][gemini-dashboard.html]]
-and listed at [[file:read-what-a-run-produced/review/][the review index]]. It proposes one
-screen rather than three readings of the same run: five figures across the top --
-NPV, Delta, Gamma, positions and books -- over a single table of NPV, Delta and
-Gamma by book, with a total row, and with every figure and every row carrying a
-change badge against a switchable baseline. It has no archive, no per-trade rows,
-no book tree and no error handling.
-
-What we take from it:
-
-1. *A change against a named baseline.* Every aggregate figure, every book row
-   and the total row carries its change and its percentage. This prototype does
-   that, and names the baseline by its run instance id and its start time, so a
-   reader knows exactly what they are compared against.
-2. *The tile pattern.* A label, the value, a note under it and a change badge.
-   The agreed design already had the first three; the badge is the review's
-   contribution and it is kept.
-
-What we refuse, and why:
-
-1. *Multiplier-synthesised baselines.* The review multiplies each current figure
-   by a constant per metric -- 0.972 for NPV, 0.976 for Delta, 1.023 for Gamma,
-   0.992 for positions -- to invent the previous run. Every book then moves by
-   the same percentage for a metric, so the deltas are fiction: they are the
-   constant written twice. This prototype carries a second fixture run with its
-   own figures so the changes are differences between two sets of numbers, and
-   ten books move by ten different percentages.
-2. *A stress scenario as a baseline.* A stress scenario is not a previous run of
-   this report: it has no archive, no instance and no error rows of its own, and
-   its numbers answer a different question. The only sound baseline is another
-   run of the same definition.
-3. *Yesterday's official close as a baseline.* The close belongs to a different
-   run, usually of a different definition. Comparing a run with it measures two
-   differences at once and names neither.
-4. *Run numbers.* The review names its baseline =Run #1042 (2026-10-17 10:30)=.
-   A run is identified by its instance id, and the id is what a reader can look
-   up. The review also collapses the two configured analytics into a chip,
-   =rannpvsensitivity=, as if the analytic set named the run; a run is named by
-   its instance and its definition, and the analytics are named separately.
-
-What the review omits that this design requires: the book tree, the trade-level
-drill-down, and the error and partial support. The tree is how a run rolls up
-from a trade to its book and a portfolio, and the review's seven-row table cannot
-show a book that exists in one run and not another. The per-trade table is the
-detail npv.csv carries. The errors are what make a completed run's totals a
-partial answer, and a comparison built without them presents an incomplete
-change as arithmetic.
-
-The review is kept as it was drawn, and it still disagrees with two facts this
-prototype states:
-
-1. *It counts 24 books.* The prototype counts 10. A trade the engine could not
-   build writes no =npv.csv= row, and the tree groups every trade into exactly
-   one node. The 24 was an earlier fixture figure, corrected for that reason, and
-   the review's own table draws seven book rows, so 24 is not the grouping it
-   displays either.
-2. *It presumes a parser pipeline.* It draws parsed NPV, Delta and Gamma per book
-   and a total computed from them, as if a pipeline supplied the rows. Nothing
-   parses the run archive. =ores_compute_results_tbl= holds the archive location,
-   an outcome and an error message, and no parsed rows. The result store that
-   would parse the archive is designed and not built, which is why this prototype
-   labels every figure and every row a fixture on the panel that draws it.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Whether the result is read in the application at all, or exported and read
-elsewhere. The archive listing, the per-trade rows and the two downloads are the
-operations this journey needs and does not have, and they are the first thing
-the real build would have to add.
-
-* See also
-

-  PROTOTYPE. Throwaway. Mock data, no backend, no build step.
-
-  Read what a run produced, from
-  doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_read_what_a_run_produced.org:
-  the system's output message, the engine's output archive, the errors that
-  came with it, and the ORE package the run read.
-
-  Three variants, switchable with ?variant=A|B|C, and a run in view switchable
-  with ?run=<instance-id prefix>. A puts the run's figures first, B puts the
-  archive and a manifest of its files first, C puts a written summary first.
-  The variants disagree about what "the result" is, not about colour.
-
-  The fixture bar at the top of the page picks one of six mock runs: completed
-  clean, completed carrying 8 Analytics errors and 3 Configuration warnings,
-  failed, in flight, a substituting run that completed clean, and a second
-  Headline Position run a day earlier which is the baseline the completed run is
-  compared against. Beside them sits one scenario chip, results-with-errors, also
-  reachable with ?scenario=results-with-errors: the completed run that carries
-  errors drawn with its results saying they are partial. The bar at the foot
-  prints the live variant, the scenario and the state it is showing.
-
-  Variant A's result panel compares. The control under the analytics names a
-  previous completed run of the same definition, or no comparison; it defaults to
-  the previous run so the feature is visible on load, and ?baseline=none turns it
-  off. Each figure, each book row, each tree node and the total row then carries
-  its change and percentage against that run, whose instance id and start time
-  are printed beside the control. The baseline's figures are that run's own
-  fixture numbers, never this run's numbers scaled, so the books move by
-  different amounts. A change whose two sides are not both complete is marked
-  partial: the results-with-errors scenario shows the current run's case.
-
-  Variant A also plots the result, and the plot is chosen to fit the analytic:
-  horizontal bars for NPV by book and for each Greek by book, a signed bar chart
-  of the change against the baseline, and a line of NPV across the runs of the
-  same definition with the current run and the baseline marked. The book tree
-  selection narrows the bars to the subtree it narrows the table to.
-
-  The plot vocabulary is the ordinary one, and the page states the rule that
-  picks a form: one whole in few parts is a donut, and not more than about six
-  slices; one whole in many parts, or parts that must be compared precisely, is
-  horizontal bars; many wholes each split the same way are stacked bars; two
-  series over the same categories are grouped bars; two measures against each
-  other are a scatter; a change over time is a line; a contribution that sums to
-  a total is a waterfall; and a handful of exact numbers stays a table. Here that
-  gives a donut of each book's share of the run's NPV and a donut of the run's
-  problems by scope, both with the total in the hole and every percentage in the
-  legend; stacked bars of the problems by scope across the two runs the
-  comparison pairs; grouped bars of Delta against Gamma, which share the books and
-  the unit; and a scatter of each book's Gamma against its Delta, so an outlier is
-  a distance rather than a row. A waterfall is drawn nowhere: no figure on this
-  page is a contribution to a known total.
-
-  Every plot carries a title, its unit, an aria-label, a caption saying why that
-  form, and its exact numbers beside it. A plot whose figure the errors left
-  partial carries the same partial marking the figure carries and says in the
-  caption what is excluded; a donut draws the excluded part as a hatched slice of
-  its own, named excluded, so the whole of the pie is not silently smaller than
-  the run. A count with no magnitude to compare, one book, and a single run are
-  not plotted, and the page says so instead. The plots are inline SVG written in
-  prototype.js: a page opened from file:// has no build, no CDN and no network, so
-  no chart library is loaded or copied in.
-
-  Honest gaps, repeated on the page: no operation lists the files inside a
-  run's archive, no operation or route serves the archive's bytes, and no read
-  serves parsed results or the exported ORE package. The manifest and every
-  figure are drawn from this file.
-
-  The per-trade table is drawn from this file too. Per-trade results are real: a
-  run writes npv.csv into its archive with one row per trade, its NPV, its
-  base-currency NPV, its notional and its counterparty. No operation parses the
-  archive, so the table is a fixture and says so on the panel; opening a row
-  answers with that trade's result, and with the error the run recorded against
-  its TradeId where it recorded one.
-
-  The book tree is the third reading: the run's result rolled up from a trade to
-  its book, a book to its portfolio, and a portfolio to the group portfolio
-  above it. It is a fixture for two reasons the panel states. The archive carries
-  no book column -- npv.csv's columns are exactly TradeId, TradeType, Maturity,
-  MaturityTime, NPV, NpvCurrency, NPV(Base), BaseCurrency, Notional,
-  NotionalCurrency, Notional(Base), NettingSet and CounterParty -- so a built
-  screen joins each TradeId to trade_bookings.book_id through
-  trading.v1.trade_bookings.list, and no operation returns results already
-  grouped by book. And no operation parses the archive, so no node has a figure
-  behind it. The portfolio tree is assembled from portfolios.list, which carries
-  parent_portfolio_id, because there is no
-  portfolios.list_by_parent_portfolio_id. A trade booked to no book is a real
-  state, so the tree draws an Unbooked node rather than dropping the row.
-
-  The figures are not free invention: each run names the analytics its report
-  configuration runs (Headline Position runs npv and sensitivity, Large
-  Exposures runs npv and saccr), and every measure and every manifest row is an
-  output of that named set. The set is printed on the screen and in the fixture
-  switcher, so a reader can see why these figures and not others.

-/* Read what a run produced prototype. Self-contained: plain JavaScript, mock
- * data, no framework, no build step, nothing that outlives the page.
- *
- * See doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_read_what_a_run_produced.org.
- *
- * The decision this prototype serves: how the five reporting journeys become
- * one reporting surface without a screen per journey. For this journey the
- * question is what "the result" of a run is, and how much of it belongs on the
- * screen before a person goes looking for a file.
- *
- *   A, figures-first  -- the run's numbers are the screen.
- *   B, artefact-first -- the run produced files, and the screen is a manifest.
- *   C, narrative-first-- a sentence about the run, with the files at the end.
- *
- * Every fact about a run -- its output message, its output_storage_key, its
- * state, its errors -- is a field reporting already stores, but no screen
- * reads it today. Every figure and every file row is a fixture: nothing here
- * reads a server, no operation lists the files inside an archive, and no
- * operation returns the archive, the package, or a parsed result. The amber
- * note and the gaps panel say so on the page, because a prototype that draws
- * a file list must not imply the server served it.
- *
- * The figures are not free: a report's numbers are the outputs of the
- * analytics its configuration names, and this file says which ones on every
- * run. Headline Position configures npv and sensitivity, so its measures are
- * NPV, Delta and Gamma and its archive holds npv.csv and sensitivity.csv and
- * no saccr.csv. Board Risk Dashboard configures npv, parametricVar and saccr;
- * Large Exposures configures npv and saccr. The manifest follows the same
- * rule, so a reader can see why these figures and not others.
- *
- * Field shapes are the model's: output_message, output_storage_key,
- * reporting/runs/<instance-id>/output.tar.gz, report error scope codes
- * Analytics / Configuration / Report, and severities error / warning. The
- * engine messages are drawn from real log_structured.json lines.
- *
- * One scenario sits beside the six runs: results-with-errors (?scenario=
- * results-with-errors, or its chip). It takes the run that already carries
- * eleven problems and draws the connection between the errors and the results:
- * a banner above the figures saying the results are partial, a marker on the
- * figures themselves, marked tree nodes for the books that lost trades, and one
- * row per failed trade with no price and its error. A completed run can produce
- * an archive and still not produce the whole answer, and the page must not let a
- * total read as if it did. The errors are the run's own rows, read by
- * reporting.v1.report_error_events.list_by_report_instance_id, which exists; no
- * operation is invented for it.
- *
- * The result panel also compares. A completed run carries a control that picks
- * another completed run of the same definition, started before it, or no run at
- * all; the page defaults to the previous one, so a reviewer meets the comparison
- * without hunting for it, and ?baseline=none turns it off. Each aggregate
- * figure, each book row, each tree node and the total row then carries its
- * change and its percentage against that run, and the panel names the baseline
- * by its instance id and its start time.
- *
- * The comparison is arithmetic on two fixtures, and that is the point of it. The
- * second Headline Position run below is a run of the same definition one day
- * earlier, with its own figures per book, so ten books move by ten different
- * amounts. Nothing here multiplies one run's numbers by a constant to invent a
- * baseline, because a per-metric multiplier makes every book move by the same
- * percentage and the change is then fiction. A stress scenario is not a previous
- * run of this definition, and yesterday's official close belongs to a different
- * run, so neither is offered as a baseline: the only sound comparison is another
- * run of the same definition. A run is named by its instance id and its start
- * time, never by a report number.
- *
- * A change is only as honest as the two numbers under it. When either run in the
- * comparison carries errors the change is partial: a total over the trades that
- * survived cannot be compared as if it were the whole answer. The badge carries
- * the mark and the panel says so once in words, and the results-with-errors
- * scenario shows what the current run's errors leave out. The book tree's
- * selected node drives both sides, so selecting a book compares that book across
- * the two runs.
- *
- * A's result panel also plots. The form of each plot follows the shape of its
- * numbers: NPV and each Greek by book are horizontal bars, sorted, signed and
- * drawn from a zero rule; the change against the baseline is bars of its own,
- * because a change and a level are not one series; and the run's NPV across the
- * runs of the same definition is a line, with the current run and the baseline
- * marked. A run that produced no Greek has no Greek plot, a selection of one
- * book has no bar chart, and a single run has no trend, because a plot of one
- * figure states nothing a sentence cannot. Every plot is inline SVG written in
- * this file: a prototype opens from file:// with no build, no CDN and no
- * network, so no chart library is loaded or copied in. Every plot keeps its
- * exact numbers in a table beside it, and a plot whose figure the errors made
- * partial carries the same partial marking the figure carries.
- */

-    /* -------------------------------------------------------------- plots */
-    /* Every plot on this page is inline SVG written here, because a prototype
-       opens from file:// with no build, no CDN and no network: a chart library
-       cannot be loaded, and none is copied in either. The form of each plot
-       follows the shape of its numbers. A magnitude compared across categories
-       is bars, a change over time is a line, and a category set with no
-       magnitude to compare is no plot at all.
-
-       Three rules hold every plot on this page.
-
-       - A bar starts at the zero rule, and a negative value draws a bar on the

-         silently start somewhere else.

-    /* ------------------------------------------------ the form of a plot */
-    /* The vocabulary this page draws from, and the rule that picks one form.
-       The rule is data, so the table on the page and the choice each plot makes
-       cannot disagree: every one of the six forms below carries the shape of
-       numbers it answers to, and a form is chosen by the shape rather than by
-       taste.
-
-       Bars and lines alone were too narrow. A set of parts that makes up one
-       whole is a donut; several wholes each split the same way are stacked
-       bars; two series over the same categories are a grouped bar; two measures
-       against each other are a scatter. A table stays the right answer for a
-       handful of exact numbers, and no chart replaces it. */

-#+title: Run a report and watch it finish prototype
-#+description: Three structural variants of starting a run and waiting for it, with the six phases scripted on a timer.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                                    |
-|---------------+----------------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                                     |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]                   |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues how a person starts a run and then knows when to stop
-waiting. It carries three structural variants switched with =?variant=, and it
-answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_run_a_report_and_watch_it_finish.org][Run a report and watch it finish]].
-
-It is throwaway. It reads no service, and the run it shows advances on a scripted
-timer so that the waiting can be judged at all.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-Starting a run is easy to draw. Waiting is not. The journey is over when the run
-reaches a terminal state, and the open question is whether that state arrives
-where the person is looking or somewhere they have to go back to.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | Modal and notify | Starting a run is a confirmation over the catalogue, and the run then reports itself in a strip so the person can keep working. Waiting is someone else's job. |
-| =B= | Run theatre | Starting a run opens a dedicated view of that run, with the six phases advancing left to right and the current one live. The person stays until it is terminal. |
-| =C= | Queue-first | Starting a run drops a row into a queue of that person's runs, each advancing in place, so several can be watched together. |
-
-** Six phases, seven steps
-
-The pipeline has six phases: Pre-processing, Submission, Execution, Retrieval,
-Post-processing, Finalisation. The workflow that implements them has seven steps,
-because pre-processing is four steps rather than one and retrieval and
-post-processing are a single step rather than two. The page shows both and says
-which is which, because a reader who confuses them will misread every run that
-has a step retried.
-
-Execution runs on a worker node and is not a step any ORE Studio service
-performs; the services submit the work and wait. The page marks that phase as the
-worker node's rather than the platform's. Only finalisation touches the state
-machine.
-
-** The two endings that matter
-
-A run reaches a terminal state with =output_message=, and the successful one
-reads exactly =Report execution completed.= A run can also complete and still
-carry errors, so the terminal state says so at the moment it arrives rather than
-leaving it to be discovered later. A failed run terminates with a report-scoped
-error rather than a phase stuck mid-flight.
-
-** Driving it
-
-The phases advance on a timer, one every 700 milliseconds, so a run reaches its
-end in about 4 seconds. There is a control to run the demonstration again. The
-timer is the point: a static picture of a half-finished run cannot be judged.
-
-** What is fake
-
-Everything, and the page is explicit about the part that matters: the per-phase
-position the ladder shows does not exist as a read. It lives in =ores.workflow=,
-and no reporting read serves it. The phases are scripted, nothing reads a
-server, and the definitions, parties, timings and errors are mock.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/run-a-report-and-watch-it-finish/=. Three files, plain
-HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review. The
-phase ladder is the strongest part of =B= and the most likely thing to be taken
-into whichever variant wins.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Where the progress comes from. The screen can draw a run advancing, but the
-server does not yet serve a run's current phase, so the real build needs either a
-workflow read or a reporting-side projection of one. That is a server question,
-not a layout one.
-
-* See also
-
-- [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]] — the group, and the axis this prototype turns on.
-- [[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/reporting.org][Reporting journeys]] — the five journeys these answer to.

- * is how a person starts a run and then knows when to stop waiting. Three
- * structures answer it, and they disagree about structure rather than colour:
- *
- *   A, modal-and-notify. The catalogue stays the page. A dialog confirms the
- *      run, then the page returns to the catalogue and a strip at the top

-#+title: See a report's results by counterparty prototype
-#+description: Three structural readings of one run's results by counterparty: a ranked list, a group tree, and a proportional map, with the two cases a screen must not drop drawn as stated cases.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item      | Where |
-|-----------+-------|
-| Prototype | [[file:see-a-reports-results-by-counterparty/][the prototype]] |
-| Journey   | [[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_see_a_reports_results_by_counterparty.org][See a report's results by counterparty]] |
-| Group     | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]] |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues how one run's results read by counterparty, rather than
-by book. It carries three structural variants switched with =?variant=, and it
-answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_see_a_reports_results_by_counterparty.org][See a report's results by counterparty]].
-
-Every figure on the page is a fixture, and the panel that draws it says so. The
-two facts that make it a fixture are on the page: no operation returns results
-grouped by counterparty and nothing parses the run's archive, and =npv.csv=
-names the counterparty as a name rather than identifying it by id.
-
-One control sits beside the variants: the report's analytics, either =npv,
-saccr= or =npv= alone. A run that does not run =saccr= has no exposure, so the
-exposure column and every exposure figure go away rather than reading as zero.
-The page opens on =npv, saccr=, because that is the report this journey is
-mostly read on.
-
-Two cases are drawn as stated cases whose whole point is that they are not
-dropped: a counterparty the party can see with no result in the run, and the
-trades that carry no =counterparty_id= because their =counterparty_scope= is
-=intra_entity=.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-A run's results are one table of trades. Read by book, that table answers
-whether a book is in line. Read by counterparty it answers a different question:
-*who does this run face, how much of it is each name, and which name carries the
-concentration?* That question is asked by a credit or market-risk reader before
-sign-off and by a desk asking what one name contributed. The three variants
-disagree about which instrument answers it.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | Ranked list | The answer is an ordered table: one row per counterparty, largest first, a group row above its members, and the totals at the foot. The reader scans the top and has the answer. |
-| =B= | Tree | The answer is a hierarchy: counterparties grouped by their parent, each node carrying its rolled-up aggregate, expanding to its members. A group total and its parts are visible at once, which is the fact a flat list hides. |
-| =C= | Map | The answer is concentration: a bar of the run whose segments are as wide as each counterparty's share of NPV, with the selected counterparty read beside it. The eye answers "how concentrated" before any number is read. |
-
-=A= is the densest of the three: seven columns, every figure legible, and a
-group row that cannot be mistaken for a member because the member rows are
-indented under it. =B= gives up the flat ranking to make the nesting the
-subject: the same aggregates, but arranged so that a group's figure can be
-checked against the members beneath it. =C= gives up the table: a segment under
-two percent wide cannot carry a name, so the bar carries width and the legend
-beneath it carries the code, the full name, the aggregate NPV, the notional, the
-trade count, the exposure and the share. The variant is an argument about what a
-reader looks at first, not about what the page knows.
-
-** A group and its members
-
-A counterparty nests through =parent_counterparty_id= on
-=ores_refdata_counterparties_tbl=, so a banking group and its legal entities are
-both real records. Credit reads the group; the desk reads the entity it faces.
-The page therefore keeps both, and the group's figure is arithmetic rather than
-a stored field: it is the sum of its members plus the trades booked to the group
-itself, recomputed every time the page draws. A parent that disagrees with its
-children cannot appear.
-
-The fixture has two groups and they are deliberately different.
-=ACME FINANCIAL GROUP= owns no trades and holds =ACME BANK PLC= and
-=ACME BANK INTERNATIONAL=, so its figure is exactly its two members.
-=MERIDIAN CAPITAL GROUP= holds =MERIDIAN CAPITAL= and
-=MERIDIAN CAPITAL UK= *and* carries trades of its own, so its figure is larger
-than its two members together. A reader who checks one against the other learns
-how the roll-up works.
-
-Each member is ranked where it sits, and the group is ranked by the aggregate
-that includes its members, which is why the group sits above =ACME BANK PLC=
-even though the member is the largest single name on the page.
-
-** The two stated cases
-
-=BLUE RIVER PENSION= is a counterparty the party can see through
-=refdata.v1.party_counterparties.list_by_party_id= and this run produced nothing
-for. It is drawn as a row or a node or a legend line with a trade count of zero
-and dashes where the figures would be, and the page says it is not a measure of
-zero. A zero trade count is a fact about the run; a zero NPV would be a figure
-the run never produced.
-
-The trades whose =counterparty_scope= is =intra_entity= are the second case.
-=ores_trading_trades_tbl= allows =counterparty_id= to be null only under that
-scope, so the run can hold trades that no name claims. They are drawn under a
-heading of their own, with their notional, their NPV, their trade count and
-their netting sets, and they are selectable like any counterparty. The page says
-what they do to the totals: the counterparty rows add up to less than the run,
-and the amber segment, row or node is that difference. Dropping them would make
-every total reconcile against nothing.
-
-** The trade, its netting sets and its errors
-
-Selecting a counterparty, a group or the unassigned trades opens the panel
-beside or below the list. It states the four aggregate figures, then the trades
-the aggregate is made of, one row each, with the netting set from the trade's
-booking and the error the run recorded against that trade where it recorded
-one. A group's panel adds its members' trades, labelled with the member code, and
-says in words how the group's figure was summed.
-
-The page draws five of 2,318 trades for =ACME BANK PLC= and says so, because the
-aggregate is a population figure and the row list is a sample of it. The errors
-are drawn for the trades shown, and the panel states how many errors the run
-records in all and how many of those are recorded against the analysis and name
-no trade. That last count is the honest limit of this whole screen: the error
-scopes are =Trade=, =Analytics=, =Curve=, =Configuration= and =Report=, and none
-of them is a counterparty, so an error recorded against the analytic alone
-cannot be attributed to a name and the page refuses to divide it across them.
-
-** What is fake
-
-Everything. The counterparties, their short codes and full names, the parents,
-the trades, the netting sets, the errors, the population counts and every
-aggregate are drawn from the file. Nothing reads a server, and there is no
-backend to read: no BFF route serves reporting.
-
-The figures are chosen so that the arithmetic holds. The four figures an
-aggregate has are each a sum of the same population, so the ranked list, the
-tree and the legend all agree with each other and with the totals row. The
-totals are =59,753,609= USD of NPV over =6,848= trades, of which =412= trades
-carrying =1,205,000= USD name no counterparty. The counterparty rows therefore
-sum to =58,548,609= USD, not to the run.
-
-The names follow the seed's own shape: party =ACMCOR=, and counterparties in the
-style the fixtures already use, such as =ACME BANK PLC=, =NORTHGATE CLEARING=,
-=MERIDIAN CAPITAL=, =HANSA PFANDBRIEF=, =PACIFIC TRUST= and
-=KESTREL ASSURANCE=. The trade types are ORE's own, and the netting set codes
-are the kind a party writes.
-
-The exposure figures are the output of the =saccr= analytic, and they exist only
-while the control says =npv, saccr=. That is not a display toggle: a run whose
-configuration does not name =saccr= produced no exposure, and the page draws the
-absence rather than a column of zeros.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/see-a-reports-results-by-counterparty/=. Three files,
-plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step. The page opens
-from =file://= with no server and no session. =?variant=A|B|C= chooses the
-structure, =?analytics=npv= drops the exposure, and =?counterparty=<code>=
-selects a name on load.
-
-** The verdict
-
-No verdict yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and has not been
-taken up. It has no Gemini review.
-
-The reading of the three: =A= is the one a credit reader can work from today,
-because a ranked list is scanable and its totals are in one place. =B= is what
-makes the group structure arguable at all, and it is the variant that would be
-hardest to give up if the group roll-up turns out to be the reason for the
-screen. =C= is the one that answers the question a limit conversation actually
-starts with, and it is the only variant that shows the unassigned population as
-a share of the run rather than as a line at the bottom.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Whether the counterparty view is a reading of the result on the same screen as
-the book view, as the journey proposes, or a screen of its own. Whether a reader
-wants both readings at once, side by side, or one at a time with a switch. And
-the real question behind all three variants: whether the result store that would
-parse the archive groups by counterparty itself, or whether every client joins
-trades to counterparties for itself. The page cannot answer that, because no
-such read exists to judge.
-
-* See also
-

-#+title: See the reports a party runs prototype
-#+description: Three structural variants of reporting's front door, with mock data, on a throwaway prototype page.
-#+type: knowledge
-#+level: cross
-#+filetags: :prototype:ui:reporting:
-#+created: 2026-10-17
-#+updated: 2026-10-17
-
-| Item          | Where                                                 |
-|---------------+-------------------------------------------------------|
-| Prototype     | [[file:see-the-reports-a-party-runs/][the prototype]] |
-| Gemini review | none                                                  |
-| Group         | [[file:index.org][Reporting prototypes]]                |
-
-* Summary
-
-This prototype argues what the front door of reporting is, before any of it is
-built. It carries three structural variants of the same screen, switched with
-=?variant=, and it answers to
-[[file:../../knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_see_the_reports_a_party_runs.org][See the reports a party runs]].
-
-It is throwaway. It is not production code, it reads no service, and every value
-on it is mock data.
-
-* Detail
-
-** The question
-
-A party runs a number of reports, some on a schedule and some on demand, and each
-of them has a latest run that either went well, went wrong, or never happened.
-The open question is what a person lands on when they open reporting. The
-journey can answer that five ways and still be true to itself, which is why this
-is a prototype and not a specification.
-
-** The three variants
-
-Switch with the bottom bar, or with =?variant=.
-
-| Variant | Name | The structural argument |
-|---------+------+-------------------------|
-| =A= | Index-first | The catalogue is the page: one row per report, its schedule, its owner, and the health of its latest run. A run is a detail reached from a report. |
-| =B= | Ledger-first | One dense table of runs across the party, newest first, report as a column. The catalogue is a filter, not a page. |
-| =C= | Attention-first | Only what needs a human: failed runs and runs that completed carrying errors. Clean runs exist behind a filter, off by default. |
-
-The variants disagree about structure, not colour. A starts from the thing that
-is scheduled. B starts from what happened. C starts from what is wrong, and is
-the only one that hides work rather than ranking it.
-
-** The health words, and the thing a reader gets wrong
-
-The latest run of a definition is one of five: =failed=, =completed with errors=,
-=running=, =never run=, =completed clean=. The summary tallies them, and each row
-carries its error count split into errors and warnings.
-
-The point the page exists to make is that **a completed run is not necessarily
-clean**. A row that completed while carrying errors is drawn apart from a clean
-one without opening anything. A definition that has never run is not clean
-either: nothing ran and nothing was checked.
-
-** What is fake
-
-Everything. The definitions, parties, schedules, owners, run times and error
-counts are mock. Nothing reads a server, and the application has no reporting UI
-today. The page says both, at the top, in the strip and the note.
-
-** Where the code lives
-
-=doc/prototypes/reporting/see-the-reports-a-party-runs/=. Three files, plain
-HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework and no build step. The site build finds
-the directory and deploys it where it sits.
-
-** The verdict
-
-None yet. This page is on the branch that proposes it and waits for review.
-Whichever variant is chosen, the health tally and the split error count stay:
-they are the part the other four prototypes depend on.
-
-** What it does not settle
-
-Whether the five journeys become one area, one screen or two. This prototype
-argues the front door only, and the area behind it is judged from the other four.
-
-* See also

-/* Reporting prototype: see the reports a party runs. Self-contained: plain

- * outlives the page.
- *
- * See the reports a party runs, from
- * doc/knowledge/journeys/reporting/journey_see_the_reports_a_party_runs.org.
- *
- * The screen answers "which reports does my party run, and how did each one
- * last go?" Every row is a fixture: the definitions, the runs and the errors
- * are mock, no operation serves them, and nothing here reads the server.
- *
- * Three variants disagree about the front door of reporting:
- *   A index-first     -- the catalogue of definitions is the page.
- *   B ledger-first    -- one dense table of runs is the page; the catalogue is
- *                        a filter.
- *   C attention-first -- only failed runs and runs carrying errors are shown;
- *                        clean runs sit behind a filter that is off by default. */

+std::vector<trading::domain::range_bound>
+fx_instrument_mapper::forward_range_bounds(const accumulatorData& d) {
+    std::vector<trading::domain::range_bound> rows;
+    rows.reserve(d.RangeBounds.RangeBound.size());
+    int sequence_number = 0;
+    for (const auto& rb : d.RangeBounds.RangeBound) {
+        trading::domain::range_bound row;
+        row.sequence_number = ++sequence_number;
+        if (rb.startDate)
+            row.start_date = to_optional_domain_date(std::string(*rb.startDate));
+        if (rb.RangeFrom)
+            row.range_from = exact_decimal(*rb.RangeFrom);
+        if (rb.RangeTo)
+            row.range_to = exact_decimal(*rb.RangeTo);
+        if (rb.Leverage)
+            row.leverage = static_cast<double>(*rb.Leverage);
+        if (rb.Strike)
+            row.strike = exact_decimal(*rb.Strike);
+        if (rb.StrikeAdjustment)
+            row.strike_adjustment = exact_decimal(*rb.StrikeAdjustment);
+        rows.push_back(std::move(row));
+    }
+    return rows;
+}

     BOOST_LOG_SEV(lg, info) << "FxAccumulator roundtrip passed. Amount: " << instr.fixing_amount;
